18
tests that c ould be conducted. However, estimates of the chamber contents were computed
assuming that the fuel in a normal flame test (for example) was either fully or not at all oxidized,
e.g., for unsustained ignition in the latter case.
The CIR facility was equipped with a 3-axis SAMS sensor head and the acceleration measurements,
along with relevant documentation, are accessible via the home page for the Principal Investigator
Microgravity Services (PIMS) , https://gipoc.grc.nasa.gov/wp/pims/home/. To be clear, the
acceleration measurements are not archived with the ACME experiment data in the Physical
Sciences Informatics (PSI) website, www.nasa.gov/PSI.
All ACME experiments will be constant volume (i.e., rather than constant pressure) studies, where
the chamber’s free volume will be about 90 liters. Burner flows will generally be constrained to
limit the pressure rise, and tests will typically be 0.5-2 minutes in duration.
The chamber’s free volume is approximately 83 liters depending on the installed hardware.
The ACME experiments will be configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. Instead, the
experiments will be commanded from the ground, specifically from the Telescience Support
Center (TSC) at the NASA Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, Ohio. They can be conducted in a

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign, p.18
text:
nominally automated mode using pre -programmed scripts. However, it will also be possible to
effectively operate the experiments in a “manual” mode, where changes can be made in response
to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. For
example, a flow rate could be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit. Step and ramp
changes can be made in the flow rate(s) or electric field pot ential. The TFP fiber array can be
translated uniformly through a soot -free flame to get a continuum measurement of the
temperature field. In summary, ACME’s experiment control will allow for broad flexibility.
The TSC is now also referred to as the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). ACME tests
were always conducted in a nominally automated mode.
B. Hardware Shortcomings
From the Flame Design PI, Rich Axelbaum:
“The only significant disappointment with the project was with the diagnostics,
particularly with respect to gas temperature and soot volume fraction. They were not at
the level that the team would have hoped. Much of this was due to the fact that the
diagnostics were outdated by the time they were used in our experiments on the ISS, and
thus the diagnostics and calibrations were not at the level that we expect in a laboratory
experiment. Of course, the ISS has constraints that limit the ability to incorporate state-

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign, p.18
text:
of-the-art diagnostics, and this likely made this weakness unavoidable, but it would have
been valuable to have had more flexibility in terms of being able to upgrade the
diagnostics with more modern cameras and instrumentation.”
ACME’s sintered spherical burners did not always yield spherically symmetric flames which are
centered on the burner’s center, where that combination is important for true spherical
symmetry. While nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center bec ame
increasing offset from the burner center as the flow rate was increased. It is very likely that the
sintered attachment of the sphere to the supply tube is more porous than the sintered sphere

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign, p.19
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023
19
itself because the flame is seen to be shifted toward the supp ly tube. There was significant
improvement when the starting burner (serial number 1002) was replaced mid -way through
round 1 with an alternate burner (serial number 1003), which continued to be used for spherical
flame testing throughout the remainder of ACME operations. Nonetheless, the symmetry was
not perfect, which is a shortcoming of the Flame Design data.
On 27 Dec. 2021 (GMT 361), it was determined that the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array
was not aligned to the ACME Data Camera (DataCam ) as intended, i.e., so that the fibers would
be orthogonal relative to the camera. Unfortunately, this was the fourth day of testing in which
the fiber array wasn’t aligned, where it regrettably wasn’t recognized earlier. Given the
importance of the TFP-derived measurements of the flame temperature, testing was halted until
the array was aligned (with other crew tasks) by astronaut Raja Chari on 17 Jan. 2022 (GMT 017).
The signal from the standard ACME radiometer array used in round 1 of Flame Design testing was
saturated for nearly every test, yielding non -useful data. For round 2, that sensor array was
replaced with the one designed for Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI -G) which yielded
satisfactory measurements.

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign, p.19
text:
ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and oxidizer did
not always perform adequately, where the flow rates were not always appropriately steady or at
the intended value. However, the resulting effects on the flame behavior are tentatively assumed
to be minor.
In addition to sections 3.A-B, shortcomings are discussed in Appendices B and C of this report and
in the ACME Engineering Implementation document. The latter document includes discussion of
deviations and waivers (in section 4.B), etc.
4. Preliminary Results
A. Changed Test Plans
A change was made to the CIR combustion chamber’s pressure limit on 17 Jan. 2022 (by astronaut
Raja Chari) to enable Flame Design testing at chamber pressures of up to 3 atm in the final round-
2 test days, whereas the limit had been 1.5 atm in preceding testing. In his request for this change,
Flame Design PI Rich Axelbaum explained:
“One of the fundamental goals of Flame Design is to achieve sooting limits. We are unsure
if we will be able to attain a range of sooting flames with the current ambient fuel
constraints. One way to increase soot formation, and thus the range of the test matrix,
is via higher pressures, so this capability can help to ensure we me et our science goals.
Another fundamental goal of Flame Design is to understand flame extinction. Our recent

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign, p.19
text:
analysis suggests that pressure is a critical variable when predicting flame extinction, and
in can influence flame chemistry in ways that we had not anticipated. Obtaining
extinction data over a wide range of pressures could also be valuable for spacecraft fire
safety.”
An additional normal-flames test day was added to the start of the second round of testing (even
though that was focused on inverse flames) to acquire data useful for calibrating the Thin Filament
Pyrometry (TFP) measurements. With that goal, the added test day, conducted on 28 Oct. 2021

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign, p.20
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023
20
(GMT 301), was carried out with the long (near) thermocouple rake, where all other Flame Design
tests were conducted with the short (far) rake. In his request for this additional test day, the PI
stated in part:
“The ability to validate the TFP is very important for most of the ACME experiments. Thus,
measuring the near-field temperatures under conditions where we have TFP data would
be highly desirable, almost required. … These results would be the only measurem ents
ACME has with a direct comparison with TFP, and since we already know exactly which
flames to run to get good data, we know that we will be successful in obtaining this data
and validating the TFP data. … Reiterating, this extra day would directly benefit all of the
temperature data of Flame Design, and all of the spherical flame ACME experiments, by
providing at least one direct validation of the TFP method. As you know, we have
uncertainties about the accuracy of the TFP technique we are using in the ACME rig, and
having these T/C measurements could have a profound impact on the ACME results.”
As discussed in the previous section, the decision was made to use the CFI-G radiometer array in
Flame Design’s second round of testing rather than the standard ACME array that often saturated
in the earlier testing.

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign, p.20
text:
Coiled igniter tips were also used in the second round of testing instead of the loop igniter tips
used in the first round, where the coiled were believed to be more robust.
Other changes to the test plans were minor in comparison.
B. Overview of Experiment Test Operations
While not yet prepared, additional details will be made available in the ACME/ Flame Design
Experimental Procedure document.
The narrative description of the experimental procedure is an excerpt from the ‘Methods /
Experimental’ section of the following conference paper.
Y.-C. Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Stocker, U. Hegde, and D. Dunn -Rankin, “Electric Field Effects on
Flames in Microgravity on the International Space Station,” 2018 Spring Technical Meeting of
the Central States Section of The Combustion Institute, Minneapolis, MN, 20-22 May 2018.
While the paper was written for the Electric -Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E -FIELD
Flames) experiment, much of the discussion applies to ACME in general, including the Flame
Design investigation. The figure referenced in this excerpt is not i ncluded herein. Clarifications
and additional information, not in the conference paper, are included in boxed notes like this.
The CIR experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. Thus far, ACME’s activity

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign, p.20
text:
has included the majority of the crew members, regardless of their nationalities. Most often the
astronauts and cosmonauts exchange gas bottles, mass flow controllers, and igniter tips. In the
latter case, the igniter tip exchange can occur after failure or proactively before failure when the
crew already has changes to make changes in the interior of the insert. While these activities may
seem mundane, the crew play a critical role in setting up the hardware for each experiment. As
an extreme example, there were crew activities on 8 separate days in Sept.-Oct. 2017 to configure
the CIR and ACME hardware for the first ACME experiment, namely the Coflow Laminar Diffusion
Flame (CLD Flame) experiment. In contrast, only two crew days were required to reconfigure the

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign, p.21
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023
21
hardware for the first E-FIELD Flames tests because of the initial use of the same coflow burner.
Planning is critical because crew activity is scheduled three weeks in advance, for which detailed
procedures must be prepared and uplinked to the ISS.
As a correction, including two maintenance activities, there were 11 crew days in Sept.-Oct. 2017
to prepare for the initial CLD Flame testing on the space station.
All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations
Center (GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio. Typically , four to six people staff four consoles during the
testing. The CIR hardware is controlled from the Rack Officer (RO) and Data Management Officer
(DMO) consoles, and the ACME hardware is controlled from the Payload Developer (PD) console.
Two shifts of personnel are scheduled to staff these three consoles on test days because they
typically last 14 hours with the many pre - and post-testing activities. Given that the tests are
remotely commanded, the operations are carried out in the day and evening in Cleveland, e.g.,
from 7 AM to 9 PM. A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are normally conducted in a period of 10 hours
of less. Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per two weeks. On intervening

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign, p.21
text:
weekdays, the image dat a is downlinked and the crew often swap one or both gas bottles.
Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2 -shift day for the RO and
DMO consoles, where it is always necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors
and that data is not missing. Those two positions are also staffed to guide and oversee the crew
activity. As a result, the CIR consoles are normally actively staffed on four weekdays per week. A
team of four carry out the detailed planning for the CIR a nd ACME console staff, and the daily
operational plans typically exceed 50 pages on days including testing.
The science console allows for review of the analog video and non-imaging telemetry (at 1 Hz) in
near real time but doesn’t allow for commanding. In the case of E -FIELD Flames, arrangements
were made so that the analog video is streamed to a secure computer at UC Irvine to allow the
research team to participate in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s
planned parameters. That te am does not see the telemetry during the testing, but is in
communication via phone and e -mail with their NASA research partners at the GRC ISS Payload
Operations Center (GIPOC). While there are many preparatory steps, the tests are ultimately
conducted using an uploaded software script and parameter files. In advance of the test day, the

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign, p.21
text:
UC Irvine science team plans the nearly 60 parameters in the voltage sweep script and specifies
other parameters that are configured outside of the script, such as camer a settings. It is also
possible to effectively conduct tests in a ‘manual’ mode, where parameters are changed in
response to the analog video downlink or telemetry. For example, the electric field potential can
be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit.
Provisions were made to enable the investigators from all ACME experiments to remotely view the
analog video while they communicated verbally with NASA science personnel in the operations
center. All ACME flame tests, including those for Flame Design, were conducted in a nominally
automated manner using software scripts and extensive parameter files.
Typically, ten E-FIELD Flames tests are conducted per test day. Despite the short test durations,
the low rate results from several unavoidable factors. After a test is conducted, the 125-Hz non-
imaging data is downlinked for immediate review by the science team. A small sample of images
are often downlinked to ensure that the camera exposures are appropriate, where the times for

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign, p.22
text:
ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023
22
those images are typically selected based on non-imaging data to provide extreme examples. The
review helps to verify parameters or plan for adjustments in subsequent tests, e.g., to select the
voltage range after determining where the ion current saturates for the given fl ame conditions.
After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber atmosphere after which the chamber is
vented (to space) back to atmospheric pressure, if needed. Midway through a day’s E -FIELD
Flames tests, the atmosphere is circulated for 15 minu tes through a filter cartridge filled with
molecular sieves to capture any soot and adsorb at least a portion of the combustion products,
e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products. The tests are only
conducted when both Ku and S band communication is available through NASA’s Tracking and
Data Relay Satellite (TDRS) System. Depending on the various orbits, there are periodic
communication outages with a loss of signal (LOS) that can be a short handover (from one satellite
to another) or can last as long as 30 minutes.
An average of 16 tests were conducted per Flame Design test day, where ignition was typically
unsuccessful (e.g., un-sustained) in a couple of tests.
In contrast to E-FIELD Flames, recirculation during Flame Design inverse-flame test operations was

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign, p.22
text:
only conducted prior to venting at the end of a test day. During normal -flame testing, it was
usually conducted once in the midst of testing, as done with E-FIELD Flames. Exceptions were test
days 19115, 19123, and 19137 (the first three days with flames); 19161 (when no flames were
ignited); 19206 (the last test day in the first round of testing), and 21301 (the first day of the second
round of testing). Another exception was on 19150 when it was carried out duri ng the midst of
testing and then again when the combustion chamber was vented and refilled for additional tests
on the same day.
A variety of constraints limit the number of tests that can be performed, both overall and on a
daily basis. The next combustion experiments in the CIR will feature solid fuels and focus on flame
spread and material flammability. That follow -on plan limits the duration of ACME operations,
where each ACME experiment is allotted four months for testing. Although it requires additional
crew time, these allotments are split into two rounds so that the investigators have a break from
testing for careful review of the early results so that they can maximize the scientific outcome of
their second round. This paper reports on early results from the first round of E-FIELD Flames.
While nitrogen is available from the space station, the combustion testing is limited by the

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign, p.22
text:
available gas bottles that were and are launched to support the tests. For E -FIELD Flames and
most of ACME’s experiments, the test matrices used to plan those gas resources were established
in 2010. At that time, NASA limited the scope of the ACME tests matrices with the intent of
focused experiments with limited objectives rather than comprehensive experiments. As s uch,
the general target was 50 tests per experiment. For most ACME experiments, the limiting gas
constraint is the oxygen/nitrogen bottles used to fill the chamber. This resource constraint is
exacerbated by the CIR because it is equipped with a pair of redundant safety timers to limit the
fuel that can flow into the combustion chamber (where the timers can be set for the oxidizer flow
in the case of inverse flame testing). The timers can only be reset by venting the combustion
chamber. Therefore, the timer limit combined with other constraints effectively corresponds to
the day’s maximum flow time for the fuel (or more generally, the limiting reactant). For E -FIELD
Flames, the safety timers are set to the maximum value of 999 seconds, which corresponds to the
10 tests typically completed per day.

title: ACME/Flame Design: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign, p.23

The maximum limit of 999 seconds for the valve safety timers was used for all ACME testing.
Another constraint is the available time in a day, where the console personnel and ISS resources,
such as the video downlink, are planned for a limited number of hours. When necessary for the
research, NASA does have continuous 24 -hour/day operations for some non -CIR experiments.
But as discussed, the ACME tests are typically two minutes or less in duration, so the testing is
almost always limited to the planned durations.
Data limits are yet another constraint, where the on -orbit hardware can store a limited amount
of data. More importantly, 127,000 MB is the most that can be reasonably managed in a two -
shift transfer and downlink day. Therefore, tests days are limited to this amount of data, where
image data from select cameras is often archived at reduced rates to mitigate this challenge.
Nonetheless, the limit sometimes forces decisions to abandon recorded images.
This detailed description of operations and hardware provides the context under which the ACME
experiments are conducted. …

C. Summary of Preliminary Results
Abstract for Critical temperature and reactant mass flux for radiative extinction of ethylene
microgravity spherical diffusion flames at 1 bar (2023):
In microgravity combustion, where buoyancy is not present to accelerate the flow field and strain
the flame, radiative extinction is of fundamental importance, and has implications for spacecraft
fire safety. In this work, the critical point for r adiative extinction is identified for normal and
inverse ethylene spherical diffusion flames via atmospheric pressure experiments conducted
aboard the International Space Station, as well as with a transient numerical model. The fuel is
ethylene with nitrogen diluent, and the oxidizer is an oxygen/nitrogen mixture. The burner is a
porous stainless-steel sphere. All experiments are conducted at constant reactant flow rate. For
normal flames, the ambient oxygen mole fraction was varied from 0.2 to 0.38, burner supply fuel
mole fraction from 0.13 to 1, total mass flow rate, mtotal , from 0.6 to 12.2 mg/s, and adiabatic
flame temperature, Tad , from 2000 to 2800 K. For inverse flames, the ambient fuel mole fraction
was varied from 0.08 to 0.12, burner supply oxy gen mole fraction from 0.4 to 0.85, mtotal from

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign, p.25
text:
2.3 to 11.3 mg/s, and Tad from 2080 to 2590 K. Despite this broad range of conditions, all flames
extinguish at a critical extinction temperature of 1130 K, and a fuel-based mass flux of 0.2 g/m2 -
s for normal flames, and an oxygen- based mass flux of 0.68 g/m 2-s for inverse flames. With this
information, a simple equation is developed to estimate the flame size (i.e., location of peak
temperature) at extinction for any atmospheric-pressure ethylene spherical diffusion flame given
only the reactant mass flow rate. Flame growth, which ultimately leads to radiative extinction if
the critical extinction point is reached, is attributed to the natural development of the diffusion -
limited system as it approaches steady state and the reduction in the transport properties as the
flame temperature drops due to increasing flame radiation with time (radiation-induced growth.)
Abstract for On the existence of steady state gaseous microgravity spherical diffusion flames in
the presence of radiation heat loss (2023):
Whether steady-state gaseous microgravity spherical diffusion exist in the presence of radiation
heat loss is an important fundamental question and has important implications for spacecraft fire
safety. In this work, experiments aboard the International Space Station and a transient numerical

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: FinalRpt_ACMEFlameDesign, p.25
text:
model are used to investigate the existence of steady -state microgravity spherical diffusion
flames. Gaseous spherical diffusion flames stabilized on a porous spherical burner are employed
in normal (i.e., fuel flowing into an ambient oxidizer) and inverse (i.e., oxidizer flowing into an
ambient fuel) flame configurations. The fuel is ethylene and the oxidizer oxygen, both diluted with
nitrogen. The flow rate of the reactant gas from the burner is held constant. It is found that steady-
state gaseous microgravity spherical diffusion flames can exist in the presence of radiation heat
loss, provided that the steady-state flame size is less than the flame size for radiative extinct ion,
and the flame develops fast enough that radiation heat loss does not drop the flame temperature
below the critical temperature for radiative extinction (1130 K). A simple model is provided that
allows for the identification of initial conditions that can lead to steady -state spherical diffusion
flames. In the spherical, infinite domain configuration, the characteristic time for the diffusion -
controlled system to effectively reach steady -state is found to be on the order of 100,000 s.
Despite a narrow r ange of attainable conditions, flames that exhibit steady -state behavior are
observed aboard the ISS for up to 870 s, even with the constraint of a finite boundary. Steady -

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.2
text:
Task Description:
NOTE Update August 2020: New grant issued for Flame Design - A Novel Approach to Clean Efficient Diffusion
Flames, with grant number 80NSSC20M0072, which continues to 4/30/2022. NOTE (September 2015): Continuation of
Flame Design - A Novel Approach to Clean Efficient Diffusion Flames (NNX09AO53A).
The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons.
These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely
affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many
methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing
pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance
penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The
approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within
the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants.
This effort is a collaborative effort between the PI (Principal Investigator), the Co-Is (Co-Investigators), and staff at

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.2
text:
NASA Glenn Research Center. The division of labor has Richard Axelbaum directing normal gravity experiments and
computations at Washington University, David Urban providing guidance for the flight experiments, and Peter
Sunderland directing experiments and numerical simulations at University of Maryland.
Rationale for HRP Directed Research:
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For
example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants.
Task Progress:
We have completed Round 1 (normal flames) and Round 2 (inverse flames) of Flame Design testing and are processing
and analyzing the data. We are running Sphdif simulations and publishing the findings.
Three journal papers were published this year and one other was submitted. One conference paper was published and
presented. Kendyl Waddell defended and published his Ph.D. dissertation.
Our work on the numerical model has continued. We have run multiple cases with the University of California San
Diego (UCSD) mechanism. We continue to investigate the boundary conditions for radiation and conduction. We
simulated ethylene flames to perform parametric studies in an attempt to find conditions that are favorable to steady state
flames.

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.2
text: February 2024 Update per PI. See Bibliography for additional information. (Ed., 2/15/24) Despite a range of conditions, all flames extinguish at a critical temperature of 1130 K, a fuel-based mass flux of 0.2 g/m2-s for normal flames, and an oxygen-based mass flux of 0.68 g/m2-s for inverse flames. With this information, we have developed a simple equation to estimate the flame size (i.e., location of peak temperature) at extinction for any atmospheric-pressure ethylene spherical diffusion flame given only the reactant mass flow rate. Flame growth, which ultimately leads to radiative extinction if the critical extinction point is reached, is attributed to the natural development of the diffusion limited system as it approaches steady state and the reduction in the transport properties as the flame temperature drops due to increasing flame radiation with time (radiation-induced growth). Reference: Irace PH, Waddell KA, Constales D, Sunderland PB, Axelbaum RL. "Critical temperature and reactant mass flux for radiative extinction of ethylene microgravity spherical diffusion flames at 1 bar." Proc. Combust. Inst. 2023 Jan 1;39(2):1905-13. https:// Despite a narrow range of attainable conditions, flames that exhibit steady-state behavior are observed aboard the

Task Description:
NOTE Update August 2020: New grant issued for Flame Design - A Novel Approach to Clean Efficient Diffusion
Flames, with grant number 80NSSC20M0072, which continues to 4/30/2022. NOTE (September 2015): Continuation of
Flame Design - A Novel Approach to Clean Efficient Diffusion Flames (NNX09AO53A).
The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons.
These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely
affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many
methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing
pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial
performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these
concerns. The approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion
flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and
minimize pollutants.
This effort is a collaborative effort between the PI (Principal Investigator), the Co-Is (Co-Investigators), and staff at

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.7
text:
NASA Glenn Research Center. The division of labor has Richard Axelbaum directing normal gravity experiments and
computations at Washington University, David Urban providing guidance for the flight experiments, and Peter
Sunderland directing experiments and numerical simulations at University of Maryland.
Rationale for HRP Directed Research:
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For
example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants.
Task Progress:
We have completed Round 1 of Flame Design testing and are processing the data. This includes making videos from
HiBMs still images, converting video from the ops camera from ts to mp4 format, plotting the digital data for all tests,
and measuring flame diameters. We have finalized the test matrix for Round 2.
We are organizing the results of Flame Design Round 1 (flame diameter, fiber temperature, PMTs, radiometers, etc.).
Particular focus has been placed on using two-color ratio and ratio intensity pyrometry to obtain fiber temperature. We
continued to plot and analyze the thermocouple data.
We are processing HiBMs data to obtain soot volume fraction and are using the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.7
text:
Experiments (ACME) images to obtain soot temperature. Fiber temperature is being used to measure flame temperature
at the sooting limit. We have compiled all of our radiative extinction data, excluding extinction temperature.
We have performed thin-filament pyrometry for several International Space Station (ISS) flames based on color ratios
and based on grayscale intensity.
We have completed soot temperature measurements of ethylene and methane tri-axial flames using two-color pyrometry.
We performed narrow-angle radiometer measurements of radiant emissions in ethylene tri-axial flames. Soot volume
fraction measurements using color pyrometry and an absolute intensity calibration have been performed. In our research
on double luminous zones, we have made our chemiluminescence images quantitative and have chosen some of them to
be displayed as color contour plots of intensity at specific wavelengths. Thermocouple probing of the double luminous
zones was performed. Work continued on the imaging of excited species.
An analytical model of steady-state diameters of gas-fed spherical diffusion flames was created.
Our work on the numerical model has continued. We have run multiple cases with the University of California San
Diego (UCSD) mechanism. We continue to investigate the boundary conditions for radiation and conduction. Because

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.7
text:
burner heating can significantly affect the flame diameter and lifetime, we have started to implement a heat balance at
the burner surface to solve for burner temperature and better conserve enthalpy. We simulated ethylene flames to
perform parametric studies in an attempt to find conditions that are favorable to steady state flames. We compared the
simulation results with experimental results. Work is underway to update the globally implicit solver to the
time-splitting method. We modified the SphDiff code to plot the radius of stoichiometric mixture fraction as a function
of time, both for non-reacting and reacting flows. We added 2nd order upwind scheme. We modified the transient term
in the conservation of mass equation so that it captures the density change due to temperature and concentration
changes. We added an automatic temperature initialization scheme from an analytical droplet combustion model.

This effort is a collaborative effort between the PI (Principal Investigator), the Co-Is (Co-Investigators), and staff at
NASA Glenn Research Center. The division of labor has Richard Axelbaum directing normal gravity experiments and
computations at Washington University, David Urban providing guidance for the flight experiments, and Peter
Sunderland directing experiments and numerical simulations at University of Maryland.
Rationale for HRP Directed Research:
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For
example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants.
Task Progress:
Many laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) tests were performed. The system was optimized and the
signal/data processing methodology was improved. We obtained calibration data of the relation between atomic ratio
and intensity ratio of major elements (C,H,O,N) from a McKenna flat-flame burner. We reduced the burden on the
transition stage by cutting down the distance from the measured point to the transition stage (for ethylene-air
counter-flow burner). We measured the C/O, H/O, C/H atomic ratios along the center line of ethylene-air counter-flow
diffusion flame. We used the acoustic system (LIBT) to measure the temperature profile on the center line of an

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.10
text:
ethylene-air counter-flow diffusion flame. All the results have been compared to the OPPDIF simulation and
Wengdong's previous data, and we have verified that the LIBS measurement is reliable and repeatable.
At Washington University in the last two months, we have performed experiments to show the PM emissions from the
pure ethylene flame and comparing PM (particulate matter) data of newly bought low pressure impactor [Electrical
Low-Pressure Impactor (ELPI), model ELPI+, Dekati] and Scanning Mobility Particle Spectrometry (SMPS, model
3080, TSI Inc.). A rich ethylene flame was chosen as it produces soot at a uniform rate. A co-flow diffusion flame
burner was used, which comprised of two coaxial channels for the flow of fuel and air, respectively. Particle sampling is
achieved with an N2-diluted sampling probe. The flow of dilution N2 through the annulus gap provides the negative
pressure needed to sample the flue gas as well as cool down and dilute the particle-laden flow. The dilution ratio (DR)
is controlled by N2 flow rate and the physical dimension of the annulus gap, and CO2 is chosen as the tracer gas for
dilution ratio measurement. A high flow rate of dilution N2 (~45 SLPM) is applied and the dilution ratio is controlled to
a range of 30 – 200. The probe samples the whole particle stream while maintaining quasi-isokinetic sampling, and is

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.10
text:
expected to cause little bias for particle measurements. The ELPI and SMPS (scanning mobility particle spectrometer)
data show similar trends. The experiments were also conducted to know the efficiency of ELPI with respect to time to
get the correct PSD (particle size distribution) data. It was found that after 2 minutes of measurements, ELPI have to be
cleaned as it creates a virtual mode owing to the partly over filing of ELPI stages. In the future, a new dilution system
will be used and PM data will be compared between SMPS and ELPI at dilution ratio of the order of 10000 using rich
ethylene flames.
At University of Maryland (UMD), the possible appearance of double luminous zones in normal diffusion flames was
investigated in the literature and in the laboratory. Additional published flame lengths were added to our draft paper on
flame lengths. Oxygen concentrations were measured in the chimney for inverse diffusion flames. A presentation on
double luminous zones was made at ASGSR (American Society for Gravitational & Space Research) in Seattle.
At UMD we tested IDFs (inverse diffusion flames) with CO2 as diluent in both fuel side and oxidizer side. These did not
have double luminous zones. We also tested IDFs with Ar and He as diluent. These had the most remarkable double
luminous zones we have seen to date.

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.10
text:
At UMD, work continues on improved imaging of species in normal and inverse diffusion flames. Interference filters
have been acquired to allow the imaging of OH*, CH*, C2*, and CO2*. A Matlab script for Abel deconvolution has
been modified for the resulting images. We have imaged our normal and inverse diffusion flames with various optical
filters to identify the source of the blue emissions observed. We also have applied deconvolution to these images.
Work has progressed on identifying the species responsible for double blue zones in normal and inverse gas jet diffusion
flames. Bandpass filters allow imaging of C2* (515 nm), CO2* (455 nm), CH* (430 nm), and OH* (310 nm). The
images are deconvolved, and corrections for CO2* emissions are made in the images of C2* and CH* emissions.
WashU and UMD have been working together to begin welding B-type thermocouples (0.0015 in, 38 micron). These
will initially be used to measure temperatures of co-flow diffusion flames at various stoichiometric mixture fraction.
The injection port of the single droplet generator has been modified to allow for continuous operation with a Hencken
flat flame. Droplet generation in the previous design was unstable when run with a flame. The single droplet generator
will allow for the study of preferential vaporization in nonpremixed flames. We modified the design of the droplet

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.10
text:
generator to be able to maintain a steady droplet stream with flame. Drawings were sent to machine shop and parts have
been modified.
A new student has started at Wash U and he has been learning high-speed videography, PDPA, and manufacturing of
fine-wire thermocouples. We are also developing a new method of making temperature measurements with high-speed
videography.
The spherical flame code has been demonstrated for the first time by the new team of Ph.D. students. Work at UMD has
emphasized the numerical model. The current graduate students are now able to simulate spherical normal and inverse
diffusion flames. They have implemented an improved method of choosing the initial temperature profile.
The numerical modeling of spherical diffusion flames has progressed. This indicates that some normal flames of
ethylene burning in air may be able to reach steady state. Furthermore, flames that continue burning with peak
temperatures as low as 1000 K are observed. Previously no flames were predicted with these temperatures below 1100
K.
We completed the final review of “Science Protocol on Intent to Conduct an International Collaborative Research Effort
Entitled Flame Design,” to support collaborative research with Russian Scientists.
Employing the principles developed by Long to support ACME (Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments)

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.10
text:
research projects, WashU is developing capabilities to measure particle temperatures through direct photography.

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.11
text:
Based on recent findings, the new graduate student at Washington University is beginning to construct a tri-coflow
burner to test a theory of applying Flame Design concepts to control heat flux. We have modified an existing burner to
create a triaxial coflow flame. The inner nozzle supplies air or oxygen enriched air, the middle nozzle supplies fuel
(methane) or nitrogen diluted fuel, and the outer nozzle supplies air or oxygen enriched air. The inner oxidizer creates an
inner flame sheet, resulting in two distinct flame zones. The goal of this project is to maximize radiation heat transfer in
methane combustion by using flame design concepts to create a soot favorable environment at the inner flame sheet and
then oxidize soot particles before they are released to the ambient environment. We have been taking high speed videos
of the flame sheet interactions and are preparing to take radiation measurements.

methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing

concerns. The approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion

This effort is a collaborative effort between the PI (Principal Investigator), the Co-Is (Co-Investigators), and staff at

computations at Washington University, David Urban providing guidance for the flight experiments, and Peter

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.13
text:
Sunderland directing experiments and numerical simulations at University of Maryland.
Rationale for HRP Directed Research:
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For
example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants.
Task Progress:
The laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) measurement method has been improved at Washington University
in St. Louis. This includes a new oscilloscope setup and preparation for better acoustic monitoring. We have
synchronized the new oscilloscope with the LIBS system. We completed work on noise filtering of the acoustic
measurements. We performed Matlab programming on automated acoustic aided LIBS measurements. We performed
high temperature LIBS tests in a Hencken burner, LIBS tests in a McKenna burner under same equivalence ratio and
different temperature, and acoustic aided LIBS measurements in a McKenna burner with varying equivalence ratio. We
adapted a maximum likelihood estimation method instead of average in LIBS data processing; compared and correlated
the baseline for different element emission lines; and worked on the scalar measurement. We investigated the
compositional effects in laser-induced backward transfer (LIBT) measurement and investigated the screening methods

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.13
text:
of LIBT measurement by looking into the statistics. We investigated the simultaneous composition and temperature
measurement using laser induced plasma. We explored the water-gas-shift equilibrium in higher hydrocarbon flames and
investigated the potential of inferring molecular profiles from LIBS measured elemental compositions. We investigated
the water-gas-shift equilibrium in higher hydrocarbons using detailed mechanisms for heptane and toluene. We
developed a plasma model to simulate the sound wave generation as a function of laser energy input and local gas
properties and to optimize the measurements using a CCD based spectrometer.
Wendong Wu successfully defended his Ph.D. in May, 2017, at Washington University in St. Louis. The collaboration
between Washington University and Shanghai Jiaotong University will continue in the field of laser plasma diagnostics.
Graduate student Pan Du has joined the Flame Design team.
At the University of Maryland, we continue to examine the effects of dilution on lengths of normal and inverse gas jet
diffusion flames. The method of measuring flame lengths was refined to examine only the blue intensities in the recorded
images. Both normal and inverse flames now correlate together according to the theory of Roper. We have also

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.13
text:
characterized the double flame structure visible in some inverse diffusion flames. We imaged the double flames at 310
and 430 nm. We are measuring oxygen concentrations and temperatures in and above the double flames. This will help
to determine if oxygen in this region contributes to the formation of the double luminous zones. A paramagnetic oxygen
analyzer is being used, which has a mole fraction range of 0-1 and an accuracy of 0.001%.
At the University of Hawaii Manoa, Beei-Huan Chao has retired and resigned from his role as Flame Design
Co-Investigator. His invaluable contributions to Flame Design are greatly appreciated and will be missed going forward.
Prior to his retirement, progress was made on analytical studies of C/O ratio in diffusion flames. We examined extinction
of spherical diffusion flames attached to a burner and revisited reactant leakage of diffusion flames. We revisited
Linan's 1974 paper following the “total enthalpy” concept.
The research team published two journal papers, four conference papers and abstracts, and one Ph.D. dissertation.
The flight experiment was supported in various ways. For example, the research team responded to issues raised by
NASA engineers in refining the test matrix and ACME requirements document. The research team also aided staff at
NASA Glenn with burner characterization drop testing in the 2 s drop facility.

text:
Task Description:
NOTE: Continuation of Flame Design - A Novel Approach to Clean Efficient Diffusion Flames (NNX09AO53A).
The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons.
These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely
affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many
methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing
pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance
penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The
approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within
the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants.
This effort is a collaborative effort between the Principal Investigator, the three Co-Investigators, and staff at NASA
Glenn Research Center. The division of labor has Richard Axelbaum directing normal gravity experiments and
computations at Washington University, David Urban providing guidance for the flight experiments, Peter Sunderland

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.16
text:
directing numerical simulations at University of Maryland (UMD), and Beei-Huan Chao directing analytical work and
computations at University of Hawaii.
Rationale for HRP Directed Research:
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For
example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants.
Task Progress:
Summary of Accomplishments
• The research team published 6 conference papers and abstracts during this period.
• Work at Univ. of Maryland has started a new experimental study on the effects of dilution on the stoichiometric
lengths of normal and inverse gas jet diffusion flames Two new graduate students were added to this project at UMD:
Zhengyang Wang (Ph.D.) and Mohamed El Makawy (M.S.). They have generated predictions of these effects from the
model of Roper (1977). Stoichiometric lengths of over 250 flames have been measured. Physical constants in the model
of Roper have been adjusted such that it predicts these reasonably well.
• Work at Washington University continued to pursue normal gravity experiments of soot formation in diffusion flames,
numerical modeling, chemical kinetics, water-gas shift reaction rates, and laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.16
text:
(LIBS). The LIBS measurement method has been improved. We now use a gated spectrometer to utilize C, H, N, O
atomic lines instead of ionic lines in atomic ratio measurement. We improved accuracy with acoustic aid and automated
baseline correction. Shot-to-shot variation is analyzed with relative standard deviation.
• Work at Univ. of Hawaii continued to pursue analytical and computational studies of soot formation, radiation, and
extinction in diffusion flames. Also being investigated are ignition behavior and effects of C/O ratio in diffusion flames.
• The flight experiment was supported in various ways. For example, the research team responded to issues raised by
NASA engineers in refining the test matrix and ACME requirements document. The research team also aided staff at
NASA Glenn with burner characterization drop testing in the 2 s drop facility.
Scientific Context, Hypothesis, and Research Objectives
The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons.
These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely
affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many
methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.16
text:
pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance
penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The
approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within
the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants.
This effort is a collaborative effort between the PI, the three Co-Is, and staff at NASA Glenn Research Center. The
division of labor has Richard Axelbaum directing normal gravity experiments and computations at Washington
University, David Urban providing guidance for the flight experiments, Peter Sunderland directing numerical simulations
at University of Maryland, and Beei-Huan Chao directing analytical work and computations at University of Hawaii.
Additional Accomplishments
W. Wu, G. Yablonsky, R.L. Axelbaum, Observation of Water-Gas Shift Equilibrium in Diffusion Flames, Combustion
and Flame, accepted. The kinetic behavior of the water-gas-shift (WGS) sub-system has been studied computationally
for hydrocarbon diffusion flames in the counterflow geometry. Of specific interest was the spatial domain in which the

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.16
text:
reactions in the WGS-complex exhibit characteristics that lead to species concentrations approaching those expected
from equilibrium. Two scenarios were observed for WGS equilibrium:
(1) Full equilibrium in which every step of the WGS-mechanism is nearly in equilibrium;
(2) “Apparent” equilibrium, which is achieved via opposing but coherent shifts away from equilibrium for the two key
elementary reactions that constitute the WGS reaction. This interesting phenomenon is caused by the supply of the H
radical, which participates in the forward reaction of one step and the reverse reaction of the other. This new form of
apparent equilibrium differs from well-known “quasi” equilibrium, which is typically caused by the combination of a
fast reversible step and slow irreversible step.
Parametric domains where found in which these two scenarios are observed. For a given fuel type it was shown that the
two scenarios can be separated by the location of stoichiometry. On the oxidizer side, full equilibrium of the overall
WGS reaction is achieved, while on the fuel side, apparent equilibrium can occur.
Z. Wang, M. El Makawy, P.B. Sunderland, B. Chao, R.L. Axelbaum, The Effects of Reactant Dilution on Lengths of
Laminar Jet Diffusion Flames, Abstract, ASGSR, Cleveland OH (2016). Many past studies have examined the

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.16
text:
stoichiometric lengths of laminar gas jet diffusion flames. These are found to be independent of pressure and burner
diameter for fixed fuel mass flow rate. However, some studies report flame lengths increase when inert is added to the
Page 2 of 3
Task Book Report Generated on: 02/28/2024

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.17
text:
fuel stream, whereas others report no change. Furthermore, measurements of effects of inert in the ambient gas are
sparse, as are measurements for inverse flames. The analytical model of Roper (CNF 29:219, 1977) accounts for the full
range of reactant dilution and inverse flames, but has only been tested for fuel-air systems.
This work examines the stoichiometric lengths of normal and inverse steady methane/oxygen/nitrogen jet flames burning
on a 3.0 mm coflowing burner inside a glass chimney. Nitrogen dilution is such that methane mole fractions vary from
0.15 – 1 and oxygen mole fractions vary from 0.18 – 1. The measured flame lengths vary from 3 – 53 mm.
Stoichiometric lengths are measured from visible emissions of the blue flame sheets. Reactant flow rates are measured
with calibrated rotameters.
The predictions of the Roper model are compared with the measured flame lengths. For normal flames the agreement is
best for a mass diffusivity at 25 C of 17 mm2/s and a temperature of 0.94 times the adiabatic flame temperature. This
contrasts to values used by Roper for methane/air flames of 20 mm2/s and 1500 K, respectively. For the present
conditions the predictions match the measurements with a R2 coefficient of determination of 0.91.
For fixed fuel flow rate, inert addition to the fuel stream is found to increase flame length, but this effect is negligible for

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.17
text:
fuel mole fractions above 0.5.
A simplified approximation of the Roper model has been obtained for normal methane/nitrogen/oxygen diffusion
flames. This removes the requirement to specify adiabatic flame temperature and stoichiometric mixture fraction. The
simplified model predicts flame length from the methane flow rate and mole fraction and the oxygen mole fraction.
W. Wu, R.L. Axelbaum, Interpreting Flame Structure by Mixture Fraction Measurement Using Laser-Induced
Breakdown Spectroscopy, Abstract, ASGSR, Cleveland OH (2016). Measuring mixture fractions in a broad range of
combustion systems with a suitable spatial and temporal resolution is critical not only for understanding the flame
behavior, but also for the validation of rapidly developing numerical models. Instead of deriving the mixture fraction
from measured molecular profile, a new approach of obtaining such quantities from atomic ratios measured by laser
induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) is introduced in this study. The atomic ratios for C, N, H, and O (e.g., C/O,
H/O, and N/O) for the LIBS system were first calibrated in an ethylene-air premixed flat flame, where the equivalence
ratio of the pre-mixture was varied from 0.60 to 1.80. Then the atomic ratio distributions along the centerline of an

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.17
text:
ethylene-air counter-flow diffusion flame were measured to demonstrate the capability of LIBS to measure atomic ratios
between different elements throughout the entire flame. The elemental mass fractions for C, H, N, O can be thus
obtained from atomic ratio profiles. The mixture fraction distribution was calculated from elemental mass fractions.
Numerical results were compared to the experimental results and showed excellent agreement. The results of this work
demonstrate that the LIBS technique holds promise as a simple tool for measuring atomic ratios and mixture fraction in
diffusion flames.
Practical Applications. This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in
terrestrial combustors. For example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants.
Plans for Upcoming Year Including Use of NASA Facilities. In the coming year we plan to continue with our
publications of experimental and numerical work. We plan to perform additional simulations at Washington Univ.,
Univ. of Hawaii, and Univ. of Maryland. We plan to continue efforts to advance to flight tests and spherical burner
development.

W. Wu, P.B. Sunderland, B.-H. Chao, D.L. Urban, R.L. Axelbaum, Recent Advances in Flame Design, A Spaceflight
Combustion Experiment, Abstract, ASGSR, Alexandria, VA, 2015.
Flame Design is a spaceflight combustion experiment that will examine several unusual aspects of spherical diffusion
flames fueled by gases. Its emphasis is on soot formation and flame extinction. This experiment, and associated
ground-based work, attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent
constraints, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. This presentation will introduce the
overall concepts of Flame Design. It will summarize observations in the NASA Glenn 2.2 s and 5 s drop facilities,
which have yielded important insights into soot formation and flame extinction behavior. Detailed numerical modeling
of spherical diffusion flames have aided the understanding of the observations. Recent advances in Laser-Induced

diagnostic is well suited to use in spaceflight experiments.

This effort is a collaborative effort between the PI, the three Co-Is, and staff at NASA Glenn Research Center. The
division of labor has Richard Axelbaum directing normal gravity experiments and computations at Washington
University, David Urban providing guidance for the flight experiments, Peter Sunderland directing numerical simulations

at University of Maryland, and Beei-Huan Chao directing analytical work and computations at University of Hawaii.
Rationale for HRP Directed Research:
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For
example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants.
Task Progress:
Summary of Accomplishments:
• The research team published 4 peer-reviewed journal articles during this period. This work is summarized below.
• Work at Washington University continued to pursue normal gravity experiments of soot formation in diffusion flames,
numerical modeling, and chemical kinetics.
• Work at Univ. of Maryland continued to pursue numerical models of spherical diffusion flames, including soot
formation and extinction.
• Work at Univ. of Hawaii continued to pursue analytical and computational studies of soot formation, radiation, and
extinction in diffusion flames.
• The flight experiment was supported in various ways. For example, the research team responded to issues raised by
NASA engineers in refining the test matrix and ACME requirements document. The research team also aided staff at
NASA Glenn with burner characterization drop testing in the 5 s drop facility.
V.R. Lecoustre, P.B. Sunderland, B.H. Chao, R.L. Axelbaum, Modeled Quenching Limits of Spherical Hydrogen

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.23
text:
Diffusion Flames, Proceedings of the Combustion Institute 34 (2013) 887-894. Hydrogen-air diffusion flames were
modeled with an emphasis on kinetic extinction. The flames were one-dimensional spherical laminar diffusion flames
supported by adiabatic porous burners of various diameters. Behavior of normal (H2 flowing into quiescent air) and
inverse (air flowing into quiescent H2) configurations were considered using detailed H2/O2 chemistry and transport
properties with updated light component diffusivities. For the same heat release rate, inverse flames were found to be
smaller and 290 K hotter than normal flames. The weakest normal flame that could be achieved before quenching has an
overall heat release rate of 0.25 W, compared to 1.4 W for the weakest inverse flame. There is extensive leakage of the
ambient reactant for both normal and inverse flames near extinction, which results in a premixed flame regime for
diffusion flames except for the smallest burners with radii on the order of 1 micron. At high flow rates
H+OH(+M)?H2O(+M) contributes over 40% of the net heat release. However at flow rates approaching quenching
limits, H+O2(+M)?HO2(+M) is the elementary reaction with the largest heat release rate. The corresponding author for
this paper was P.B. Sunderland.

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.23
text:
F. Xia, R.L. Axelbaum, Simplifying the complexity of diffusion flames through interpretation in C/O ratio space,
Computers and Mathematics with Applications, 65 (2013) 1625-1632. Understanding the structure of diffusion flames is
often complicated by the dependence of flame structure on the boundary conditions, e.g. composition, temperature and
flow field (e.g., strain rate in a counterflow flame.) In this paper, the local carbon-to-oxygen atom ratio (C/O ratio) is
applied as a variable to interpret the flame and soot zone structures of counterflow diffusion flames from numerical
results with detailed chemical kinetics and transport. Radical pool and soot precursor zones are shown to be clearly
delineated in C/O ratio space. The boundary of these two zones, as well as the flame location, are shown to be
independent of both stoichiometric mixture fraction (Zst) and strain rate when interpreted in C/O space. The kinetic ratio
is used to study the characteristics of key chemical reactions and to identify regions of equilibrium for these reactions.
The results of this paper indicate that the C/O ratio is a valuable variable for interpreting flame structure and soot
precursor chemistry for diffusion flames. The corresponding author for this paper was R.L. Axelbaum.
F. Xia, G.S. Yablonsky, R.L. Axelbaum, Numerical Study of Flame Structure and Soot Inception Interpreted in

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.23
text:
Carbon-to-Oxygen Atom Ratio Space, Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, 34 (2013) 1085-1091. The utility of
interpreting flame results in carbon-to-oxygen atom ratio (C/O ratio) space, as opposed to physical space or mixture
fraction space, is evaluated. Flame and soot zone structures of counterflow diffusion flames have been studied for C2H4
and C3H8 and interpreted in C/O ratio space as a function of stoichiometric mixture fraction (Zst). The
Burke-Schumann results expressed in C/O ratio space demonstrate how a clear and direct understanding of how
structure is affected by Zst can be realized in C/O ratio space because, unlike physical or mixture fraction space, the
flame location is independent of stoichiometric mixture fraction. Numerical results with detailed chemical kinetics also
indicate that C/O ratio space is a fundamental variable in the sense that, for a given fuel, the location of the flame zones
and critical reactions is invariant with Zst and strain rate. Two zones are clearly observed, namely the radical pool and
the soot precursor zone located on the fuel side of the flame. The onset threshold of soot precursors (C6H5 and C6H6)
for the high temperature side of the soot precursor zone is characterized by the depletion of radicals. The role of the
hydrogen radical in flame structure and soot inception is demonstrated by studying its production and consumption

name: ACME/Flame Design
title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.23
text:
channels in C/O ratio space. Finally, a modified (C/O)* is given to interpret the physical meaning of C/O ratio. The
numerical results in this work indicate and explain the advantages of applying C/O ratio space in the analysis of flame
structure and soot precursor chemistry. The corresponding author for this paper was R.L. Axelbaum.
F. Yi, R.L. Axelbaum, Stability of Spray Combustion for Water/Alcohols Mixtures in Oxygen-Enriched Air,
Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, 34 (2013) 1697-1704. The feasibility of burning fuels that are heavily diluted
with water was evaluated. This concept could potentially be utilized to directly generate steam for a variety of
applications, including power generation and enhanced oil recovery. Two water-soluble fuels, ethanol and 1-propanol,

title: ACME/Flame Design: TaskbookRpts, p.24
text:
were heavily diluted with water and sprayed into a swirl-stabilized burner and the blow-off limits were obtained to
identify the flame stability. The blow-off limit was experimentally determined as the lowest O2 concentration where a
flame could exist under a given oxidizer flow rate. For the present experimental system, stability maps were determined
as a function of fuel concentration and oxidizer flow rate for different types of nozzles and both alcohols. Contours of
temperature and overall fuel mass fraction in the droplets were obtained for a flame burning 15 wt% ethanol in an
oxidizer of 50% O2 and 50% N2. The results revealed that preferential vaporization of ethanol over water plays an
important role in enhancing flame stability. To further understand this, a model of bi-component droplet vaporization
was employed for both the diffusion limit and distillation limit modes of liquid mass transfer. The results confirmed the
preferential vaporization of ethanol and demonstrated that it is necessary to account for the non-ideal solution behavior
of the alcohol-water mixture to appropriately model the vaporization process. The model also demonstrated that for this
experimental system, droplet vaporization was better characterized by the distillation limit mode with enhanced mass
transfer by convection. The corresponding author for this paper was R.L. Axelbaum.

ACME Critical Design Review– 24
Glenn Research Center
ZIN Technologies
PDR RFA-004 Disposition
RFA # 04
Originator: Al Linne
Originator Concurrence: 7 November 2013
Statement of
Concern
Recommended Action Closure Rationale
A detonation analysis has
not been completed.
Perform a detonation analysis on the
expected ACME gas mixtures. This
should be done prior to the ACME Phase
0/1 Flight Safety Review, since it may
inform some of the hazard analysis. Also,
the results of this analysis could drive the
consumables usage and could limit the
amount of science performed.
An ACME detonation analysis has been performed
for the Inverse Flame Experiment, which is the the
worst case hazard. It was chosen because of the
possible oxygen interaction with ACME CIA
hardware (i.e. materials compatibility). The
analysis validated that the present configuration
could safely meet requirements. The analysis has
not impacted the design.
A full detonation analysis of all experiments will be
completed prior to the Phase 2 Flight Safety
Review.

Originator Concurrence: 7 November 2013
Statement of Concern Recommended Action Closure Rationale
A number of different oxygen
percentages were discussed &
identified in the PDR presentation
and documentation. What oxygen
percentage was used in the
design and does this cover the
ranges requested by the PI.
Determine the worst case oxygen
percentage (and pressure) that could
potentially be in the CIR chamber with
ACME installed, based on credible failures
to CIR & ACME equipment and use this
oxygen percentage as the design point for
ACME. This will drive integrated
safety/hazard analyses as well as ACME
material compatibility.
Also, based on the resulting worst case
oxygen percentage determine if an
oxygen compatibility assessment needs to
performed for the ACME Chamber Insert
Assembly.
Oxygen compatibility with the ACME CIA has
been assessed and is documented in the
Draft Materials Identification/ Usage List
(MIUL), which is a review item for the CDR.
An Integrated Hazard Analysis has been
completed and the worst-case oxygen
percentages and pressures have been
identified and addressed in the Hazard
Report (see ACME Hazard Report 5,
documented in ACME-SDP-001).

The project has done a good job of

have not yet been vetted with the PIs.

requirements that the GRC science and

uncover additional operational
requirements.

Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME)
PURPOSE: ACME is focused on advanced combustion
technology via fundamental microgravity research. The
primary goal is to improve efficiency and reduce pollutant
emission in practical terrestrial combustion. A secondary
objective is fire prevention, especially for spacecraft.
RESEARCH: ACME includes six independent experiments
investigating laminar, gaseous, non -premixed flam es. They
are being conducted with a single set of modular hardware
in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International
Space Station (ISS).
STATUS: ACME set-up and check-out was carried out by the
ISS crew in Sept.-Oct. 2017, where science test ing began in
November. The first round of testing for the Coflow Laminar
Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment of Marshall B. Long
et al. was completed in Feb. 2018, where 130 methane
flames (at a range of concentrations) were ignited. The first
round of testing for the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar
Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment of Derek
Dunn-Rankin et al. was completed on May 18 , where 1 20
coflow flames were ignited . On May 20, b urners and
additional hardware for the next three ACME experiments
are scheduled to launch . The ACME hardware should be
reconfigured on May 22 by astronaut Ricky Arnold (NASA)
for CLD Flame ’s second round , where the ethylene flame

20 August 2018
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME)
PURPOSE: ACME is focused on advanced combustion
technology via fundamental microgravity research. The
primary goal is to improve efficiency and reduce pollutant
emission in practical terrestrial c ombustion. A secondary
objective is fire prevention, especially for spacecraft.
RESEARCH: ACME includes six independent experiment s
investigating laminar, non-premixed flames of gaseous fuels .
The experiments are being conducted with a single set o f
modular hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)
on the International Space Station (ISS) . While the ISS
astronauts set up the experimental hardware, the ACME tests
are remotely commanded from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload
Operations Center.
STATUS: ACME setup and checkout were carried out by the
ISS crew in Sept. -Oct. 2017 . Thus far, a dozen astronauts
from Germany, Italy, Japan, Russia and the United States
have supported the ACME research. Since November 2017,
over 300 flames have been ignited for the Coflow Laminar
Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) and Electric-Field Effects on
Laminar Diffusion Flames (E -FIELD Flames) experiments led
respectively by Profs. Marshall B. Long (Yale University) and
Derek Dunn-Rankin (University of California, Irvine).
A second round of CLD Flame tests is currently underway and

focused on improving practical combustion on Earth, BRE is
