title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.3
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
3
1. Overview
The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which tests are conducted within
the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS).
The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. James G . Quintiere of the Department of Fire
Protection Engineering at the University of Maryland. The experiment has two Co -Investigators (Co-Is),
namely Prof. Peter B. Sunderland, of the same U. Maryland department, and Dr. John L. de Ris (FM Global,
retired). The ISS research also benefitted greatly from the work of Parham Dehghani, a doctoral student
in the Fire Protection Engineering department.
Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NA SA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME
including BRE and the rest of the ACME investigations. In preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki
Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University ( CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Sc ientist. For
ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team includes Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam
who are also with CWRU.
The ISS operations were conducted in two separate rounds of testing during Increments 58-59 and 63-64.

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.3
text:
More specifically, the first round of testing was conducted from Feb. to April 2019, while the second -
round testing occurred from Sept. 2020 to Jan. 2021. The first round of tests was limited to ethylene and
the 25-mm BRE burner, while the second round also included tests with methane and the 50-mm burner
(although not together).
2. Science Overview
A. Background
This background is the Executive Summary from the experiment’s Science Requirements Document
(SRD) of June 2013.
The goal of this research is to establish the burning conditions possible in a microgravity quiescent
environment. The approach is to do this using a burner to emulate (BRE, Burning Rate Emulator)
the burning for real condensed fuels, representative of common liquids and solids. This will be
done for quasi-steady burning conditions, albeit ideal in some cases, but the BRE will range over
a wide spectrum of real fuel properties. The key properties governing steady burning are (1) the
heat of gasification, (2) the surface re-radiation heat flux, and (3) the heat of combustion. Flame
radiation is also relevant in general and can be represented in terms of the laminar smoke point.
Its importance in microgravity flames needs study, but the first three properties are key.
Currently NASA assesses the flammability hazard of materials for use in space flight by an upward

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.3
text:
flame spread “pass-fail” test (Test 1), and supplements with data from the Cone Calorimeter (Test
2). The latter test has the capability of measuring the three properties listed above. Hence, the
successful application of the BRE in microgravity can enhance the usefulness of Test 2.
Fundamental and ad hoc testing in microg ravity at quiescent conditions has shown that quasi-
steady flames can be supported on candle-wicks, droplets, jets and, at very low ambient velocities,
small plastic samples and a burner flame. The established flames tend to have spherical or semi-

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.4
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
4
ellipsoidal shapes. Our preliminary work burning ethanol on planar wicks of 1 × 4 cm suggest
similar shapes in aircraft and drop tower tests. But this work showed instabilities in the drop
tower, and needs further exploration. Theoretical analysis based on microgravity jet flame length
correlations suggests that a 50 mm diameter planar material could support quasi -steady
combustion in microgravity for some liquid and plastic fuels. The analysis indicates that burning
depends on diameter, so several additional burner sizes will be needed to examine this effect.
Gas burners like the BRE have been used to successfully simulate burning of a wide range of fuels
in terms of their B numbers and configurations over a range of Grashof numbers. We have
successfully show n that for planar burning at different angle orientations that a burner can
emulate the flame standoff distribution, and even match the onset of unsteadiness to turbulent
flow. Theoretical analyses of such a problem are limited by the inability to accurately deal with
flame radiation, turbulence and variable properties. A burner simulation can be far superior as it
inherently contains these effects.
The construction of a 50 mm diameter prototype BRE burner with flame heat flux sensors has

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.4
text:
enabled us to emulate both a methanol and heptane pool fire of the 50 mm diameter, reproducing
its color, flame character and shape, and heat of gasification for nearly the same surface
temperatures. We show that the BRE is capable of displaying the burning conditions in terms of
the fuel properties of heat of combustion, heat of gasification, and surface re -radiant heat flux
(with some likely effect of smoke point). A preliminary 3 -D plot of steady burning gives a
flammability mapping in terms of these v ariables under conditions of gravity and atmospheric
variations. A mapping in microgravity can demonstrate the burning conditions for a wide range
of real materials in terms of these properties. In addition the effect of external radiation can
indirectly be assessed. The 50 mm burner has been redesigned, along with a 25 mm burner, to
reduce edge effects, provide improved heat flux sensors with temperatures, and cooling water
has been dropped from the both the burner and the heat flux sensors in microgravity
experiments.
The primary objective is to observe the burning behavior (including extinction) in long -duration
microgravity for methane/nitrogen and ethylene/nitrogen mixtures on a porous circular burner
of 25 and 50 mm diameter at various pressures, a mbient oxygen, and CO2 (desired, to assess

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.4
text:
extinguishment). Ignition will not be directly studied in microgravity studies, as we believe
normal-gravity experiments are sufficient for its study. Another objective is to obtain conditions
that can be relate d to microgravity behavior of condensed fuels that embrace the scope of real
liquid and solid fuels.
We think these results can establish fuel properties that directly relate to the fire hazard in
spacecraft, and these properties can be derived from NASA Test 2. The BRE is an efficient, safe,
and comprehensive technique for achieving these results.
This version of the Science Requirements Document has been refined since the Science Concept
Review (Aug 28, 2012). The panel wrote at that time that they “s trongly encourage continued
development of the BRE experiment for implementation into the ACME and testing on the ISS.”
We have tried to address most of their recommendations and suggestions. In addition, work has
progressed to include the development of two papers, and the commencement of drop facility
testing of the BRE. Those results have shown quasi-steady flames, and are very encouraging.

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.5
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
5
B. Rationale for Microgravity
This is the ‘Justification for Extended Duration Microgravity’ section (2.5) of the experiment’s SRD
from June 2013. Equations are not included here, but they can be found in the SRD.
Fire in a spacecraft microgravity environment is a likely event based on limited accident data, tests
to burn materials, and research that has explored simple burning scenarios. Indeed, NASA screens
the use of materials on spacecraft by its flammability Test 1.
Currently NASA Test 1 and Test 2 are incapable of directly analyzing material fire hazards in
spacecraft. There is no predictive methodology to extrapolate from these tests. However, NASA
Test 2, the Cone Calorimeter, is capable of determining heats of combustion and gasification, and
surface reradiation in burning. Steady (or quasi -steady) burning rate data from the BRE in flight
experiments will establish a flammability mapping in terms of these properties for microgravity.
In addition, using Eq. (2), the results can establish the necessary heat flux condition for other fuels
to burn in microgravity. The BRE is an efficient way to achieve quasi-steady burning. While
microgravity tests of condensed fuels have been performed and are planned, they are limited in
their ability to reveal sufficient information about the diverse condensed fuels that exist aboard

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.5
text:
the ISS. Moreover the time to achieve quasi-steady burning rate of solid fuels can be of the order
of minutes as dictated by the time response of the solid. The BRE can be turned on and off quickly,
and its quasi-steady condition is only dependent on the gas phase phenomenon. While this time
is shorter, it can still be on the order of 10 seconds or more.
The proposed tests cannot be performed in parabolic aircraft owing to considerable g -jitter
disturbances. While limited testing is possible in drop facilities, the characteristic times for the
gas phase (approximately 20 s) and the burner surface temperature (approximately 40 s) preclude
consideration of quasi -steady conditions. Preliminary testing in the NASA 5.2 s drop facility
indicated the approach to quasi -steady burning, but longer tests are needed to confirm this
tendency. The longer duration testing in the ISS with the efficient oper ation of the BRE can
produce results only limited by the gas-phase response time.
C. Science Objectives
The proposed objectives text presented here is the ‘Experimental Objectives’ section (2.2) of the
experiment’s SRD from June 2013. ISS testing was not carried out to address the desired second
objective, where NASA effectively limited this experiment to the first and third objectives.
The BRE flight program seeks to establish the burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.5
text:
ambient in terms of material properties. The specific flight objectives are as follows.
1. Observe burning behavior in long -duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2
mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2
ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA-
considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 %
oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can
be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels.
2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired).
3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.6
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
6
D. Science Success Criteria
This text is from the BRE portion of the ‘Success Criteria’ section of the ACME Integrated Science
Requirements Docume nt (ISRD, ACME -SRD-001.B) from Sept. 2013, which is revision B of the
version prepared for the Requirements Definition Review (RDR). Achievement of superior success,
as defined below, was effectively ruled out by NASA because its plan didn’t include the desired
tests.
6.5.1. Minimum Success
- Obtain color video, burner surface temperature, and burner heat flux for two C2H4
flames that burn for at least 20 s and then extinguish.
6.5.2. High Success
All of the above plus:
- Obtain a flammability map for C2H4.
6.5.3. Complete Success
All of the above plus:
- Obtain a flammability map for CH4.
- Measure peak temperatures (using filament and/or soot pyrometry) as a function of
time for at least 5 flames.
- Measure temperature distributions (using filament and/or soot pyrometry) at or near
quasi-steady conditions for at least 5 flames.
- Measure temperature distributions (using filament pyrometry) near the extinction
limit for at least 5 flames.
- Measure soot volume fraction profiles at (or near) quasi -steady conditions and near
the extinction limit for at least 5 flames.
6.5.4. Superior Success
All of the above plus:
- Complete the desired parts of the test matrix.

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.7
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
7
3. Hardware Overview
A. General Description
This section is copied from section 2.A of the April 2021 version of ‘ACME Engineering
Implementation’ which should be consulted for additional details. References to other sections
within the boxed text of this section refer to the ACME Engineering Implementation document.
This section provides a general description a general description of the ACME engineering from
the ‘3.0 Experimental’ section of the following 2014 conference paper:
Dennis P. Stocker, Fumiaki Takahashi, J. Mark Hickman, and Andrew C. Suttles, “Gaseous
Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station ,” Spring
Technical Meeting of the Central States Section of the Combustion Institute, Tulsa, OK, 16–
18 March 2014.
IMPORTANT: The 2104 paper from which this section was extracted proceeded completion of the
spaceflight hardware which was mostly launched in 2017. As a result, it does not accurately
describe the final engineering in some regards . Therefore updates, clarification s, additional
details, shortcomings, references, etc. have been included in boxed notes like this following the
original description. As a minor note, the sizes of figures were adjusted in this report, but none
were cropped.
As previously discussed, the ACME experiments will be conducted within the Combustion

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.7
text:
Integrated Rack (CIR) using a chamber insert, depicted in Figure 2, which was designed to
accommodate gas delivery to a variety of exchangeable burners. Besides the chamber insert,
other ACME-unique hardware includes a high -definition color camera and an avionics package,
which is for data acquisition and control.
Figure 2: Design of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) chamber
insert that will be used in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on ISS.

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.8
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
8
ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of
burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter. As
depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4
to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1
and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two
flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm). Most burners
will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux
transducers. The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring
of the pressure differential across the outlet surface. The igniter will have a crew -exchangeable
tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper -motor drive will allow for
precise positioning.
Figure 3: ACME burner types, including from left to right, gas-jet burners, a co-flow burner,
porous spherical burners, and flat porous burners for the BRE experiment.
Ultimately, the spherical burners were limited to a single diameter of 6.35 mm, and the fabricated
gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm.

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.8
text:
However, only the larger gas -jet burner was used during the spaceflight tests. The burners are
addressed in detail in section 3.C.
Unfortunately, the spherical burners have not always yielded spherically symme tric flames,
presumably as a result of (1) greater burner flow through the joint between the porous sphere and
supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local
flame quenching.
Two types of igniter tips have been used during ACME testing. Most tests have been conducted
using a loop igniter tip like those which had been successfully used in the droplet combustion
experiments which preceded ACME research in the CIR. However, some tests were conducted with
a coil igniter tip, where that included the second round testing for both the Burning Rate Emulator
(BRE) and Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames ( s-Flame) experiments, with the
exception of the latter’s first day testing. The CFI -G investigation will also use the coil igniter tip.
For more information about the igniter tips, see section 3.D.
The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the
delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner. The
maximum fuel flow is 2 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), whereas much higher flows, e.g., 10 slpm (on

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.8
text:
a nitrogen basis), are possible for the oxidizer and nitrogen lines. The crew can exchange the mass
flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges that maximize the flow accuracy. The gas delivery
system enables on -orbit dilution of the fuel or oxidizer (but not both simultaneously), coflow,
inverse flames (e.g., oxidizer delivery to the center of a coflow burner) , and premixed flames,

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.9
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
9
although the latter are not planned for any of the current ACME experiments. Gases can also be
delivered premixed to the space station where that is necessary in some circumstances, such as
the blending of different fuel gases. CIR’s standard bottle sizes are 1, 2.25, and 3.8 liters but ACME
will sometimes use smaller bottles as a hazard control to limit the deficient reactant (e.g., fuel)
that can be released into the combustion chamber.
Thus far, ACME tests were not conducted with carbon dioxide as a diluent. Furthermore, the fuel
diluted with helium was premixed prior to launch rather than on orbit. Ultimately, oxidizer flows
of up to 20 slpm (on a nitrogen basis) were possible, while the nitrogen flow was limited to a
maximum of 5 slpm. ACME has not used gas bottles smaller than 1 liter as indicated above; the
bottle fill pressure was instead limited as an additional hazard control.
ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and
two illumination systems, of which three cameras are part of the CIR facility and are already in
use on orbit. All but one of the cameras is mounted outside of the chamber. Collectively, the
imaging systems will enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.9
text:
volume fraction; and operational support. However, it is unlikely that all functions would be
exercised at any one time as will become apparent in the subsequent discussion.
Color imaging is provided by two cameras: a high -definition digital camera mounted outside of
the chamber and a standard analog camera mounted on the chamber insert (with a turning
mirror). Both cameras are part of the ACME hardware that is now in development . The analog
camera signal will be downlinked in near real time to support the experiment operations. Light -
emitting diodes within the chamber can be used to illuminate the igniter and burner to both
support the operations and provide reference images. The 12-bit digital camera records at up to
30 full frames (1360x1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent
control of the zoom, iris, and focus. The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly
with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging. Color imaging can
also be carried out with a blue -green BG7 Schott glass filter, which balances the color planes to
avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green. The natural flame
color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is pyrometry and

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.9
text:
measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23 -24]. Alternately, CH*
imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430 -nm
bandpass filter with a 10 -nm full width at half -maximum transmission (FWHM). A 450 -nm
bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract
interfering broadband soo t emission. However, the filter assembly rotates slowly so such
subtraction effectively requires a separate test with each filter and of course reproducible flame
conditions.
The video from the analog operations (i.e., ops) camera, also referred to as the internal camera,
is not archived in space. The video is instead recorded on the ground in the operations center. Its
gain was sometimes adjusted for improved imaging of dim flames, e.g., approaching extinction.
The sensitivity of the color digital camera, often referenced as the ACME DataCam (i.e., Data
Camera), to the dim microgravity flames was such that it was often used with long exposure times
and thus low framing rates, for example on the order of 1 frame per second. The clear “filter” is
of fused silica. Unfortunately, the thickness of the blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter and the added

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.10
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
10
antireflective (AR) coating caused too great a reduction in the red, so it doe s not balance the
intensity of the three color planes as intended and thereby can limit the accuracy of temperature
determination. Meanwhile, rather than the 450 -nm bandpass filter described above, the high
definition color camera was equipped with a bandpass filter for imaging formaldehyde emissions.
For more information, see the Data Camera Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-010 Rev. A).
Imaging of the dim hydrogen flames in the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames
(s-Flame) experiment was particularly challenging with these, if not all, cameras.
Pyrometry can alternately be accomplished with CIR’s monochrome High-Bit Depth Multispectral
(HiBMs) camera, equipped with a Liquid-Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF), which allows for imaging at
multiple spectra, but requires a quasi-steady flame for measurement at each desired band. This
camera has a telecentric optical system and is recorded at 512x512 and 30 frames per second
(fps). Although it has a 1024x1024 pixel array, binning has been necessary because of signal loss
through the LCTF. Both soot pyrometry and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) are possible, where
ACME is equipped with a crew -replaceable array of 5 silicon carbide (SiC) fibers. The fibers are

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.10
text:
orthogonal to the flame axis and the array can be translated along the flame axis to the desired
position downstream of the burner, e.g., based on the downlink of the analog video. During set
up, the crew can manually orient the array so that it is orthogonal to either ACME’s color digi tal
camera or the HiBMs camera with the LCTF. An alternate fiber array including a platinum wire
will be used for inflight characterization, which in combination with preflight calibration will
enable determination of the soot volume fraction [24].
In contrast to the preceding paragraph , ACME did not use a HiBMs camera for pyrometry, but
instead relied on use of ACME’s color DataCam for such temperature measurements . For an
example of how this can be done, see the techniques described in the following papers:
P.B. Kuhn, B. Ma, B.C. Connelly, M.D. Smooke, and M.B. Long, “Soot and Thin-filament Pyrometry
Using a Color Digital Camera,” Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, 33 (2011) 743-750.
B. Ma, M. B. Long, “Absolute light calibration using S -type thermocouples,” Proceedings of the
Combustion Institute, 34 (2) (2013) 3531-3539.
Thus far, TFP tests have been conducted with 14 -micron fibers spaced apart by 5 mm for a total
span of 20 mm (in the case of 5 intact ceramic fibers), neglecting optional translation of the array.

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.10
text:
Tests have been conducted using arrays with and without the platinum wire in the furthest
downstream position. Tests have also been conducted with some of the fibers broken and
subsequently removed, leaving only three fibers in the final testing for the BRE and Coflow Laminar
Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiments and at least the initial testing for the Cool Flames
Investigation with Gases (CFI-G).
CIR has a second HiBMs camera, without a filter, that will be used in combination with CIR’s
illumination package for alternate measurements of the soot volume fraction. This will be
accomplished via an extinction technique previously employed in microgravity [3,6,26], where the
camera and the collimated light source (with its two fiber-coupled laser diodes) are positioned at
opposite windows. The images are recorded at 1024x1024 and 30 fps. Thus far, the primary
purpose of this combined system has been the measurement of the droplet diameter for
determination of the droplet burning rate.

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.11
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
11
A HiBMs camera without the Liquid Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF) has been used throughout much,
but not all, of ACME’s operations. In the first round of the CLD Flame experiment, it was used
without a filter for flame imaging, but this proved to be largely unsuccessful because the camera
is very insensitive to blue. Afterward, it was equipped with a red filter corresponding to the CIR
illumination package for the rest of the ACME testing. Unfortunately, that filter is sufficiently
broad that signif icant incandescence can pass through the filter limiting its utility for
determinations of soot volume fraction via light extinction, e.g., through the technique described
in the following papers:
D.L. Urban, Z.G. Yuan, P.B. Sunderland, K.C., Lin, Z. Dai, and G.M. Faeth, “Smoke-Point Properties
of Nonbuoyant Round Laminar Jet Diffusion Flames,” Proceedings of the Twenty -Eighth
Symposium (International) on Combustion 28 (2000) 1965-1972.
F.J. Diez, C. Aalburg, P.B. Sunderland, D.L. Urban, Z. -G. Yuan, G.M. Faeth, “Soot properties of
laminar jet diffusion flames in microgravity,” Combustion and Flame, 156 (2009) 1514-1524.
P.S. Greenberg and J.C. Ku, “Soot Volume Fraction Imaging,” Applied Optics, 36 (22) (1997) 5514-
5522.
Nonetheless, soot volume fraction can also be determined from the color DataCam images.

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.11
text:
During ACME operations, the HiBMs camera is typically archived at 15 fps because of data limits
for transfer and downlink operations. And because operations are constrained by the data limits,
image data from this camera are sometimes deleted without downlinking to enable additional
testing. And in some testing, HiBMs images aren’t even acquired given their lesser value.
Unfortunately, the HiBMs backlight illumination is significantly obstructed by the bracket for the
electrode mesh further limiting its utility for the E -FIELD Flames experiment. This was a design
trade-off necessitated primarily by ACME’s large number of cameras and other optical
instruments.
CIR’s Low-Light-Level Ultraviolet (LLL -UV) package is a monochrome camera with an intensifier
(for 280-700 nm) and a 310-nm bandpass filter (with a 10-nm FWHM) for OH* imaging. Again as
a result of the signal loss through the filter, binning is employed such that the OH* images are
recorded at 512x512 and 30 fps.
During ACME operations, the LLL -UV camera has only been used for the Structure and Response
of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment.
While not discussed in the preceding section, another intensified camera was used throughout
ACME testing, although its image data was sometimes deleted or not even acquired to allow the

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.11
text:
performance of additional tests. This was the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) camera which was
generally configured with its CH* filter, where an exception is some s -Flame testing with
particularly dim flames. Due to design trade-offs, its Field of View (FOV) was partially obstructed
by the arms of the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array when it was moved inwards to the
flame. More information about this camera can be found in its characterization report, CIR-RPT-
4600.
The ACME chamber insert will also be equipped with non -imaging optical diagnostics including
both thermopile radiometers and Photomultiplier Tubes (PMTs). There is a crew -exchangeable
linear array of radiometers of which there are two versions supporting the initial set of

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.12
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
12
experiments. The array has a fixed position which is parallel to the chamber axis and centered
(along the chamber length) relative to the chamber windows and thus most of the other
instrumentation. One array is equipped with a single wide -view radiometer with two narrow -
view radiometers that are downstream and two more that are upstream, where all view s are
orthogonal to the chamber axis, as depicted in Figure 4. The narrow -view radiometers are
intended to support studies of gas -jet flames, where ACME can accommodate shorter burners,
making the “lower” detectors useful. The other array, also seen in Fig. 4, provides for three wide-
view measurements of the flame, where one view is masked to nominally block radiant emission
from the burner. It was specifically designed for the BRE experiment but will be a resource
available to other ACME experiments. Given that the radiometer array can be exchanged by the
crew, alternate arrays could be developed.
Figure 4: Crew-exchangeable radiometer arrays on the ACME chamber insert: (top) standard
(ACME) array of 5 radiometers, and (bottom) array with three radiometers, designed for the BRE
experiment, where the lowest detector is masked to avoid view of the burner.

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.13
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
13
A third radiometer array was developed for the CFI -G experiment, where it is important to
understand that only a single radiometer array can be used at a time.
The narrow-view radiometers in the standard array are only fully sensitive in small spots, but they
are each sensitive in a much greater Field of View (FOV) than represented in the preceding figure.
They do not have lenses; their FOV is a result of an aperture where most of their FOV is within the
penumbra which is only visible to a portion of the sensor. Figures representing the measured FOVs
of the as-built standard and BRE radiometer arrays are found in section 3.F of this document.
Unfortunately, the radiometers in the BRE array typically saturated in the first round of BRE
testing, so the standard array was used in its second round. However, those radiometers similarly
saturated in many of round 2 tests. In this regard, each of ACME’s BRE and standard radiometers
have a fixed gain. Meanwhile, each sensor in the radiometer array developed for the CFI -G
investigation has two fixed gains, i.e., a high gain and low gain.
For more information about the standard radiometer arr ay used for most ACME testing, see the
Radiometer Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-011). Meanwhile, you can learn about the other

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.13
text:
radiometer arrays from the BRE Radiometer Characterization Report (ACME -RPT-012) and the
Cool Flames Radiometer Characterization Report (CIR-RPT-4600).
An additional wide -view radiometer, that is fixed and not crew exchangeable, is positioned
downstream of the burner and flame at 30 o from the chamber axis. This detector is primarily
intended to support the spherical flame experiments and will have a quicker response than the
more sensitive detectors that will used in the linear arrays. Like the radiometers on the two linear
arrays, it will have a spectral range of nominally 0.2 -11 micron and its field of view will be
established by an appropriately selected aperture.
The FOV of the off-set radiometer is also shown in section 3.F. Learn more about this sensor from
the Radiometer Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-011).
To detect the quenching of dim flames, the chamber insert will be equipped with a set of three
PMTs. Each PMT will have a wide-angle view, a sight line that is orthogonal to the chamber axis,
and will be centered (along the chamber length) relative to the chamber windows so that it is
aligned with most of the other instrumentation. The PMTs’ spectral r ange will be 230 -700 nm,
i.e., visible and near ultraviolet, but one will have a 310-nm bandpass filter and another will have

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.13
text:
a 430-nm bandpass filter (where both are with a 10-nm FWHM). The pair of detectors will enable
measurement of OH* and CH* emissio n, respectively. The third PMT will be equipped with a
neutral density filter to prevent saturation. Like many other components, the PMT array can be
removed from the chamber insert by the crew.
Unlike the radiometers, each PMT had a readily adjustable gain. However, the PMT signals
sometimes saturated when the gains were set too high. See the PMT Characterization Report
(ACME-RPT-013) to learn more about the three Photomultiplier Tube (PMTs).
The chamber insert is also equipped with six far -field thermocouples to measure the spread of
the thermal field in the spherical flame experiments. They are of limited utility for other
experiments because they are positioned upstream of the burner tip. Therefore, they will

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.14
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
14
generally not be installed by the crew to reduce the chance of accidental damage. There will be
two versions of a four-thermocouple rake to allow a choice of near and far measurements. Other
arrays could be designed to support future experiments, but they cannot extend downstream of
the burner tip without interfering with other (e.g., optical) measurements.
The two lone thermocouples, which are both at nominally 200 mm from the center of the spherical
burner, have been installed throughout ACME testing. The tip of one was seen to be slightly bent
early in testing, as discussed and depicted in section 3.G of this report.
Only the short (or far) version of the radiometer rake has been used thus far, where factors include
the need for crew time to switch between rakes and the heat loss th at could result from
thermocouples in the long (close) rake. The short (far) rake’s thermocouple tips should nominally
be at 45, 60, 100, and 100 mm from the spherical burner center. For thermocouples at the same
distance from the burner center, the angl e between the rays from the burner center to the two
thermocouples should be 90 degrees. The bead size of the thermocouples was not measured, but
it is undoubtedly at least twice the size of the 0.2 mm diameter wire.

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.14
text:
The two thermocouples closest to the burner outlets on each four-thermocouple rake are type B,
while the others are type K.
Experiment-unique hardware is also mounted on the chamber insert. For example, to
accommodate the E-FIELD Flames experiment, the insert is equipped with a high -voltage supply
and a crew-removable electrode mesh which can be set between +10 and -10 kV. The circular mesh
is orthogonal to the chamber axis and is positioned (during set up) at either ~35 or ~50 mm
downstream of the insulated burner. The ion current between the burner and electrode mesh will
be determined via measurement of the voltage drop across a known resistor and application of
Ohm’s Law.
Additional images of the chamber insert can be seen in subsequent sections of this report. The
hardware specific to E-FIELD Flames is discussed further in section 2.B.
Additional supporting measurements will be made, where the chamber pressure is a simpl e
example. The ACME experiments will use the CIR’s gas chromatograph for pre - and post-test
analysis of the chamber atmosphere, e.g., for oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide,
and fuel gases. Acceleration measurements will be provided by the Space Acceleration
Measurement System (SAMS) [27], which is the primary instrument for such measurements on
ISS and previously served that role for the space shuttle.

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.14
text:
The CIR’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP) was not used for the CLD Flame or
E-FIELD Flames investigations and thus far was only sometimes used during BRE, Flame Design,
and s-Flame testing. Its use requires significant time and as such effectively reduces the number
of tests that can be conducted. However, estimates of the chamber contents were computed
assuming that the fuel in a normal flame test (for example) was either fully or not at all oxidized,
e.g., for unsustained ignition in the latter case.
The CIR facility was equipped with a 3-axis SAMS sensor head and the acceleration measurements,
along with relevant documentation, are accessible via the home page for the Principal Investigator

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.15
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
15
Microgravity Services (PIMS) , https://gipoc.grc.nasa.gov/wp/pims/home/. To be clear, the
acceleration measurements are not archived with the ACME experiment data in the Physical
Sciences Informatics (PSI) website, www.nasa.gov/PSI.
All ACME experiments will be constant volume (i.e., rather than constant pressure) studies, where
the chamber’s free volume will be about 90 liters. Burner flows will generally be constrained to
limit the pressure rise, and tests will typically be 0.5-2 minutes in duration.
The chamber’s free volume is approximately 83 liters depending on the installed hardware.
The ACME experiments will be configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. Instead, the
experiments will be commanded from the ground, specifi cally from the Telescience Support
Center (TSC) at the NASA Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, Ohio. They can be conducted in a
nominally automated mode using pre -programmed scripts. However, it will also be possible to
effectively operate the experiments in a “manual” mode, where changes can be made in response
to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. For
example, a flow rate could be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit. Step and ramp
changes can be made in the flow rate(s) or electric field potential. The TFP fiber array can be

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.15
text:
translated uniformly through a soot -free flame to get a continuum measurement of the
temperature field. In summary, ACME’s experiment control will allow for broad flexibility.
The TSC is now also referred to as the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). Thus far, the
ACME tests have always been conducted in a nominally automated mode.
B. Hardware Shortcomings
In terms of hardware, BRE’s primary challenge was that the sensors for measuring the thermal
radiation, which had fixed amplification, often saturated. Although the measurements were not
documented as required to meet experiment success, they were considered sufficiently critical
that BRE was equipped with its own radiometer array, featuring three thermopile detectors.
Estimates had been made of the signal levels based on 5 -second drop tests since the hot gases
tend to blanket the flame in the absence of buoyancy and thereby remain within the view of the
radiometers. As a result, the signal levels are strongly dependent on gravity. The estimates were
not part of the science requirements and may not have been sufficiently tracked in the hardware
development. Furthermore, the ISS tests lasted as long as 5 minutes, which is over four times the
envisioned BRE test duration and 60 times the duration of the drop tests. With the fixed

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.15
text:
amplification of the radiometer signals, the data was frequentl y lost - other than the knowledge
that the limits were exceeded. Saturation of the radiometers was partially mitigated in the round
2 testing through use of ACME’s standard array instead of the one developed specifically for BRE
which was used in the first round of testing.
The outlet surface of the 25 -mm BRE burner (used in all but two of the BRE test days) became
scratched and worn, as seen in Fig. 5(a), through ISS stowage and/or handling. This degradation
presumably occurred following its removal after the first round of testing as seen in Fig 5(b). The
scratches are not evident in Fig. 5(c) taken when the 25-mm burner was removed at the end of
its use, but the outlet surface was clearly no longer uniformly black. These changes are important
because of their effect on the absorptivity of the burner’s copper outlet plate. Note that Figs. 5(b)

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.16
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
16
and (c) were rotated to nominally correspond to Fig. 5(a), i.e., with the offset heat flux transducer
toward the image top and embedded thermocouples toward the bottom.
(a) ISS063e088291 detail, 14 Sept. 2020
(b) ISS059e017084 detail, 9 April 2019 (c) ISS064e026386 detail, 25 Jan. 2021
Figure 5. Changes in the appearance of the 25-mm BRE burner outlet

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.17
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
17
As discussed in the preceding section, the ACME DataCam is unfortunately not as sensitive as had
been hoped to the dim microgravity flames. As a result, it was often used with a long exposure
time limiting the framing rate, or a high gain amplifying noise in the image.
On 3 Sept. 2020 (20247), the first day of BRE’s second round, the gas flow didn’t always transition
as to the desired flow rate as intended. The intended igniter arm was missing (but found before
the next test day) and use of an alternate arm led to the concerns about ignition success and the
decision to ignite at the same successful flow conditions and subsequently adjust th e fuel flow
rate to the desired test value. The first attempt was successful, but the transition time was then
shortened to save fuel, but it was reduced to the degree that it unfortunately prevented the
intended flow transition. Unfortunately, this shortcoming wasn’t discovered until during a review
of the data days later. As a result, the tests on that day were generally conducted at the same
fuel flow rate, which was meant to be a variable. Therefore, a make-up test day was conducted
on 28 Jan. 2021 (21028) to address the science loss.
More generally, ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel and

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.17
text:
nitrogen have unfortunately not always performed adequately, where the flow rates have not
always been appropriately steady. Steps were made to mitigate such behavior, e.g., by zero-ing
the MFCs prior to each test, but they were not completely successful. Furthermore, when an MFC
is used at a small fraction of its maximum flow rate, the actual flow rate sometimes diffe rs from
that desired.
During testing on 23 Dec. 2020 (20358), it was discovered that the lowest of the 14-micron silicon
carbide fibers on the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array had broken. After some
discussion, testing continued that day. Given that the translating array had five ceramic fibers,
the loss of one was not a significant science loss. But it was a concern for crew safety. Recovery
plans were developed and enacted on January 18 to remove the broken fragments from the harp-
like array. Unfortunately, the next fiber was broken during the deli cate operations where the
fibers are only spaced 5 mm apart. As a result, the last two BRE test days were conducted with
only three rather than five fibers in the TFP array. ACME does have alternate fiber arrays, but
there were months of testing remaining and the decision was made to continue testing with only
3 fibers.
Ignition was not always successful. As an extreme example, it was discovered on 1 April 2019

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.17
text:
(19091) that the hot-wire igniter tip had failed on the preceding test day, preventing further flame
testing until it could be replaced. While such circumstances are uncommon for ACME operations,
BRE tests were sometimes conducted under conditions, e.g., for igniter activation and
deactivation, which led to momentary flashes without sustained ign ition. Given that unplanned
crew time is required to replace failed igniter tips, the BRE ops team limited - to varying degrees
- the igniter voltage and the time that it was energized within the flame. The latter was known
from earlier research in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) to degrade the hot-wire igniter tip
and hasten its demise. It is notable that the flashes of flame (across the burner surface)
sometimes continued briefly after the igniter was deactivated and retracted. In one case on the
first day of testing, there was excess fuel and a ‘fireball’ was ignited which promptly quenched.
Ignition also sometimes failed due to a software limitation where the fuelFlowIgnitionDeltaMs
parameter which specifies the relative timing of the fuel flow and igniter activation must be evenly
divisible by 100 (ms). This limitation wasn’t initially understood and the igniter sometimes didn’t
energize as a result.

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.18
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
18
While it rarely occurred, BRE tests sometimes automatically aborted (due to the controlling
software script), where that is typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter. As a
result, there is little lost other than the time associated with the failed test attempt. Such aborts
typically occur because of communication issues with an Image Processing and Storage Unit
(IPSU).
In addition to this section (3), shortcomings are discussed in Appendices B to E of this report and
the ACME Engineering Implementation document.
4. Preliminary Results
The burner has shown that quasi-steady burning is possible for real solids with a flat surface of 25 mm
diameter. Up to now most flammability studies in microgravity have focused on flame spread with a
wind for concurrent spread and at least a self -induced wind for opposed flow sp read. We already
knew that this would be possible from normal-gravity research. The burning of liquids, as in a wick of
a candle flame and small droplets, has been shown to produce steady flames. However, many droplet
flames were found to extinguish owi ng to radiative cooling of the flame. We see this as well in the
extended ISS microgravity tests. However, this extinction was predominately seen for nominal
ambient conditions of 21% oxygen and 14.7 psia. At conditions of 27% oxygen, 10.2 psia and 34%

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.18
text:
oxygen, 8.2 psia, the flames generally persisted for 3 minutes or more. These are all atmospheric
conditions that NASA is considering for future spacecraft.
A. Changed Test Plans
While BRE’s proposal included desired testing with carbon-dioxide-diluted atmospheres, NASA’s
plan for the ISS investigation did not include desired testing. Therefore, the exclusion of that
testing was not a change in plans.
The most significant change was the use of ACME’s standard radiometer array rather than the
BRE radiometer array in BRE’s second round of testing. This change was made because the BRE
array was found to generally saturate during the ISS tests. The ACME array had a greater range
but nonetheless still often saturated during testing.
Significant changes were made to the ignition procedure in the early first -round testing, both
relative to the preceding ACME experiments and in the first few days of BRE testing . Compared
to the other ACME burners (neglecting the outer plenum of the coflow burner), the BRE burners
have a much greater internal volume. Therefore, the fuel flow was begun before the igniter was
energized, where that period ranged from a few seconds to roughly 1 minute. The duration was
typically about 15 and 30 seconds for the 25- and 50-mm BRE burners, respectively. In contrast,
the fuel flow has commonly been started when the igniter is energized in the other ACME

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.18
text:
investigations.
Despite the duration of fuel flow prior to igniter activation, there was concern about
understanding the composition of the gas initially flowing from the burner. Therefore, on the
second BRE test day (20 Feb. 2019, i.e., 19051), a no -flame ‘test’ was run before each flame test
in which the burner was flushed with nitrogen at 0.15 slpm for 15 seconds. A shortcoming of this
measure was that the time between the nitrogen flushing and the start of the fuel flow was not

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.19
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
19
precisely controlled. Therefore, the software script used to run the BRE tests was subsequently
altered to allow specification of a ‘pre-flow’ with a specified wait time between the pre-flow and
the start of the gas flow for the flame. Although the script allowed for a pre -flow of nitrogen
and/or fuel, only nitrogen was used for the pre-flow during BRE’s ISS testing. The revised script
was implemented on BRE’s third test day (25 Feb. 2019, 19056) where a nitrogen flow rate of 0.15
slpm for 15 seconds continued to be used throughout the remainder of the first round.
A wait time of 2 minutes was used in the first two 19056 tests, while a 1 -minute wait was used
for the remainder of testing on that day. During the remaining round -one test days, the wait
duration was consistently 50 seconds. With the script change, the basic non -imaging data file
captured the data during both the pre-flow and in the flame test, but it is important to understand
that data was not acquired throughout the wait duration. Therefore, one should pay close
attention to the time stamp when reviewing BRE data prior to the start of the fuel flow because
the listed time abruptly jumps.
Although the script wasn’t significantly modified, there were changes to the ignition procedure in

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.19
text:
the second round of BRE tests. It was concluded that the nitrogen pre-flow wasn’t needed for the
first test of the day or the first test after the chamber was evacuated and refilled. The wait time
between the pre-flow and the start of the fuel flow was also increased to 5 minutes throughout
the second round, whereas it was 50 seconds in most of the first -round tests. This was done to
ensure that the atmosphere in the chamber was quiescent prior to the start of the fuel flow. Pre-
flow durations and flow rates were also somewhat different. In the tests o n the first round-two
test day (202 47), which featured the 50 -mm burner, the pre -flow was a t ~0.5 slpm for 5 or 10
seconds. On the two subsequent test days (20261 and 20279), the pre-flow was at 0.19 slpm for
3.2 seconds. For the remaining test days (20339, 20346, 20352, 20358, 21020, and 21028) , the
pre-flow was instead 0.16 slpm for 5 second s, where that includes the final test day which also
featured the 50 -mm burner. As such, the pre -flow differed significantly between the two test
days with the larger BRE burner.
A few minor changes were made to the script after the addition of the pre -flow to flush the
burner’s internal volume:
~2020-03-17 flow ramp hold was fixed so that the hold values were achieved exactly
~2020-12-18 ignition detection was disabled prior to igniter arm retraction so that the

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.19
text:
retraction wasn’t interrupted
The first change was implemented between the first and second rounds of testing , while the
second was made during the second round. The final version of the script will be included in the
upcoming ACME/BRE Experimental Procedure document.
While a minor f actor, BRE made use of the coiled type of igniter tip in second -round testing as
compared to the standard loop -type igniter used in the first round. BRE ignition seemed to
require significant ignition energy and the coiled igniter design is believed to be more robust. The
coiled igniter tip was developed as an alternate after ignition challenges with the Coflow Laminar
Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment in late 2017. The development of the coiled igniter tips
continued even though it was later determ ined that the igniter had not been properly aligned
with the burner outlet in the early CLD Flame testing. The two igniter designs are discussed and
depicted in the ACME Engineering Implementation document.
In contrast to BRE’s success criteria (discussed in section 2.D), which identified the importance of

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.20
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
20
measuring the flame temperature, BRE’s first round testing seldom made use of Thin Filament
Pyrometry (TFP). In contrast, TFP data was acquired in a significant fraction of the second-round
testing. In this regard, TFP use was important because the BRE flames quickly became non-sooty
even with oxygen concentrations of up to 40% (by volume) so measurements couldn’t be made
via soot pyrometry.
Tests were conducted as planned at atmospheres bein g considered for future spacecraft,
featuring elevated oxygen concentrations and reduced pressures (nominally maintaining the
oxygen partial pressure), but more of the testing was conducted at roughly atmospheric pressure
with elevated oxygen concentrations. The latter tests were carried out in a broader exploration
of material flammability in microgravity.
B. Overview of Experiment Test Operations
While not yet prepared, additional details will be made available in the ACME/BRE Experimental
Procedure document.
The narrative description of the experimental procedure is an excerpt from the ‘Methods /
Experimental’ section of the following conference paper.
Y.-C. Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Stocker, U. Hegde, and D. Dunn -Rankin, “Electric Field Effects on
Flames in Microgravity on the International Space Station,” 2018 Spring Technical Meeting of

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.20
text:
the Central States Section of The Combustion Institute, Minneapolis, MN, 20-22 May 2018.
While the paper was written for the Electric -Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E -FIELD
Flames) experiment, much of the discussion applies to ACME in general, including the BRE
investigation. The figure referenced in this excerpt is not included h erein. Clarifications and
additional information, not in the conference paper, are included in boxed notes like this.
The CIR experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. Thus far, ACME’s activity
has included the majority of the crew members, regardless of their nationalities. Most often the
astronauts and cosmonauts exchange gas bottles, mass flow controllers, and igniter tips. In the
latter case, the igniter tip exchange can occur after failure or proactively before failure when the
crew already has changes to make changes in the interior of the insert. While these activities may
seem mundane, the crew play a critical role in setting up the hardware for each experiment. As
an extreme example, there were crew activities on 8 separate days in Sept.-Oct. 2017 to configure
the CIR and ACME hardware for the first ACME experiment, namely the Coflow Laminar Diffusion
Flame (CLD Flame) experiment. In contrast, only two crew days were required to reconfigure the

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.20
text:
hardware for the first E-FIELD Flames tests because of the initial use of the same coflow burner.
Planning is critical because crew activity is scheduled three weeks in advance, for which detailed
procedures must be prepared and uplinked to the ISS.
BRE has its own unique burners and it was the first ACME experiment conducted with large flames,
as compared to those in the CLD Flame and E-FIELD Flames investigations. That required changes
to some optical elements for BRE as well as subsequent ACME experiments. BRE was also the first
experiment to use the CIR facility’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP). As a
result, the initial BRE set-up included 9 days of crew activity, mostly by Canadian astronaut David
Saint-Jacques, although that includes 4 days in which hardware was either gathered or stowed.

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.21
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
21
All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations
Center (GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio. Typically , four to six people staff four consoles during the
testing. The CIR hardware is controlled from the Rack Officer (RO) and Data Management Officer
(DMO) consoles, and the ACME hardware is controlled from the Payload Developer (PD) console.
Two shifts of personnel are scheduled to staff these three consoles on test days because they
typically last 14 hours with the many pre - and post-testing activities. Given that the tests are
remotely commanded, the operations are carried out in the day and evening in Cleveland, e.g.,
from 7 AM to 9 PM. A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are normally conducted in a period of 10 hours
of less. Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per two weeks. On intervening
weekdays, the image data is downlinked and the crew often swap one or both gas bottles.
Transferring and downlinking data from a da y’s tests also requires a 2 -shift day for the RO and
DMO consoles, where it is always necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors
and that data is not missing. Those two positions are also staffed to guide and oversee the crew
activity. As a result, the CIR consoles are normally actively staffed on four weekdays per week. A

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.21
text:
team of four carry out the detailed planning for the CIR and ACME console staff, and the daily
operational plans typically exceed 50 pages on days including testing.
The science console allows for review of the analog video and non-imaging telemetry (at 1 Hz) in
near real time but doesn’t allow for commanding. In the case of E -FIELD Flames, arrangements
were made so that the analog video is streamed to a secure comput er at UC Irvine to allow the
research team to participate in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s
planned parameters. That team does not see the telemetry during the testing, but is in
communication via phone and e -mail with their NAS A research partners at the GRC ISS Payload
Operations Center (GIPOC). While there are many preparatory steps, the tests are ultimately
conducted using an uploaded software script and parameter files. In advance of the test day, the
UC Irvine science team plans the nearly 60 parameters in the voltage sweep script and specifies
other parameters that are configured outside of the script, such as camera settings. It is also
possible to effectively conduct tests in a ‘manual’ mode, where parameters are change d in
response to the analog video downlink or telemetry. For example, the electric field potential can
be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit.

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.21
text:
Provisions have been made to enable the investigators from all ACME experiments to remotely
view the analog video while they communicated verbally with NASA science personnel in the
operations center. Thus far, all ACME flame tests, including those for BRE, have been conducted
in an automated manner using software scripts and extensive parameter files.
Typically, ten E-FIELD Flames tests are conducted per test day. Despite the short test durations,
the low rate results from several unavoidable factors. After a test is conducted, the 125-Hz non-
imaging data is downlinked for immediate review by the science team. A small sample of images
are often downlinked to ensure that the camera exposures are appropriate, where the times for
those images are typically selected based on non-imaging data to provide extreme examples. The
review helps to verify parameters or plan for adjustments in subsequent tests, e.g., to select the
voltage range after determining where the ion current saturates for the given flame conditions.
After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber atmosphere after which the chamber is
vented (to space) back to atmospheric pressure, if needed. Midway through a day’s E -FIELD
Flames tests, the atmosphere is circulated for 15 minutes through a filter cartridge filled with

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.21
text:
molecular sieves to capture any soot and adsorb at least a porti on of the combustion products,
e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products. The tests are only

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.22
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
22
conducted when both Ku and S band communication is available through NASA’s Tracking and
Data Relay Satellite (TDRS) System. Dependin g on the various orbits, there are periodic
communication outages with a loss of signal (LOS) that can be a short handover (from one satellite
to another) or can last as long as 30 minutes.
About eight flames were ignited per test day in BRE’s first round, neglecting the day in which no
tests were conducted because the igniter had unknowingly failed at the end of the preceding test
day. The nominal durations were typically planned for 2 or 3 minutes but some tests were 5
minutes long. Meanwhile the secon d round of BRE had roughly 15 tests conducted per day, but
the durations were nominally 2 minutes at most.
Unlike E -FIELD Flames, the BRE experiment also made use of the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph
Instrumentational Package (GCIP) to measure species concentrations of the atmosphere in the
combustion chamber. There is no sampling probe and measurements are only made before,
between, or after tests when the chamber atmosphere was ‘stirred’ through use of a fan. The GC
measurements were made on roughly 60% of the test days with flames in the first round,
specifically on 19039, 19063, 19066, 19070, 19087, and 19094. In the second round, such data

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.22
text:
was acquired on less than half of the test days, specifically on 20247, 20261, 20279, and 20352.
Like E -FIELD Flames, BRE made periodic use of the adsorber cartridge, for example between
atmospheres and after GC measurements, if any, were made.
A variety of constraints limit the number of tests that can be performed, both overall and on a
daily basis. The next combustion experiments in the CIR will feature solid fuels and focus on flame
spread and material flammability. That follow -on plan limits the duration of ACME operations,
where each ACME experiment is allotted four months for testing. Although it requires additional
crew time, these allotments are split into two rounds so that the investigators have a break from
testing for careful review of the early results so that they can maximize the scientific outcome of
their second round. This paper reports on early results from the first round of E-FIELD Flames.
While nitrogen is available from the space station, the combustion testing is limit ed by the
available gas bottles that were and are launched to support the tests. For E -FIELD Flames and
most of ACME’s experiments, the test matrices used to plan those gas resources were established
in 2010. At that time, NASA limited the scope of the A CME tests matrices with the intent of
focused experiments with limited objectives rather than comprehensive experiments. As such,

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.22
text:
the general target was 50 tests per experiment. For most ACME experiments, the limiting gas
constraint is the oxygen/nitroge n bottles used to fill the chamber. This resource constraint is
exacerbated by the CIR because it is equipped with a pair of redundant safety timers to limit the
fuel that can flow into the combustion chamber (where the timers can be set for the oxidizer flow
in the case of inverse flame testing). The timers can only be reset by venting the combustion
chamber. Therefore, the timer limit combined with other constraints effectively corresponds to
the day’s maximum flow time for the fuel (or more generally, the limiting reactant). For E-FIELD
Flames, the safety timers are set to the maximum value of 999 seconds, which corresponds to the
10 tests typically completed per day.
The 999-second limit on the valve safety timers has thus far been common for all ACME testing.
However, the timers can be reset to 999 by nearly completely venting the chamber. Sufficient time

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: Final_20220201, p.23
text:
ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
23
and gas resources are needed to vent and refill the chamber and still conduct tests afterward, but
this was done on most BRE test days. The only exceptions were 19039, 19063, and 19091 where
in the last case no flames were ignited because the igniter had unknowingly failed at the end of
the prior test day.
Another constraint is the available time in a day, where the console personnel and ISS resources,
such as the video downlink, are planned for a limited number of hours. When necessary for the
research, NASA does have continuous 24 -hour/day operations for some non -CIR experiments.
But as discussed, the ACME tests are typically two minutes or less in duration, so the testing is
almost always limited to the planned durations.
Data limits are yet another constraint, where the on -orbit hardware can store a limited amount
of data. More importantly, 127,000 MB is the most that can be reasonably m anaged in a two -
shift transfer and downlink day. Therefore, tests days are limited to this amount of data, where
image data from select cameras is often archived at reduced rates to mitigate this challenge.
Nonetheless, the limit sometimes forces decisions to abandon recorded images.
This detailed description of operations and hardware provides the context under which the ACME
experiments are conducted. …

Abstract: From late 2017 to early 2022, six independent studies with flames of gaseous fuels were
conducted on the International Space Station (ISS) in the U.S. combustion research facility . An
exploration of flames at the extremes of high sooting and high dilution was conducted with a coaxial
coflow burner, where the fuel and oxidizer velocities were typically matched. An investigation of
electric-field effects also used the same coflow burner as well as a simple gas -jet burner, with a
circular electrode mesh, downstream of the burner, at voltages of either polarity up to 10 kV. A
study focused on material flammability in a quiescent atmosphere emulated th e burning of
condensed-phased fuels using cylindrical burners with a flat perforated outlet instrumented to
measure the heat flux to the burner, i.e., emulated fuel. Three studies of soot processes, flame
dynamics, and low -temperature combustion used poro us spherical burners, yielding a nominally

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: ACME CSSCI paper 20220402, p.1

Keywords: flames, microgravity, non-premixed, laminar
1. Introduction
Microgravity, i.e., apparent near weightlessness, is a unique environment for conducting
combustion research. Many flames are dramatically influenced by the near elimination of buoyant
convection, where the resulting effects are often advantageous [1-2]. For example, it is possible
to create spherically symmetric flames enabling one -dimensional analysis. More generally, the
effective elimination of flicker yields quasi -steady flames. Furthermore, the length scales are
increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of their structure. Microgravity flames tend
to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere than normal-gravity flames and exhibit a
much broader range of characteristics. For example, the long residence times in microgravity
flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free due to
radiative heat loss. Even neglec ting soot, microgravity flames can be appropriate for studies of
limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. It is also possible to study

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: ACME CSSCI paper 20220402, p.1
text:
momentum-dominated flames at low velocities. And of course, microgravity is the appropriate
environment for studies related to spacecraft fire safety.
Although microgravity combustion research has long been conducted in drop facilities and
research aircraft flying parabolic maneuvers, spacecraft like the International Space Station (ISS)
offer significant advantages. Drop durations, which are ~5 s or le ss in NASA drop facilities, are
too short for soot to achieve quasi -steady conditions. They are also too short to first establish a
flame and then vary conditions such as the flow rate, for example, to investigate stability or
extinction limits. Meanwhile, low-momentum flames can be dramatically disturbed by the g-jitter

present in aircraft testing, which is nominally ±0.02 g for a ~20 s duration. The jitter can be
avoided by floating an experiment within the aircraft, but that reduces the test duration to mere
seconds. As a result, space -based testing is often necessary to get microgravity conditions of
sufficient duration and quality for combustion research.
The recent research was preceded by two earlier studies with laminar non-premixed flames of
gaseous fuels conducted in the ISS’ Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) using a crew-operated
coflow apparatus consisting of a gas-jet burner centered within a fan -driven flow duct. On-orbit
tests for the Soot Processes In Coflow Experiment (SPICE) of David L. Urban and Peter B.
Sunderland were conducted in 2009 and 2012 [ 3]. ISS t esting for the Structure & Liftoff In
Combustion Experiment (SLICE) of Marshall B. Long, Mitchell D. Smooke, Fumiaki Takahashi,
and Dennis P. Stocker was carried out in 2012 [4-7]. This pair of studies were in turn preceded by
three investigations with non -premixed flames of gaseous fuels co nducted during space shuttle
missions in 1997 and 2003 [8-16]. The flames were similarly laminar, although one study featured
mechanically induced vortices.
Tests for six independent experiments with flames of gaseous fuels were conducted on the ISS

name: ACME BRE
title: ACME BRE: ACME CSSCI paper 20220402, p.2
text:
from Nov. 2017 to Feb. 2022 as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments
(ACME) project [2]. On-orbit preparations began in Sept. 2017, neglecting SLICE which was a
planned precursor to ACME’s Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) inves tigation.
Table 1 provides an overview of each study, where the first investigator listed is the Principal
Investigator. Additional information, including preliminary findings, about each of the six
experiments will be presented after a description of the experimental hardware and operations.
The ACME experiments are primarily focused on energy and environmental concerns, but
there is a secondary emphasis with the Burning Rate Emulator ( BRE) experiment on spacecraft
fire prevention. The primary objective is to gain fundamental understanding that can enable
improved efficiency and reduced emissions in practical combustion processes on Earth, for
example through the development and verification of models for chemical kinetics and transport
processes in computational simulations. In addition to enhanced performance, improved modeling
capability can lead to reductions in the time and cost for combustor design. Some specific goals
are to improve our understanding of combustion at fuel lean conditions where bo th optimum
performance and low emissions can be achieved, cool flame chemistry, flame stability and

name: ACME BRE

extinction limits, materials flammability, oxygen -enriched combustion which could enable
practical carbon sequestration, soot control and reduction, and the use of electric fields for
combustion control.
2. Methods / Experimental
The ACME research was conducted using a single modular set of hardware with the Combustion
Integrated Rack (CIR) [2]. That facility is shown on the left in Figure 1 with NASA astronaut
Kate Rubins reconfiguring hardware for a different investigation on 3 Feb. 2021 . The CIR
provides a nominally 100-liter combustion chamber, gas delivery, venting, water cooling, imaging,
and other general functions needed to carry out an array of combustion research. The facility was
launched in 2008 and then used from 2009 to 2017 for a set of investigations featuring the
combustion of liquid droplets. That research notably led to the discovery of non -premixed cool
flames [17-22] which inspired ACME’s Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G).
ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a
variety of burners (but only one at a time) on the chamber axis. Tests were conducted with gas-

(BRE) investigation. The resistively heated igniter has a crew -exchangeable tip and arm ( to
accommodate the various burners) and its stepper-motor drive allowed for precise positioning and
retraction from the flame.
The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers, visible on the left of Fig. 2, for the
delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium), and nitrogen to either the burner or the chamber.
The crew exchange d the mass flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges to improve flow
control and accuracy. The gas delivery system enable d on-orbit dilution of the fuel or oxidizer
(but not both simultaneously), coflow, and inverse flames, where the oxidizer issue d from the
burner into the chamber filled with a gaseous fuel. Gases were also delivered premixed to the
space station where that was necessary in some circumstances, such as the blending of different
gaseous fuels. ACME tests were most often conducted with methane and ethylene where other
fuels included hydrogen, ethane, propane, n -butane, and hydrogen/methane mixtures. Nitrogen
dilution was common, but tests for the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s -
Flame) study were also conducted with helium as the inert in both the fuel and oxidizer.

The chamber insert provide d an assortment of non -imaging instrumentation such as a crew -
exchangeable array of thermopile detectors to measure thermal radiation. There is al so a set of
PhotoMultiplier Tubes (PMTs) which provided measurements of chemiluminescent emissions
from the excited -state species CH* and OH* as well as a broadband measurement. A crew -
exchangeable thermocouple rake, intended for studies of spherical flames, can be installed. While
not shown in Fig. 2, the chamber insert is also equipped with a translating, crew -exchangeable
array of 14-micron silicon carbide fibers for making measurements of flame temperature via Thin
Filament Pyrometry (TFP) [e.g., 23-25,31-34].
Figure 2: ACME chamber insert used within the CIR facility
Five different cameras and two illumination systems were used in the recent research, although
usually only a fraction of th em were used because of operational constraints. There is an analog

camera mounted on the chamber insert f rom which color video was always downlinked in near
real time during testing. Th e other four cameras were mounted around the periphery of the
combustion chamber. A high-definition color camera, carefully characterized prior to launch, was
always used. Both provide flame imaging, but the high-definition camera can furthermore be used
to optically determine the CH* concentration, flame or soot temperature (via pyrometry), and soot
volume fraction [e.g., 23-25]. The latter can also be determined using a gray -scale camera with
an opposed collimated light source via a light extinct ion technique [36-37]. Two intensified
cameras were used, one filtered for OH* emissions, while the other allows for imaging of CH* or
alternately CH2O* emissions associated with cool flame chemistry.
All ACME experiments are constant volume (rather than constant pressure) studies, where the
chamber’s free volume is approximately 83 liters depending on the installed hardware. The tests
were typically only a few minutes in duration, limiting the pressur e rise, vitiation of the chamber
atmosphere, and acquisition of data which was an operational constraint.
The ACME experiments were configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. Instead, the
tests were commanded from the ground, specifically from the NAS A Glenn Research Center in

name: ACME BRE
