testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy
Project Scientist. For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team includes Drs. Uday G. Hegde
and Vedha Nayagam who are also with CWRU.
The experiment had two Co-Investigators, the first of which was Prof. Felix Weinberg of London’s Imperial
College. Prof. Weinberg was a pioneer in researching the effects of electrical fields on flames in
microgravity, but unfortunately died in 2012 (see http://www.imperial.ac.uk/news/117808/tribute-felix-
weinberg/) before the hardware was built and the tests w ere conducted on the ISS. The second Co -
Investigator was Dr. Sunny Karnani who did his doctoral research in preparation of the spaceflight
experiment and afterward worked for ClearSign Combustion Corp., which marke ts Electrodynamic
Combustion Control (https://www.clearsign.com/technology/electrodynamic-combustion-control/). The
corporation provided some support to the E -FIELD Flames research effort, but Karnani left Cl earSign to
conduct research for the U.S. Army, effectively ending his intimate role in the project prior to the

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Data Interpretation 2 Oct. 2020
4
3. Tests Conducted
This text is an excerpt from the “Results” section of the ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation
Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 (which is included in the ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final
Report).
A total of 219 flames were ignited for the E -FIELD Flames experiment, with 142 and 77
respectively ignited during Increments 55-56 and 57-58. Note that the investigation’s testing was
completed during Increment 57, so no flames were ignited during Increment 58. The first and
second rounds of testing respectively occurred in March -May 2018 and September -November
2018. The two rounds of tests resulted in 120 and 99 ignited flames conducted with coflow and
gas-jet burners, respectively. The coflow burner was developed for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion
Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, where CLD Flames’ second round occurred between the two
rounds of the E-FIELD Flames experiment. The ‘interruption’ in the E -FIELD Flames testing was
intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail
and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome.
E-FIELD Flames does not have living subjects lik e a life science experiment, but the tests are
independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene. Both are
source: data/raw/PSI-22/Science Documents/PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf#page=4

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document, p.4
text:
simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry i s well understood. Methane (CH4) is the
primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the absence of
carbon-carbon bonds. Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting because of its carbon
double bond. For both fuels, t ests were conducted with pure fuel and fuel mixed with nitrogen
over a broad range of dilutions. For limited cases, the fuel and nitrogen was premixed on the
ground prior to launch. ACME bottles were launched with methane concentrations of 30%, 40%,
45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis). Similarly, bottles were launched
with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 50%, and 100%, again with a balance of nitrogen (on a
volume basis). But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to
the burner, allowing for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations.
In all cases, the coflow was 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).
No samples (e.g., of soot) were collected f or E -FIELD Flames; all of the ISS results were
electronically transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all currently planned
ACME experiments.
source: data/raw/PSI-22/Science Documents/PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf#page=4

4. Data Interpretation
This key section provides (1) a general description of the raw experimental data and associated files and
(2) guidance on data conversions, e.g., to engineering units . Only limited guidance is provided for the
processing of image data, with the important exception of the conversion of the ACME DataCam images
from the raw Halcon object (HOBJ) format.
A. Non-Imaging Data
Data and files discussed in this section include the following:
Data Output File
Mass Flow Controller (MFC) Setpoint File
Fuel Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA) data
Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) data
Some ACME experiments featured measurements made with the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph
Instrumentation Package (GCIP), but it was not used for the E-FIELD Flames experiment and a such
that data type is not addressed in this document.
1. Data Output File
The basic ACME non-imaging measurements for each test are together in a file described in
Section 8.1 Data Output File on page 124 of Software Interface Design Description ( ACME-
DOC-010 Rev D). The test number is made up of the year (2-digts), day of year (3 digits), and
test (a letter and single-digit number). As such, the example, 18073A3 is test A3 conducted
on the 73rd day of 2018. But the test could also be early on the next (e.g., 74th) day because
source: data/raw/PSI-22/Science Documents/PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf#page=6

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document, p.6
text:
the day portion of ACME test numbers is not ch anged when operations continue past
midnight (whether GMT or Eastern) into the start of the next day.
Tests numbers that only differ by the final digit (e.g., 18073A1, 18073A2, and 18073A3) are
normally similar and occasionally identical, where the number is indicative of the variant or
repeat. Letters I and O are not used because of their similarity to 1 and 0. While initially used
in ACME testing, the letter E ceased to be used because Excel software (for example) by
default interpreted it as represent ing an exponential which was inconvenient. As a related
aside, ACME tests are often not conducted in order and some planned tests are regularly not
conducted at all. The latter results in additional letter gaps if the tests from a day are sorted
alphabetically. However, ACME testing often begins with test A1, where the final digit begins
with 1 and is increased from there with variant or repeat tests for the same letter.
The basic data is in a CSV format, i.e., with comma-separated values, which can be opened by
spreadsheet software such as Microsoft Excel. The first row is a header and provides a limited
summary of the hardware and operational conditions. The header is explained in Section 10.1
Metadata Header of ACME-DOC-010 Rev D, which begins on page 126.
source: data/raw/PSI-22/Science Documents/PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf#page=6

Additional conversion is required for the measurements of the gas flow rates found in second
through fourth columns of the data file. By column (e.g., in Excel), the flow rates are for:
B MFCA1StaticMixerFlow oxidizer (or inert) gas
C MFCA2BypassFlow nitrogen
D MFCA3FuelFlow fuel
The ACME MFCs are Hastings HFC -D-302 with default standard temperature and pressures
(STP) of 0 Celsius and 760 torr for computations of volume tric flow or velocity. It is very
important to understand that slpm, i.e., standard liters per minute, is a measurement of the
mass (or alternatively molar) flow rate wh ich is independent of the actual temperature or
pressure. This is discussed for examp le in the MFC manual, where chapter 9 (on page 39) is
“Volumetric vs. Mass Flow.”
Conversions for the actual gases can be made with information provided in the manual on
subsequent pages and the spreadsheets GasDataTables.xls and Inside gas mix calculator .xls
which were both provided by the MFC manufacturer. First, open GasDataTable s.xls and
enable content, and then open Inside gas mix calculator.xls and enable content. From this,
one should be able to enter mixtures and compute appropriate Gas Conversio n Factors
(GCFs).
Alternatively, the conversions above can be made with spreadsheets prepared by the ACME
source: data/raw/PSI-22/Science Documents/PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf#page=8

text:
engineering team, where options include the following:
ACMEFlowCalculator.xlsx
ACMEFlowAndPressuresRawDataConversion.xlsx
Computation of gas veloci ties, for example for the gas -jet and coflow burners, depends on
burner dimensions. For the coflow burner, ACME mechanical design engineer Adrian Drake
indicated the following:
“The inner diameter of the inner tube is .085 inches. Its cross sectional area is .00567
in^2, or 3.66 x 10^-6 m^2.
The flow of the outer tube is a little tricky to calculate, based on where and how you
measure. There’s an internal step in the outer tube that can’t be seen from outside, and
blocks the flow to the outer honeycombs. Because of this, when we calculated the cross-
sectional are of the outer tube, it measures from the inner step.
The outer tube’s outer diameter at that step is 0.984 inches. Its cross section area at that
diameter is .7605 in^2. From this we have to subtract the inner tube’s outer
diameter: .095 inch diameter, so area is .00709. Subtract from the Outer Diameter and
we get .7534 in^2, or .000486 m^2.”
source: data/raw/PSI-22/Science Documents/PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf#page=8

file is briefly discussed in section 8.2 Mass Flow Controller Setpoint File on page 124 of ACME-
DOC-010 Rev D.

3. Fuel Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA) data
Relevant pressure, temperature, etc. data from the CIR is not found in the data output file
discussed in section 4.A.1 of this document. Instead, it is found in 1-Hz files with names such
as 18073A3_ACME_CAM3_Exposures.txt which are again in a comma-separated values (CSV)
format despite the misleading txt suffix. As such, these files can be opened with standard
spreadsheet software.
Columns A and B (e.g., in Excel) both include timestamps, which can slightly differ (e.g., by a
second), where column A is from the Image Processing and Storage Unit for Gigabit ethernet
cameras (IPSU-G, which is also referred to as IPSU -5). The IPSU -G was used to record the
image data from the ACME Data Camera (DataCam) and the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI)
intensified camera. Meanwhile, column B provides timestamps for the CIR’s FOMA Control
Unit (FCU), where the FOMA is the Fuel Oxizidizer Management Assembly. The headings for
the first two columns are therefore:
IPSU5 TimeStamp FCU TimeStamp
Columns C-W have data from the IPSUG, of which the most significant is column T , named
IPSUG_CAMERA_3_MAN_EXP(N/A). That column provides the ACME DataCam exposure
time in microseconds and is the source of the file name. The headings for these columns are

4. Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) data
The Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) in which the experiment was conducted, was equipped
with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS), but it was not utilized for ACME testing because
of the need for crew time to enable and disable the isolation (by respectively removing and
installing alignment guides) on each test day. However, the CIR was equipped with a 3 -axis
SAMS sensor head. The acceleration archives, along with relevant documentation, are
accessible from https://gipoc.grc.nasa.gov/wp/pims/home/, the home page for the Principal
Investigator Microgravity Services (PIMS).
The following guidance for the SAMS data was provided by Kenneth Hrovat (NASA Glenn): In

combustion chamber and is sometimes referred to as the internal camera. Its primary

The NTSC video (named for the National Television System Committee) from the ops camera
is at 29.97 frames per second (fps) or nominally 30 fps. It is not recorded on the space station
but is streamed to the ground in near real time and is recorded on CIR consoles at the Glenn
ISS Payload Operations Center ( GIPOC) in a Transport Stream (TS) format using VLC Media
Player which can be freely downloaded from https://www.videolan.org/vlc/. That software
has a snapshot function allowing for convenient extraction of still images, e.g., for making
measurements of flame dimensions.
2. ACME Data Camera (DataCam)
ACME’s prim ary camera is a high-definition (1360 x 1024), 12 -bit color camera mounted
outside the chamber on CIR’s optical bench. It is equipped with a motorized lens with
independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus. It has a filter barrel with a fused silica
window (for color imaging), a blue -green BG7 Schott glass filter, and bandpass filters for
imaging CH* and HCHO (formaldehyde) chemiluminescence.
It was characterized prior to launch to enable temperature measurements via soot pyrometry
and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP), soot volume fraction, and quantitative determination of
the CH* concentration.

Images are normally downlinked within a week of the testing, but selected images are often
downlinked during a test day. Regardless, the images are downloaded in a wrapped Halcon
object (HOBJ) format, which are not readily opened with typical image processing software.
Most ACME investigators are processing the HOBJ files using the OMA2 software developed
by Prof. Marshall Long (Yale U.), the lead for ACME’s CLD Flame experiment. Th e OMA2
software is freely available in both Mac and cross-platform (Qt) versions, where the latter can
be used with both PC and Linux operating systems.
The OMA2 read-hobj function was also rewritten as a Python function by Dr. Jesse Tinajero
(Yale U.), where Python is an open source programming language that is easily obtainable for
MacOS, Linux, and Windows operating systems. The Python script to open the HOBJ files can
be downloaded from https://github.com/mblong/hobjExample.

15
The HOBJ files can also be readily viewed and processed using ImageJ or its preloaded Fiji
variant, where both can be freely downloaded. In either software package, the HOBJ files can
imported (rather than opened) as raw files with the following settings:
Image type 16-bit unsigned
Width 1360
Height 1024
Offset to first image 6244
However, imported DataCam image s will be monochrome unless a Bayer filter (e.g., as
described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayer_filter) i s subsequently implemented. It
should be possible to install a plug-in to accomplish that color conversion. As another option,
Python and Matlab both have image demosaicing functions.
NASA is also working (at the time of this writing) toward providing converted images from the
ACME DataCam, where the general priority is to support the ongoing ACME testing rather
than covert images for experiments like E-FIELD Flames which have already been completed.
In order to use the ACME DataCam for quantitative measurements it is critical to avoid
saturation, for example by using a camera gain of zero. Another employed approach was to
not use the camera’s white balance which by default multiplies the red and blue by 1.41 and
1.68, respectively, because that could inadvertently lead to saturation. Such multiplication
source: data/raw/PSI-22/Science Documents/PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf#page=15

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document, p.15
text:
can be done after the HOBJ file is converted and the colors demosaiced, where in OMA2 the
white balancing is accomplished with the commands:
*rgb 1.41 1 1.68
clip 4095
In summary, the white balance, if desired, needs to be done after the fact through software
because it was generally not done with the hardware to avoid the risk of saturation.
Note that the ACME images will be naturally dark because of the use of the 16-bit file format
with 12 -bit image data. As such, adjustments to the imag e brightness will generally be
necessary even if the images are not demos aiced. Furthermore, cameras’ CCD arrays are
susceptible to radiation damage while in orbit. As a result, the images feature hot pixels which
increase in number over the months and years in space. As such, it will appear as if there is a
star field within the combustion chamber. Therefore, the images should ideally be processed
to remove the bright outlying pixels. The radiation damage is also obvious in the ops camera
imaging.
Although the DataCam was typically set for imaging at 30 fps, that is trumped by the exposure
settings which were often long because of the dim nature of the microgravity flames. As a
result, the framing rate was typically far less. Different exposures could have been selected
for different phases of the tests, e.g., prior to ignition and during the test, so the framing rate
source: data/raw/PSI-22/Science Documents/PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf#page=15

sequence of different exposure durations is used to enable appropriate photography under
uncertain or varying flame intensities. Bracketing is also used to simultaneously accomplish
multiple imaging objectives, e.g., to appropriately image both brightly glowing soot (or TFP
fibers) as well as the much dimmer blue portion of the flame.

actual framing rate) was often varied during the test, where that could be seldom or often if
bracketing was employed, i.e., where a repeated sequence of images was taken at different
exposures.

document because (despite the file naming) they primarily include pressures, flow rates, and
temperatures from the CIR’s Fuel Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA).

Due to the use of a turning mirror, the DataCam images should be flipped vertically if upright
images are desired, i.e., where the burner is at the bottom and the flame extends upward. In
this regard, note that the DataCam provides images in a ‘landscape’ format with the image’s
long dimension orth ogonal to the burner and chamber axis. This is contrary to a n ACME
science requirement specifying that the long dimension be aligned with the experimental axis
to provide images in a ‘portrait’ format. In this regard, the science requirements were not
always met, e.g., because of design tradeoffs, etc.

reproducible. Therefore, the scaling of the image data should be established for each day of

This intensified camera was typically configured with a CH* bandpass filter and was generally

interference with the electrode mesh and the electric field itself.

4. High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera and CIR illumination package
The HiBMs camera was used in combination with an opposed backlight, i.e., the CIR ’s
collimated illumination package. The resultant imaging was used in preceding droplet
combustion experiments for measuring droplet diameter , but it may also be useful for
determining the soot volume fraction via light extinction. However, the camera’s red filter ,
corresponding to the red illumination, is broad enough to permit significant soot
incandescence to pass through the filter. As a result, this imaging is unlikely to be useful for
soot volume fraction measurements for all conditions. After post-processing on the ground,
the images were made available in the TIFF format and as such are readily op ened. The
grayscale images were typically archived at 15 fps.

Soot and Electric Fields
➢ Soot particle charge
▪ Soot particles may be originally charged, especially if they are formed
through an ionic route
▪ Soot particles gain a net charge through ion-attachment
▪ Measurements indicate that in the hottest zone, soot particles may be
charged to equilibrium, but this is not always the case and the initial
particle charge seems to depend upon the material burnt
▪ Net charge of soot particles in flames is generally positive even in the
flame region where a large excess of electrons exist
▪ Soot particle primary size is found to be ~20 nm in non-electric flames;
size can be reduced in electric fields
➢ Electric field effects on soot in laminar diffusion flames
▪ Ion wind can induce partial premixing (changes reaction zone)
▪ Ion precursors can be removed or reduced in number
▪ Soot residence time can be changed (increased or decreased)

ACME/E-FIELD Flames - Impacts, Benefits, and Products
Prepared by Dennis Stocker, ACME Project Scientist, dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov, 216-433-2166
Impacts, Benefits, and Products
This text is the ‘Impacts, Benefits, and Products’ section from the 2019 version of the final report.
The impact of this work is, as the original objectives identified, the delivery of a unique data set of chemi-
ion behavior in flames under sufficiently stable and symmetric conditions that models and theories can
be evaluated against the results. As an example, the very distinctive shape of the V-I curve in microgravity,
when matched in models, will give a very good indication that the feedback between ion driven wind and
changes in flame shape and burning behavior that then further change the ion current is captured
accurately.
These results have already garnered the interest of other groups working on electric field effects on
flames.
The use of electric field effects on flames can be as sensor (variations of ion current as associated with
combustion behavior) or actuator (ion -driven wind changes the flame shape and characteristics). This
work, as was originally planned, provides quantitative evaluation of the sensing and response potential of

text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Experimental Procedure 23 July 2020
2
1. Introduction
The narrative description of the experimental procedure is from the ‘Methods / Experimental’ section of
the following conference paper:
Y.-C. Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Stocker, U. Hegde, and D. Dunn -Rankin, “Electric Field Effects on Flames in
Microgravity on the International Space Station,” 2018 Spring Technical Meeting of the Central States
Section of The Combustion Institute, Minneapolis, MN, 20-22 May 2018.
This description also appears in Section 4.B Overview of Experiment Test Operations of the E-FIELD Flames
Final Report. Note that the referenced Figure 4 (showing the coflow burner geometry) is not included in
this document.
The CIR experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. Thus far, ACME’s activity has
included the majority of the crew members, regardle ss of their nationalities. Most often the astronauts
and cosmonauts exchange gas bottles, mass flow controllers, and igniter tips. In the latter case, the igniter
tip exchange can occur after failure or proactively before failure when the crew already ha s changes to
make changes in th e interior of the insert. While these activities may seem mundane, the crew play a
critical role in setting up the hardware for each experiment. As an extreme example, there were crew

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_procedure_20200723, p.2
text:
activities on 8 separate days in Sept.-Oct. 2017 to configure the CIR and ACME hardware for the first ACME
experiment, namely the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment. In contrast, only two
crew days were required to reconfigure the hardware for the first E -FIELD Flames tests because of the
initial use of the same coflow burner. Planning is critical because crew activity is scheduled three weeks
in advance, for which detailed procedures must be prepared and uplinked to the ISS.
All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center
(GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio. Typically , four to six people staff four consoles during the testing. The CIR
hardware is controlled from the Rack Officer (RO) and Data Management Officer (DMO) consoles, and the
ACME hardware is control led from the Payload Developer (PD) console. Two shifts of personnel are
scheduled to staff these three consoles on test days because they typically last 14 hours with the many
pre- and post-testing activities. Given that the tests are remotely commanded, the operations are carried
out in the day and evening in Cleveland, e.g., from 7 AM to 9 PM. A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are
normally conducted in a period of 10 hours of less. Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_procedure_20200723, p.2
text:
two weeks. On intervening weekdays, the image data is downlinked and the crew often swap one or both
gas bottles. Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2 -shift day for the RO
and DMO consoles, where it is alway s necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors and
that data is not missing. Those two positions are also staffed to guide and oversee the crew activity. As
a result, the CIR consoles are normally actively staffed on four weekdays per week. A team of four carry
out the detailed planning for the CIR and ACME console staff, and the daily operational plans typically
exceed 50 pages on days including testing.
The science console allows for review of the analog video and non-imaging telemetry (at 1 Hz) in near real
time but doesn’t allow for commanding. In the case of E-FIELD Flames, arrangements were made so that
the analog video is streamed to a secure computer at UC Irvine to allow the research team to participate
in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s planned parameters. That team does not
see the telemetry during the testing, but is in communication via phone and e -mail with their NASA
research partners at the GRC ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). While there are many preparatory
steps, the tests are ultimately conducted using an uploaded software script and parameter files. In

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_procedure_20200723, p.2
text:
advance of the test day, the UC Irvine science team plans the nearly 60 parameters in the voltage sweep
script and specifies other para meters that are configured outs ide of the script, such as camera settings.

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_procedure_20200723, p.3
text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Experimental Procedure 23 July 2020
3
It is also possible to effectively conduct tests in a ‘manual’ mode, where parameters are changed in
response to the analog video downlink or telemetry. For example, the electric field potential can be
adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit.
Typically, ten E-FIELD Flames tests are conducted per test day. Despite the short test durations, the low
rate results from several unavoidable factors. After a test is conducted, the 125 -Hz non-imaging data is
downlinked for immediate review by the scien ce team. A small sample of images are often downlinked
to ensure that the camera exposures are appropriate, where the times for those images are typically
selected based on non-imaging data to provide extreme examples. The review helps to verify parameters
or plan for adjustments in subsequent tests, e.g., to select the voltage range after determining where the
ion current saturates for the given flame conditions. After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber
atmosphere after which the chamber is vented (to space) back to atmospheric pressure, if needed.
Midway through a day’s E-FIELD Flames tests, the atmosphere is circulated for 15 minutes through a filter
cartridge filled with molecular sieves to capture any soot and adsorb at least a portion of the combustion

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_procedure_20200723, p.3
text:
products, e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products. The tests are only
conducted when both Ku and S band communication is available through NASA’s Tracking and Data Relay
Satellite (TDRS) System. Depending on the various orbits, there are periodic communication outages with
a loss of signal (LOS) that can be a short handover (from one satellite to another) or can last as long as 30
minutes.
A variety of constraints limit the number of tests that can be performed, both overall and on a daily basis.
The next combustion experiments in the CIR will feature solid fuels and focus on flame spread and material
flammability. That follow-on plan limits the duration of ACME operations, where each ACME experiment
is allotted four months for testing. Although it requires additional crew time, these allotments are split
into two rounds so that the investigators have a break from testing for careful review of the early results
so that they can maximize the scientific outcome of their second round. This paper reports on early results
from the first round of E-FIELD Flames.
While nitrogen is available from the space station, the combustion testing is limited by the available gas
bottles that were and are launched to supp ort the tests. For E -FIELD Flames and most of ACME’s

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_procedure_20200723, p.3
text:
experiments, the test matrices used to plan those gas resources were established in 2010. At that time,
NASA limited the scope of the ACME tests matrices with t he intent of focused experiments with lim ited
objectives rather than comprehensive experiments. As such, the general target was 50 tests per
experiment. For most ACME experiments, the limiting gas constraint is the oxygen/nitrogen bottles used
to fill the chamber. This resource constraint is exacerbated by the CIR because it is equipped with a pair
of redundant safety timers to limit the fuel that can flow into the combustion chamber (where the timers
can be set for the oxidizer flow in the case of inver se flame testing). The timers can only b e reset by
venting the combustion chamber. Therefore, the timer limit combined with other constraints effectively
corresponds to the day’s maximum flow time for the fuel (or more generally, the limiting reactant). For
E-FIELD Flames, the safety timers are set to the maximum value of 999 seconds, which corresponds to the
10 tests typically completed per day.
Another constraint is the available time in a day, where the console personnel and ISS resources, such as
the video downlink, are planned for a limited number of hours. When necessary for the research, NASA
does have continuous 24-hour/day operations for some non-CIR experiments. But as discussed, the ACME

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_procedure_20200723, p.4
text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Experimental Procedure 23 July 2020
4
Data limits are yet another constraint, where the on -orbit hardware can store a limited amount of data.
More importantly, 127,000 MB is the most that can be reasonably managed in a two -shift transfer and
downlink day. Therefore, tests days are limited to this amount of data, where image data from select
cameras is often archived at reduced rates to mitigate this challenge. Nonetheless, the limit sometimes
forces decisions to abandon recorded images.
This detailed description of operations and hardware provides the context under which the ACME
experiments are conducted. Their complexity makes the flame conditions seem trivial in comparison. It
is a simple coflow flame, with just a small j et of fuel surrounded by a weak coflow of ‘air’ which also fills
the chamber, but where tests are also conducted with no coflow. A test includes starting the gas flows to
prime the system, energizing the igniter to initiate a flame, retracting the igniter, and allowing the flame
to steady slight ly before energizing the electric field to its initial value. The flame is again allowed to
steady before beginning a voltage sweep over a specified range with steps or smooth ramps of specified
voltage changes and durations. The sweep can be in one direction or can include cycles of sweeps. After

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_procedure_20200723, p.4
text:
each test, a duplicate field sweep is made to ensure that there are no current leaks, i.e., other than the
ion current through the flame.
The first phase tests in E -FIELD Flames employ the coflow burner geomet ry shown in Figure 4, with the
fuel tube extending slightly above the burner surface. The results shown in this paper are for tests
conducted with 100% methane in a chamber atmosphere and coflow (when used) of synt hetic ‘air’ (i.e.,
21/79 oxygen/nitrogen by volume) at a nominal pressure of 100 kPa. The mesh is held at a negative
potential relative to the burner in these tests. The sweeps shown in this paper extend to at least -7 kV,
where the voltage is increased in small steps (e.g., of 100 V) lasting 1-2 seconds. The details of the voltage
changes can be seen in the resulting plots.

title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_procedure_20200723, p.5
text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Experimental Procedure 23 July 2020
5
2. Test Sequences and Parameters All E-FIELD Flames tests conducted on the ISS
were carried out using automated software w hich had its roots in ACME’s Integrated Science
Requirements Documents (ISRD, RDR version, Rev. B) and Science Operations Requirements
Documents (SORD, Rev. A). The E -FIELD Flames Science Requirements Document (SRD) is of course
pertinent but only that wh ich was incorporated in the ISRD and SORD was used by the engineering
team in developing the control software.
Multiple software scripts and corresponding parameter files were prepared to address the various
objectives explained in this excerpt from section 4.2 of the ACME ISRD. The section is fully included with
the important exception of the tables detailing the envisioned operational sequences. Given that they
were conceptual, they were left out to reduce the chance of a confused understanding of the engineering
implementation. For example, excessive electromagnetic interference (EMI) led to a change in the design
of the electric field system limiting the voltage to a single polarity on a given test day. As a result, the step
response procedure could not be carried out as detailed in Table 4.2.2 of the ISRD.
The E-FIELD experiment consists of 4 objectives corresponding to 4 series of tests using 2 different

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_procedure_20200723, p.5
text:
diffusion flame burner configurations. The first three test series provide the key fundamental
information regarding the electrical character of diffusion flames and the influence of electric fields on
soot formation; the final series focuses on electric field sensing and control of flames.
General Operations
Before any of the electric field experiments, the high voltage mesh should be installed (or moved into
position). Leak current should be measured by sweeping the voltage from 0 to 10kV and 0 to -10kV
with no flame present. A steep rise in current under these conditions indicates corona discharge and
sets the upper limit on the potential. The test sequence involves a complete repeat voltage sweep
with no flame to provide a point -by-point current leak measurement. A similar sweep should be
completed following flame extinguishment at the end of a test set. Only ion current would need to be
measured during the no-flame sweep. In addition, excessive leak current at relatively low voltage may
indicate electron emission from carbon buildup on the gas jet flame tip. If the leak current exceed s
10% of the flame ion current, cleaning of the gas jet tip is requested. Cleaning consists of a manual
wiping or possibly burning off the carbon with a modified flame condition. We expect this to be a rare

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_procedure_20200723, p.5
text:
request, but the continuous monitor of flameless ion current provides a reliable in-situ monitor. We
assume that the chamber will be emptied and refilled approximately every 7-8 tests to minimize the
oxygen concentration uncertainty in the test chamber. The exact times for settling and voltage steps
may vary (they should be reconfigurable from the ground), but a nominal expected operational
sequence for one chamber fill and the key measurement data sets are shown below.
(A) Voltage Sweep – collection of VI curves (or VCC curves) -- where the voltage is swept from 0-±5kV
(or until flame blowout) and the ion current is monitored and recorded. The sweep will consist of a
series of discrete steps, where a settling time is allowed after each voltage change. At the same time,
color and OH* video rec ords the fla me shape and luminosity (both broadband flame and soot
luminosity and OH* chemiluminescence) throughout the sweep. A typical step sweep might comprise:
15 second ignition & stabilization; 100 V/step, 0.3 sec settle between steps, and a 0.25 sec. ion current
measurement at each point, to ±5kV or blowout. Blowout can be detected by a sharp drop in ion
current. Expected run time is 50 seconds per sweep (not including a background current sweep with
the flame off). However, the time between voltage steps for fl ame adjustment and data collection

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_procedure_20200723, p.6
text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Experimental Procedure 23 July 2020
6
(B) Step Response—This test will involve the rapid change of voltage from a base level to a much
higher (or lower) level, while the ion curre nt (and flame luminosity and shape) is monitored in time
as it settles to its new steady value. The key measurable is the ion current as a function of time through
the voltage step change and the flame’s subsequent settling. As in test set (A), video, luminosity, and
chemiluminescence will record flame behaviors in response to an instantaneous change in the electric
field. A typical experiment sequence might comprise a 15 second ignition and stabilization, step
changes on the order of hundreds of volts, and recording ion current for 2 seconds between step
changes (where steps will not be limited to a single polarity). Settling time for these step changes in
zero gravity (particularly, for soot related phenomena) may need to be adjusted via uplink; the test
procedures shown are based on a nominal settling time observed in preliminary testing at 1g and the
2.2 Second Drop Tower. The range of times between voltage steps may vary between 0-100 seconds.
(C) Electric Field Effects on Soot – The following tests will demonstrate the effects of electric fields on
soot (measured by broadband emission from the flame and soot volume fraction) by slowly increasing

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_procedure_20200723, p.6
text:
the coflow air velocity, comparing the flame structure at each step to a flame affected purely by
electric forcing. Conditions will be uplinked and derived from experiments (A) and (B). Timing will
depend on the burner, but each test will be allowed at least 100 seconds. Also, note that the step
time between one coflow velocitity and the next shall be adjustable via uplink between the values of
0-10 seconds. Broad solid angle collection luminosity, flame images along with soot volume fraction
and soot pyrometry will be collected.
(D) Open Loop Sensing and Control – The experiments associated with control will be uplinked, based
on the results of the above baseline mapping experiments (A) and (B) above. Timing will depend on
the condition, but each test will be allowed at least 70 seconds. The procedure is a series of voltage
ramps (or small steps with continuous data collection). Ion current and luminosity (broadband and
CH*) fluctuations will be collected as well as flame images. The time between voltage changes for
flame adjustment and data collection shall be adjustable via uplink between the values of 0 -10
seconds.
Although four types of E -FIELD Flames tests are discussed above, it was determined by 2017 that three
types of tests could be used to address the four experimental objectives, where a separate script to
investigate effects on the soot was not needed.

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_procedure_20200723, p.6
text:
While scripts were developed for the three remaining sequences, it was later determined that the open
loop objectives could be accomplished by proper selection of parameter values with the voltage sweep
script, e.g., limiting the voltage range. Furthermore, the step response script was ultimately not employed
because of the slow response time of the high -voltage power supply. As such, all of the experiment’s
flame tests were conducted with the voltage sweep script . Therefore, that procedure is the only one to
be further discussed in this document.
The major phases of the test sequence are graphically displayed in Figure 1 , where the green and gold
lines represent the oxidizer coflow (if any), nitrogen flow (if any), and fuel flow. The gold lines represent
optional changes to flow rates, e.g., for a change in the fuel dilution after ignition. The phases are
described in d etail at the bottom of the schematic , where the nomen clature throughou t the figure
generally corresponds to parameter names.

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.2
text:
2
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
This project utilizes electric fields in microgravity combustion science to establish a fun-
damental understanding of chemi-ionization and ion-driven convection in flames. It also
uses this understanding to demonstrate electrical manipulation of sooting behavior and
stability limits in the absence of buoyancy. This work is based on prior foundation stud-
ies that included simulating zero-g combustion of small gas jet diffusion flames in an
earth-gravity laboratory, and the electric field control of flame electrodynamics. The cur-
rent SRD proposes to use the extended-duration microgravity environment to further de-
velop an understanding of electric fields in combustion processes and their potential ap-
plications.
The research centers on the fact that electrical forces, acting on charge carriers created
through chemi-ionization, can provide for measurement and manipulation of flames in
microgravity environments. For example, using the drag exercised on flame ions, electric
fields have demonstrated powerful influences on flame shape, sooting behavior, burning
velocity, extinction, and stability. The source of these influences resides in ion wind ef-
fects. In microgravity, where there are no density-driven buoyant effects to contend with,
ion winds represent an important (and perhaps the only) body force that can be applied to

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.2
text:
manipulate combustion systems. This project includes both academic study of electric
field effects and aspects for practical utilization of electrical control of combustion proc-
esses.
Our prior laboratory experiments have shown that electrical properties of flames can be
used to produce enhanced combustion performance by: (a) manipulating flame ions in
order to change flame chemistry – this is generally considered a minor influence because
flame ion concentration is typically small, but it may be critical at near-limit conditions;
(b) creating a neutral wind (ion driven convection) locally at the flame front – this proc-
ess can provide a local actuator for flame convection control; (c) using electric fields to
affect soot formation and transport – ions and soot are closely linked because there are
shared chemical pathways and because soot particles are charged by the flame ions; and
(d) using electrical properties to characterize flames – e.g., there is a relationship between
flame temperature, the carbon content of a fuel, and the ion current it can produce at satu-
ration.
In 1-g, the above-mentioned processes are confounded by complex buoyancy interactions
that cannot be unraveled. Hence, to evaluate them in detail, we propose the following
experimental objectives for an extended microgravity environment: (A) determine the

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.2
text:
relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel
flow rate and the amount of inert (nitrogen) in the fuel; (B) compare the time response of
the flame’s chemiluminescence and ion current to rapid changes in electric fields; (C)
determine sooting behavior in relation to the electric field influences; and (D) manipulate
the limit behavior of lifted flames using electric fields.
The experimental approach includes a simple gas jet diffusion flame and a co-flow burner.
The basic variations in the tests are in the burner type, the fuel type (nominally non -
sooting and sooting), and in the level of inert dilution of the fuel to vary the flame
strength. The co-flow or environment gas will have a nominal molar composition of 21%
O2 and 79% N2. The experimental concept is to ground the burner to the test chamber

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.3
text:
3
and to install an electrically active planar mesh electrode downstream of the burner
mouth. The potential of the mesh electrode can be either positive or negative, with a
steady voltage or with a time varying potential (including a rapid step change) to examine
the flame’s steady state response and time response. The data to be recorded include the
applied voltage, the ion current, the flame broadband luminosity, the CH* luminosity,
flame images of OH* and visible light showing the flame shape as a function of electric
potential and flame shape changes during transients in the electric field. In addition, a
desired measurement of temperature in and near the flame will monitor the thermal field
as a function of the electric field conditions.
The data from these measurements will allow a chemical and physical understanding of
flame ion production and information showing the potential to use these ions to electri-
cally control the flame both via modification of the local chemistry near extinction limits
and through changes in the local convection using the ion driven wind. For example, a
lifted diffusion flame near its blowoff condition is sensitive to mixing at the flame anchor
point. Therefore, electric fields acting on near-limit flames can exert a large influence
because they can affect the local mixing behavior. The role of electric fields on soot

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.3
text:
formation will be dramatic under conditions where the ion driven wind has a large influ-
ence on flow residence time (or on ion residence time, if chemical effects are found im-
portant) in sooting flames.
Generally, the convective flows driven by electric fields acting on flame ions and those
driven by buoyancy have been found to be of the same order of magnitude in earth grav-
ity. In addition, raising the temperature often increases the ion production rate and the
response to an electric field, but increasing temperature also increases the buoyancy ef-
fect, making it difficult, on earth, to separate ion wind effects from those due to buoyancy.
In the zero-g environment, it will be possible to eliminate the buoyancy confusion and
develop sufficient understanding to predict the response of flames to electric fields under
all conditions. Extended run times are crucial for all of the studies because the timescales
of flame property changes (which includes chemi-ionization) are dominated by convec-
tion (length scale/velocity) and past studies have shown that soot studies require high
quality zero gravity timescales longer than is available in aircraft and drop towers. In ad-
dition, exploring instabilities and extinction behavior in near-limit flames requires ex-
periments lasting tens of seconds.

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.3
text:
Overall, the goal of this zero-gravity study is to understand chemi-ionization behavior
and the resulting ion driven winds sufficiently well so that electrical properties of flames
can be used to characterize (by monitoring ion current) and control them (via direct
chemical or local convective influences). Electric field effects on flames have been
documented for decades (even centuries), but flames in 1-g all include buoyancy influ-
ences that affect ion generation behavior. For flames near transitions and limits, buoyant
influences always confound any understanding of the role of ion driven winds in using
electric fields to characterize and manipulate flames. The proposed study removes this
confounding influence and allows definitive measurement and analysis of the electric
field effects on jet diffusion and co-flow flames.

1 INTRODUCTION
The first subsection provides the fundamentals that link chemi-ionization in flames with
convective flows created when electric fields act on the ions generated. Later subsections
describe the variety of 1-g laboratory experiments exemplifying the scientific data we
have found valuable in linking flames to their electrical properties. For the purposes of
this SRD, the details of this introductory section are less important than the examples of
our preliminary results which inform our proposed selection of objectives and science
data end products. To focus on the proposed flight experiment, it is possible to skip di-
rectly to Section 1.4 and then refer to background information as needed.
1.1 Background and Overview of Ion Driven Winds in Flames
In addition to being a major liberator of chemical energy, hydrocarbon flames naturally
produce charged intermediate species (ions and electrons) during the chemical-to-thermal
energy conversion. Generally speaking, chemi-ions and their associated species in hy-
drocarbon flames do not participate substantially in the major heat release reaction path-
ways. Hence, the chemical kinetics of ion species in hydrocarbon flames has not been
studied as extensively as for those species or reaction mechanisms associated with igni-

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.6
text:
tion/extinction phenomena and pollutant formation. Nevertheless, many of the chemical
kinetic pathways are fairly well
articulated. Figure 1.1 shows the
chemi-ion pathways from Starik
and Titova [1] and Pederson and
Brown [2]. The major ions are
formed through reactions which
involve CH molecules. The CH
molecules are formed either from
acetylene and other C2 molecules,
or via the oxidation of CH3.
Green and Sugden [3] proposed
that CH is produced in a meth-
ane/air stoichiometric mixture
primarily via the oxidation of
CH3 through CH 3+O 
CH+H2O. Peeters et al. [4] have
used this reaction successfully in their computations, and Jones et al. [5] examined modi-
fying the rate constant of this reaction to result in a better correlation with experimental
observations. Pederson and Brown [2] used a 13-step reaction scheme for the determina-
tion of the ion profiles. Their results indicate that for a stoichiometric mixture, H3O+ is
the most important ion; its maximum concentration is more than two orders of magnitude
higher than that of C2H3O+ and C3H3 +, and three orders of magnitude higher than that of
HCO+. The latter ion is, however, an important component for the production of H3O+.
Prager, et al. examined ion chemistry more recently and found H3O+ to be dominant in
lean flames [6]. They also identified several areas of uncertainty, primarily the anion

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.7
text:
7
literature that the weak plasma nature of flames is relatively unimportant for the heat re-
lease reactions. For example, the most populous cations (positive ions) are present in
peak concentrations on the order of 1010/cc, or with mole fractions in the range of 10 ppb.
The concentration of electrons (which
make up the majority of the negative
charge carriers) is even lower than the
concentration of positive ions because
electron mobility is very high so that
relatively few electrons are needed to
balance the charge flux carried by the
more massive and more populous
positive charge carriers. Nevertheless,
the free charges in the flame make the
reaction zone a very good conductor
(similar to that of a conductive metal).
More importantly, if an electric field is
applied across the flame, the charges
can be separated into unipolar regions, as shown in Figure 1.2. In the case where the an-
ode (higher potential electrode) is close to the flame, the electrons can then easily exit the
gas phase system, leaving the positive ions to collide with neutral molecules as they mi-
grate through the unipolar space between the flame and the cathode (lower potential elec-
trode). During this migration process, the ions impart momentum to the neutral gas
equivalent to the acceleration they have achieved in the electric field between mean-free-

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.7
text:
path collisions. The collisions are so frequent, that the ions quickly establish a drift ve-
locity governed by their mobility. The collisions thereby link the ionization processes to
the neutral gas flow. This phenomenon is referred to as a Chattock wind, an ion-wind, or
more accurately an ion-driven wind, and is described in some detail by Lawton and
Weinberg [7].
In all of the applications involving electrical generation of convection, a unidirectional
gas flow is induced by using a large electric field to act on the charges of a unipolar ion
cloud in the region between the ion source and a second, usually earthed, electrode, or set
of electrodes. In these cases, the body force on a unit volume of the gas is equal to that
on the charges it contains, provided that they have a constant mobility and do not acceler-
ate. In atmospheric pressure systems, the latter condition on acceleration is met easily,
but in regions of high temperature gradients or changes in chemical composition, the con-
stant mobility condition is not. Fortunately, these regions are often of limited spatial ex-
tent and so the effects of variable mobility are usually ignored. As described, for exam-
ple in references [8,9] isothermal ion driven flow (with constant mobility) is described
generally by the coupled equations of fluid continuity and momentum along with an elec-

The above equations show that an electric field applied to the flame can create a direct

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames

text:
body force, or force per unit volume, on the system just as buoyancy does in a gravita-
tional field. Because buoyancy can be a dominant characteristic of terrestrial combustion
processes, it may seem less than obvious why physics regards gravity as a “weak force.”
However, if we consider a small magnet picking up a metal object with the entire earth
pulling in the opposite direction, it becomes obvious how much stronger the electromag-
netic forces are. It is hardly surprising, therefore, that electrical forces acting on charge
carriers can effectively substitute for gravitational influences or, more generally, provide
for vigorous combustion control in its absence (i.e., in microgravity). It is the opportu-
nity for exploiting the electric force in flames that motivates this research activity. Al-
ready, electric fields have demonstrated powerful influences on combustion processes
that include flame shape [12,13], sooting behavior [14-16], burning velocity [17,18], ex-
tinction [11,19], and stability [20,21]. The foundation of many of these results, as dis-
cussed in Lawton and Weinberg [7], reside in ion wind effects. In microgravity, where
there are no density driven buoyant effects to contend with, ion winds represent an im-
portant (and perhaps the only) body force that can be applied to manipulate combustion

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.9
text:

and exploit the electrical aspects of flames [22].

title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.10
text:

1.2 Opportunities in Microgravity for Understanding Electric Field Effects on Flames
There are at least four ways that detailed measurements of electrical properties of flames
in microgravity can be used to improve our understanding of flame electrochemistry and
to potentially improve combustion performance:
(1) Extracting flame ions in order to change flame chemistry – we have already described
that ion radicals are not considered a large contributor to combustion heat release.
However, in the situations of weak flames, as can be represented by diluted diffusion
flames in zero gravity and terrestrial flames near extinction limits, their role is likely
to be more important. In addition, in near-limit flames, ion manipulation may be used
to extend stability behavior.
(2) Creating a neutral wind (ion driven convection) locally at the flame front; this is one
of the rare and important action-at-a-distance effects on flames that can be used as a
localized actuator. A one dimensional estimate of the equation for the forces avail-
able shows that the typical values for a flame can produce ion winds with flow veloc-
ity on the order of 1 m/s and forces on the order of one or two times the buoyant force.
Although this sounds like a fairly modest wind, it has been shown to be capable of
substantial effects, including flame extinction [11,19]. The effect of the wind has

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.10
text:
been demonstrated with a candle flame in parabolic flight based microgravity [12]
and in a spherical cage drop tower [13], but there has been no systematic study of the
ion wind effect in the absence of the confounding effects of the approximately equal
influence of buoyancy. The actuation of the flame can be used to control flame per-
formance despite external fluctuations.
(3) Using electric fields to affect soot formation and transport – ions and soot are closely
linked because there are shared chemical pathways [23] and because soot particles are
charged by the flame ion attachment or electron ejection. It is possible, therefore, to
modify soot formation and to use charges attached to soot to affect soot transport. By
adjusting the soot trajectory through the reaction zone it is possible to affect the oxi-
dation of soot to prevent its eventual release or to modify the residence time of soot in
different zones of the flame. It is also possible to use the neutral ion wind to change
the mixing behavior of the flame and reduce soot in this way.
(4) Using the electrical properties to characterize the flame – there is a quantifiable rela-
tionship between the carbon content of a fuel and the ion current it can produce at
saturation [24]. This relationship is already exploited in a typical flame ionization de-

drogen flame to create an ion current in proportion to the carbon influx. In direct
flame interrogation, however, there are several confounding variables that can affect
the ion current, including flame temperature (which generally affects the O atom con-
centration) and the reaction zone volume. Flame temperature can in turn be affected
by levels of premixing, diffusion rates, fuel composition, and radiative loss. It is pos-
sible, therefore, to determine flame character from the ionization curve response.
There are also many opportunities identified for ion sensors as part of a combustion

diagnostic to determine the combustion quality [6,25].

Electric field-induced flame convection in microgravity [11,26]

eliminating the confounding buoyancy forces. Under earth gravity, diffusion flames rely

1.4 Summary of Findings and Open
Questions
The above earth gravity experiments
have resolved many questions regarding
ion driven winds in small diffusion
flames, and all of the important experi-
mental conditions and procedures have
been established. The ion pathlines and
the link between ion driven winds and
the flame shape and behavior for small
diffusion flames have been identified.
Modeling of the electrokinetics along
with the fluid dynamics has been successful, thereby providing an analytical tool for un-
derstanding the ion wind/flow coupling. The open questions regard the relationship be-
tween flame character (e.g., level of partial premixing) and the electric response. In addi-
tion, uncertainty remains regarding the chemical versus physical role of ions, and the po-
tential for dynamic manipulation of flames using electric fields.
The 1-g studies to date did not involve any quantitative analysis of soot because carbon
particles complicate the interpretation of electrical properties, but this component of
combustion is important to include because electric fields can modify soot formation and

numerical work has focused primarily on the neutral species approach, there continues to
be strong interest in the possible role of ions because there has been no satisfactory ex-

2. E-FIELD FLAMES FLIGHT EXPERIMENT
2.1 Experimental Objectives
The ultimate objective of this experiment is to develop an understanding of the mecha-
nisms of chemi-ionization in flames and to describe the interplay between convective
flows driven by those flame ions and their generation rate. With this information it will
then be possible to detect and control flame behavior electrically. In 1-g, laminar diffu-
sion flames are often controlled to a large extent by natural convection, and particularly
by the rate at which natural convection brings fresh oxidizer to the reaction zone. Hence,
the vigor with which combustion proceeds depends on local convection. As described in
Section 1, an electric field acting on flame ions produces a body force and convection
(analogous to buoyancy) which affects the combustion process. The change in the com-
bustion process can in turn affect the ion production rate, which is responsible for the
body force. This coupled interaction is very difficult to measure, study, and understand
in 1-g because buoyant forces (of approximately equal magnitude) interfere. In micro-
gravity, there is no such complication and the body force in the flame is associated en-
tirely with the ion-driven wind. 1-g experiments have demonstrated clearly that electri-
cally driven convection can be used to modify the local flow field in a manner that

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.22
text:
changes combustion behavior. For example, it can stabilize lifted flames or force them
to reattach. Electric fields have been seen to change soot formation, though whether
solely by residence time effects or their combination with chemical alterations has not
been confirmed. In addition, ions can attach to soot particles providing them with e n-
hanced mobility that can be manipulated. Furthermore, the electrical properties of flames
provide a measure of their character. For example, non-premixed flames exhibit different
relationships between ion production and ion wind forces than do premixed flames. The
hydrocarbon fuel, and in particular, the carbon/hydrogen ratio, also affects these interac-
tions. The goal of this project is to clarify and quantify this range of electrical effects and
to then demonstrate the electrical manipulation of flame stability and soot in flames using
the information obtained.
To accomplish this scientific goal, there are four fundamental experimental objectives, in
priority order, using a jet diffusion flame burner and a co-flow diffusion flame burner.
The jet flame is the more critical configuration because it has a large 1-g data foundation
and it can be more easily modeled as an ion and thermal source. In zero-g, however, it
will be primarily driven by ion wind convection (no buoyant contribution and at its low

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.22
text:
fuel flow rates, the injection momentum dies rapidly with distance from the i njector)
which may limit its operating range. The co-flow flame allows a forced convection com-
ponent to provide a wider range of flow conditions (fuel dilution and exit velocity) and a
reproducible lifted flame for stability and soot behavior studies:
A) Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as
functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of inert (nitro-
gen) in the fuel.

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.23
text:
23
For the above determination, a low-sooting and highly sooting fuel are included, and the
inert weakens the flame sufficiently to permit near-limit conditions at moderate flow ve-
locities, where the effects of electric fields will be most acute. As shown in Figure 1.10,
the resulting voltage-current (VI) curve (also known as the voltage current characteristic -
- VCC) from these experiments will identify the voltage and current at which the ion cur-
rent first saturates, the voltage at which the current begins to increase beyond saturation,
indicating a change in combustion behavior, and the voltage at which the flame extin-
guishes. These data can be analyzed further to provide the ion production per carbon
atom of fuel flux which describes the flame character (i.e., diffusion to partially pr e-
mixed), and the ion wind strength for each condition. In addition to their direct interpre-
tative value for calculating ion-driven winds and body forces, these data can also be used
in electrokinetic simulations to compute ion mobility values consistent with measured ion
currents and to help validate the numerical simulations of other researchers that include
ion species and electrical effects in their flame calculations.
B) Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.23
text:
current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethyl-
ene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream.
These data provide the dynamic system behavior of the flame. This information co m-
prises the time response of the flame (i.e., its surface area and luminosity) as compared to
the time response of the ion current. These timescales can temporally separate the direct
chemical effects of electric fields from ion diffusion and ion wind convective forcing. In
addition, the system response is required to eventually build flame models suitable for
active electrical control, assuming linear behavior over small ranges.
C) Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of
luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as func-
tions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen)
added to the fuel stream.
The interaction between soot and electric fields is very complex because it combines the
direct influence of electric fields on the chemistry, the ion wind effects on residence time
and mixing, and the electric forces on the charged soot particles themselves. The zero-
gravity environment, using the combination of the jet diffusion flame and the co -flow

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.23
text:
flame provides a wide range of conditions where these different influences can be a l-
lowed to dominate individually. For example, the forced convection environment of the
co-flow burner will minimize the influence of the axial ion-driven wind, which helps to
distinguish the direct electrical effects on ion chemistry in soot formation. In addition to
demonstrating the direct control of soot behavior by electric fields, separating the influ-
ences can help distinguish between neutral molecule addition mechanisms of soot forma-
tion and those that presume the importance of ionic species. For example, changing the
strength and polarity of the electric field can change the availability of ion precursors,
and electric convection can manipulate reactants’ time/temperature history. In addition,
charges will accumulate onto soot, and the electric field can then act directly on the soot
particles to change their residence time and path through the flame.

title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.24

D) Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to char-
acterize the combustion behavior of near-limit lifted flames and use the associated ion-
driven wind to stabilize or reattach these flames.
Because the chemi-ion current per unit flame area can be used as an indicator of flame
strength, its measure (both average and fluctuating properties) with low electric field
voltage can be used to detect flames approaching their limit condition. By adjusting the
electric field, 1-g studies indicate that an ion driven wind can be used to reduce the lift-
off height and stabilize the flame. This is an example of open loop electrical flame sens-
ing, analysis, and control.
2.2 Approach
The specific experimental objectives of the electric field experiments all examine the po-
tential for electric fields to distinguish and manipulate combustion behavior of laminar
diffusion flames, particularly with regards to stability and extinction limits and soot for-
mation and burnout. As described in Section 1, our 1-g studies have shown that small gas
jet diffusion flames can be used to study a wide range of electric field/flame ion interac-
tions, particularly as regards the changes to the flames that result from ion driven winds.

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.24
text:
These flames are compact (allowing complete optical visualization) and require very low
flow rates of fuel (on the order of 30 sccm) which makes them well-suited to the CIR ex-
periment environment. The E-FIELD Flames experiment can also take advantage of the
co-flow burner that is proposed for the CLD Flame component of the ACME flight ex-
periments. Like the gas jet diffusion flame, the co-flow burner uses very small amounts
of fuel, but unlike the jet flame, the burner isolates the diffusion flame sheet from the in-
fluence of the static ambient gas with a co-flowing gas stream. The co-flow configura-
tion allows two important aspects of
electric field/flame interaction to be
studied. First, the effects of the electric
field on the lifted co-flow flame can be
examined. There is evidence in the
literature that electric fields increase
flame resistance to lifting, though the
liftoff height itself may not change
substantially [46,47]. It is likely that
this effect is related to the ion driven
wind because the lifted flames are
sufficiently near their combustion limit
to respond to relatively small forcing.
This influence can be quantified using
the co-flow burner. There is a
controversy in the literature regarding the importance of ion driven winds in the liftoff
behavior relative to the chemical effects. The controversy cannot be resolved easily in 1-

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.24
text:
g because buoyancy confounds the flowfield. Recent experiments in our 1-g laboratory
confirm that the co-flow burner exhibits some significantly different electric field/flame

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.25
text:
25
interactions from the jet diffusion flame. Figure 2.1 shows a typ ical methane co-flow
without and with the electric field.
In addition to controlled lifted flame ion current measurements, in the slightly lifted (but
not near-limit) flame conditions, the effect of the electric field on sooting behavior can be
measured. As mentioned earlier, there remains some question regarding the role of ionic
species in soot formation, and by using the co-flow burner configuration, we will be able
to affect the flame electrically without distorting the flame with the ion-driven wind as
necessarily occurs in the simple gas jet diffusion flame.
The detailed list of flame conditions to be studied is included in Section 3 and in the Ap-
pendix (e.g., test matrix of conditions). The basic variations in the tests, however, are in
the burner type (simple gas jet and co-flow), the fuel type (methane and ethylene), and in
the level of inert (nitrogen) dilution of the fuel. The co-flow gas will be air with molar
composition of 21% O2 and 79% N2. If additional fuel gas combinations and oxidizer is
available (e.g., CO2 diluted fuel), then additional experiments can be run following the
same procedures outlined below.
The schematic approach of the E-FIELD Flames experiment is shown in Figure 2.2. The
concept is to ground the burner to the chamber through a safety bleed resistor-capacitor

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.25
text:
pair, and to install an electrically active mesh electrode downstream of the burner mouth.
A tentative electrical configuration is shown in Figure 2.3. These figures show that the
high voltage connection is attached to the mesh, with the ion current measurement being
made across a shunt resistor connected between the burner and the low potential (relative
to system ground) side of the high voltage source. This configuration requires that the
burner be electrically isolated from the rest of the chamber, but the electrical isolation (in
terms of breakdown potential resistance) can be relatively modest since the potential dif-
ference across the shunt resistor will not be significant during normal operation (e.g., on
the order of 1 V for a 100 kΩ shunt resistor and 0.1 microamp chemi-ion current). The
potential of the mesh electrode can be either positive or negative, with a steady voltage or
with a time-varying but unipolar voltage (including a step change) to examine the flame’s
steady state response and time response to such changes. The goal of the design is to
eliminate any leakage current so that all current flowing through the shunt resistor is the
result of chemi-ionization in the flame. In 1-g studies, there have been cases where soot
formed on the burner acts as a weak electron emitter (see, e.g., Figure 1.17). Even in this

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: E-FIELD_Flames_SRD_20100402, p.25
text:
situation, the leak current is small (less than 5%), but it is preferable to have a mechanism
for removing soot buildup on the burner should it occur. The removal can be manual, or
non-lifted, non-sooting flame conditions can be used to burn the soot from the burner tip
in situ.

Flying 250 miles above the Earth, the International Space Station (ISS)
provides a platform for research to improve life on Earth, enable space
exploration, and understand the universe. This Researcher’s Guide is
intended to help potential ISS combustion science researchers plan
experiments utilizing the microgravity environment in order to understand
how heat and mass transport phenomena coupled with chemistry affect

1. Microgravity, or weightlessness, alters many observable phenomena
within the physical and life sciences. Systems and processes affected by
microgravity include surface wetting and interfacial tension, multiphase
flow and heat transfer, multiphase system dynamics, solidification, and
fire phenomena and combustion. Microgravity induces a vast array of
changes in organisms ranging from bacteria to humans, including global
alterations in gene expression and 3-D aggregation of cells into tissue-like
architecture.
2. Extreme conditions in the ISS environment include exposure to extreme
heat and cold cycling, ultra-vacuum, atomic oxygen, and high-energy
radiation. Testing and qualification of materials exposed to these extreme
conditions have provided data to enable the manufacturing of long-
life, reliable components used on Earth as well as in the world’s most
sophisticated satellite and spacecraft components.
3. Low-Earth orbit at 51 degrees inclination and at a 90-minute orbit
affords ISS a unique vantage point with an altitude of approximately 240
miles (400 kilometers) and an orbital path over 90 percent of the Earth’s
population. This can provide improved spatial resolution and variable
lighting conditions compared to the sun-synchronous orbits of typical
Earth remote-sensing satellites.
Unique Features of the ISS
Research Environment

text:
8
Combustion occurs when fuel and oxygen react to produce carbon dioxide, water
and heat. For the foreseeable future, the overwhelming majority of delivered energy
in terrestrial applications will be from combustion or other chemically reacting
systems. These energy uses cover the range from electric power and transportation
to processes directly tied to the delivered material (e.g., glass and steel manufacture).
These processes produce some of the most important environmental hazards
currently facing humanity (global climate change, acid gas pollution, mercury
contamination from coal, and wild-land fires).
Despite being the subject of active research for over 80 years, combustion processes
remain one of the most poorly controlled phenomena that have a significant impact
on human health, comfort and safety. This is because the simplest combustor
(e.g., kitchen stove) remains beyond our detailed numerical modeling capabilities.
Typically, the combustion process involves a large number of chemical species
(hundreds) and reactions (even thousands). It is these species and reactions
that determine flammability limits (combustor operating ranges) and pollutant
emissions. Much of combustion research involves developing a comprehensive and
predictive quantitative understanding of this complex process. This understanding
source: data/raw/PSI-22/Science Documents/PSI-22_Science Documents_ISS Researchers Guide - Combustion In Reduced Gravity.pdf#page=8

name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
title: ACME E-FIELD Flames: ISS Researchers Guide - Combustion In Reduced Gravity, p.8
text:
usually occurs in smaller, bench-scale experiments that are amenable to detailed
study and modeling. In these bench-scale experiments, however, buoyant forces,
created by gravity and the large temperature differential between the flame and
the ambient gas, dominate and frequently obscure the physical and chemical
phenomena of interest, and hence, complicate analyses. In the absence of gravity,
buoyancy can be suppressed, and the analyses can be reduced to much simpler one-
dimensional systems.
T o understand the strong influence of gravity on flames, one can consider the
density gradients in flames. Typical flame temperatures are on the order of 2,300
degrees Kelvin, whereas ambient temperatures are approximately 300 degrees
Kelvin. This produces an eight-fold density change over the scale of a centimeter.
The resultant density gradient induces a strong velocity field that dominates all but
the highest flow fields. This flow field causes the flame to lift and point upward.
The resultant flow instabilities cause the flicker typical of flames on Earth. Figure 1
contains a gallery of 1-g to 0-g comparison flames.
By varying or eliminating the effects of gravity, we can extract fundamental data
that are important for understanding combustion systems. This approach has
been implemented to some extent in existing terrestrial reduced-gravity platforms,
source: data/raw/PSI-22/Science Documents/PSI-22_Science Documents_ISS Researchers Guide - Combustion In Reduced Gravity.pdf#page=8
