for unity Le. These results also suggest that, sim ilar to considerations fo r premixed flames, the

The general phenomena of flame surface dynamics and flame extinction will be experimentally
and computationally studied using the present burner-supported spherica l diffusion flame. The
reactivity and radiative properties of the flame can be varied syst ematically by changing the fuel
ejection rate as well as the sooting tendency of the gaseous fuel. Thus a comparison between the
experimental and theoretical extinction flame sizes, with and without substantial radiative heat loss,
can be realistically conducted to interrogate/extr act the kinetics and quantify the dependence of the
dual extinction phenomenon on the extent of radiativ e heat loss. The pres ence of flame front
instabilities, with the associated cell dimensions and pulsating frequencies, can also be readily
observed and quantified.
1.2.4 Structure and Response of Sooty Flames to a Non-Steady-State Initial Condition
It is well established that, for the same flame temp erature, soot generation can be more substantial
for diffusion flames than for premixed flames. Th e reason is that, for a diffusion flame, soot is
generated on the fuel side of the flame and he nce cannot be readily oxidized because the local
environment is deficient in oxygen. As such, we study the structure a nd response of spherical

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame_SRD_20100125, p.13
text:
diffusion flames using characteristically sooty fuels. Nonetheless, an important issue in the study of
sooty flames is that proper constr aints be placed on the system, so that a meaningful comparison can
be conducted. Arbitrarily varyin g fuels/diluents may not lead to meaningful results. A logical
constraint is to hold the total energy, and hence to a large extent the maxi mum flame temperature of
the system fixed, as parameters are changed. Th e second constraint is to hold the flame residence
time constant.
We next note that soot is expected to form in a thin layer in the region between the flame and the
burner surface, with the exact lo cation determined by the outwardly flowing fuel stream and the
inwardly directed thermophoretic force. Conseque ntly, the continuous expansion of the flame front
will lead to a corresponding movement of the s oot layer. Experimental and computational
quantification of such movements can lead to information on the soot formation kinetics as well as
the growth of the soot particle size. The pres ence of soot also provides a radiative heat loss
mechanism, and is directly related to our studies on extinction mechanisms, as discussed earlier.
The nonpremixed spherical ethylene flame will serv e as the benchmark for the characteristically
sooty flame. Ethylene is chosen because of its str onger propensity to form soot than, say, methane.

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame_SRD_20100125, p.13
text:
The flame dynamics under microgravity conditions will be specifically examined for the
aforementioned soot onset, as a function of the reside nce time (i.e. characteristic flame size) with no
strain and only curvature effects, radiative extinction, and transpor t induced instability. Since the
flame continuously expands due to fuel vapor accumula tion, it is expected that soot initiation as well
as the subsequent motion of the soot layer will be dynamically evolving as well. Their relative rates
of motion should then yield sufficient information for us to assess the intensity of the thermophoretic
force experienced by the soot particles. Furthermor e, different than the droplet flame, there is no
feedback from soot radiation to the droplet, affecting va porization rate. As a result, soot formation
kinetics and flame extinction can be studied at constant mass flow rate.
1.3 Status of Understanding from Current Investigation
Extensive experimental and theoretical progress has been made both in the preparation for the
space-based experimentation as well as to obtain new research results in their own right.

chamber developed at Princeton. Substantial effo rt was also expanded towa rds developing a porous

will be continuously updated to reflect anticipated advances.
The following is a summary of the major findings of the research performed associated with this
program.
1.3.1 Dynamics and Extinction of Diffusion Flames
1.3.1.1 Flame Front Motion

the burner surface. Tracking the subsequent outwar d movement of the flame front toward its steady-
state equilibrium or radiative extinction, a nd comparing the experime ntal behavior with
computational simulation would allow assessment of the detailed chemistry and transport
mechanisms.

Experimental data of good quality have been obtained on the transient response of burner-
generated spherical diffusion flames in the 2.2-s drop tower facility at the NASA Glenn Research
Center. These flames are maintained by constant fu el mass flow rates during an impulsive step from

respectively defined as the ratio of the horizontal and the vertical diameters of the flame and as the
distance between center of the burner and bottom of the flame divided by half of the vertical diameter
of the flame), as shown in Fig. 1.6. For the flame evolution process, fully transient calculations with
detailed chemistry and transport agree quite satisf actorily with the experime ntal data (e.g. visible

The slight disparity of the flame trajectories be tween the non-radiative and radiative cases can be
explained in terms of the effects of finite-rate reac tions and thermal expansion. As can be seen from
Fig. 1.9, due to the reduced reaction ra tes from reduced temperatures, the mass consumption rate for
the radiative case is always smaller than that fo r the non-radiative case. However, computations
reveal that there is very little reactant leakage (until the brief pe riod just preceding flame extinction)
for the radiative case despite th e smaller mass consumption rate. This phenomenon is readily
explained because the flame with radiative loss is able to accumulate more fuel mass for the same
volume as compared to the non-radiative case, due to increased gas density from reduced
temperature. As a result, during the early stage of flame expansion, the radiative flame is able to

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame_SRD_20100125, p.15
text:
maintain a smaller radius with a smaller mass c onsumption rate and smaller reactant leakage.
However, as the flame continues to expand and decrea se in temperature, the e ffect of enhanced mass
storage ability cannot compensate for that of decr easing reaction rate s, driving the flame to move
outwardly faster than in the non-radiative case in order to reduce the fuel mass flux into its
consumption zone.

The implications of tracking the flame motion in terms of evaluating chemistry and transport
effects are as follows. Since chemilluminescence is directly linked to the detailed chemistry of
intermediate species, tracking of the peak temperature position better assesses the transport
mechanisms, especially radiative loss/absorpti on, and consequently the flame structure.
Respectively, the tracking of a peak chemiluminescen t species, such as OH* and/or CH*, reinforces
the validity of the detailed chemistry. Since both chemical kinetics and transport mechanisms are
important at extinction, requisite quantitative prediction of extinction phenomena establishes closure.
Experiments have also been performed in low-pr essure environments in normal gravity. As
suggested and demonstrated by Law et al. (1980) through droplet experiments, problems involving
diffusion flame sheets are minimally dependent on th e system pressure except for buoyancy effects.
Thus by conducting experiments in low pressure and normal gravity, buoyancy effects can be
minimized without affecting much the basic featur es of the flame-sheet problem. Consequently
steady-state burner-supported, near ly spherical, diffusion flames ha ve been established and some
useful results have been obtained (Yoo et al. 2002) . Studies using this approach, however, are

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame_SRD_20100125, p.16
text:
limited by small flames and low pressures. Consequently, the experimental flames still suffer a slight
degree of asymmetry. Furthermore, the need to work in reduced pressure severely limits the pressure
range of investigation for kinetics studies. Since pressure is a sens itive parameter in kinetics, these
low-pressure, normal gravity experiments cannot replace normal-pressure, microgravity experiments.
We shall return to the topic of the establishment of micro-buoyanc y flames in normal gravity in
§1.3.1.3.
1.3.1.2 Quasi-Steady Extinction
As inferred from Fig. 1.7, radiative extinction is computationally predic ted to occur well beyond
the experimental duration of 2.2s. Howeve r, for fuel mixtures with relatively low H 2 and high CH 4
concentrations, optically thin computations predic t radiative extinction while the experimental flame
is still extant and expanding, as shown in Fig. 1.10. As expected, wide-band Planck mean absorption
coefficients (T&H), based on Tien (1968) and Hubbard an d Tien (1978), over-pre dict radiative loss
compared to the statistical narrow band (SNB) mean coefficients for the optically thin cases. With
the treatment of gas-phase self-r eabsorption effects, computations utilizing the SNB model seem to
better describe the experimental observations in te rms of the computational flame surviving beyond
the 2.2 seconds.

the experimental g-jitter was sufficiently strong as to preclude a definitive answer. 5-s drop tower
experiments showed (Fig. 1.11) an expanding spherical flame which seems to exhibit local extinction
(near the top) near the end of the drop. Nonetheless, preliminary 5- s drop tower tests have still been
unable to capture the entire flame extinction phe nomenon even for the most favorable (minimum
flame extinction time, i.e. ~2.5s) case, as shown in Fig. 1.10. Moreover, a large portion of the
experimental matrix requires mixtures with longer characteristic extinction times as seen in Fig. 1.12,
further stressing the need for longer microgravity duration. The large eff ect of g-jitter on the
experiments and the limited duration of earth-based experiments further substantiate the need for
space-based experimentation. Only by resolving su ch experimental uncertainties and limitations can
a computational adjustment of the radiative loss parameters be appropriate.

It is of critical importance to note that loca l visible luminosity from the flame provides no
indication of either flame strength or flame extinction. In particular, Fig. 1.13 shows that the peak
visible emission from CH* decreases rapidly despit e an ever increasing flame temperature. The
reason for this phenomenon of local visible luminosity decay, as observed in all of the experimental
flames, is mainly due to the ini tially enriched oxygen concentration within the reaction zone of the
transient flame structure as compared to the stea dy-state flame structure. That is, the initial,

profiles of Fig. 1.13. Consequently, the flux of oxidizer into the reaction zone is very large initially,
and gradually subsides until it attains its steady-state value. Since the computations reveal that the
main CH* production route considered fo r our flames is through the reaction C 2H+O2, rather than
C2+OH, increased oxygen concentratio n available for reaction with C 2H will result in increased
chemiluminescence from CH*. The decay of local luminosity of the flame is a consequence of the
relaxation of the local CH* luminosity to its steady- state condition from the initial, elevated value.
Consequently, experimental inves tigations of extinction phenomena for such flames should not rely
on visible observation, but rather on explicit temp erature field measurement (e.g. thin-filament
pyrometry, IR radiometer data) in the assessment of the moment of flame extinction.

1.3.1.3 Instability and Extinction
As mentioned in §1.2.1, the preceding discussion should be limited to quasi-steady flames, as
determined by satisfying gas-phase steadiness in th e reference frame of the moving flame front. The
onset of fully transient flame behavior can also lead to extinction as for the case of the 1-D thermal-
diffusive pulsating instability. Candle flames in microgravity have displaye d flickering instabilities
prior to extinction (Dietrich et al. 1994). However the geometry of these flames is not optimal for the
study and verification of the 1-D pulsating instability, as predicted by theory, because of the potential

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame_SRD_20100125, p.19
text:
15
influence from the flame holding re gion which is premixed in natu re and hence could conceivably
initiate the oscillation. To better understand the m echanism for instability, the transient behavior of
spherical diffusion flames was co mputationally simulated using de tailed chemistry and transport
(Christiansen et al. 2002). Oscillatory instability, as shown in Fig. 1.14, was observed near both the
high velocity induced limit (low mass flow rate) and the radiative induced limit (high mass flow rate)
of the isola response of flame extinction,. These os cillations typically grow in amplitude until they
become large enough to extinguish the flame.

Attempts have been made to observe oscill atory instability through low-buoyancy experiments
conducted under the influence of normal gravity. Th e approach is based on the low-pressure droplet
experiment of Law and Williams (1973) , in which the effect of buoyancy was minimized in a low-
pressure environment, typically down to 0.1 atmosphere, beyond which kinetic effects would become

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame_SRD_20100125, p.19
text:
severe. Since the present porous sphere is much la rger than the droplets, buoyancy is still significant
at such a level. In order to further reduce buoyancy, an additional arrangement was implemented
(Yoo et al. 2002). This involved injecting the oxidizer gas into an environment of low molecular
weight fuel such as hydrogen and methane. Buoyan cy is reduced because the hot, low-density flame
sphere is now situated in an environment of low molecular weight gas. In the experiments various
gases (N2, CO2, He) were used to change the Lewis number and radiative properties of the gas so that
both the transport-induced and react ion-induced limits could be achie ved. Extinction was triggered
by gradually decreasing the H 2 concentration in the ambient. Results showed that, at the transport-
induced limit, extinction is char acterized by sudden quenching of th e flame, as demonstrated by a
rapid decrease of the radiometer signal voltage. However, at the radiation-induced limit, extinction is
preceded by oscillations in the flame luminosity that grow in magnitude before extinction, in
agreement with the calculation. It is also important to note th at both calculation and experiment
showed that flame oscillation is characterized by fluctuations in luminosity instead of flame

16
movement in that the extent of th e movement is much smaller than the thickness of the flame. This
observation offers interesting implications in flame control.
Studies using this approach, however, are limited for small flames, low pressures, low molecular
weight fuels, and the inverse-fl ame arrangement. Consequently, th e extent of investigation is
severely limited, and these low-pressure, normal gravity experiments cannot replace normal-pressure,
micro-gravity experiments. Additionally, gas-phase radiative loss is significantly smaller at such low
pressures, making radiative extinction phenomena difficult to study.
1.3.2 Structure and Response of Sooty Flames to a Non-Steady-State Initial Condition
Initially, partially premixed fl ames were planned for spaceflight testing. As such, preliminary
drop-tower experiments have been conducted for oxygen/propane and oxygen/ethylene mixtures,
diluted with argon and nitrogen, issued into air. Varying amounts of oxygen were added to the “fuel”
mixture, while keeping the pure fuel mole fraction fixed and altering the rela tive proportions of inert
(i.e. N2 and Ar) such that the adiabatic flame temperature of the systems were held constant.
The effect of oxygen addition on soot suppression is shown in Fig. 1.15, which presents two cases
with the same C 3H8 fuel concentration, adiabatic flame temperature, and flow rate. The 25%C 3H8 /

not only a function of the degree of partial premixing but also of the flow rate. Figure 1.16 shows

1.4 Summary
Fundamental combustion research has reached the very exciting stage of having the potential of
being quantitatively descriptive of simple phenomena and qualita tively descriptive of complex
phenomena. Attaining the goal of complete quantitative predictability, however, is hampered by the
lack of comprehensively developed and validated chemical kinetic a nd transport data base relevant
for high-temperature chemically reacting flows i nvolving the oxidation of complex fuels. The
proposed microgravity experiments on the aerodyna mically clean, burner-generated spherical
diffusion flames are expected to yield high-qualit y diffusion flame data that, together with those
acquired from homogeneous and premixed flame expe riments, will provide the needed information

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame_SRD_20100125, p.21
text:
and constraints for such a development and valida tion. It is to be emphasized that the one-
dimensional spherical diffusion flame is probably th e most desirable flame configuration for a study
of this nature, and that this flame is only realizable in the microgravity environment.
In the course of developing and validating the fundamental data sets, our proposed experiments
and the associated computational simulations w ill be concurrently yielding quantitative and
qualitative understanding on vari ous elemental flame phenomena. For example, by studying the
motion of diffusion flames, we will be able to fu rther scrutinize the universal importance of fuel
accumulation, which was originally found to be im portant in droplet burning. Furthermore, by
requiring quantitative predictability of the flame mo tion, we will be able to assess the importance of
radiation loss and re-absor ption. Other phenomena to be stud ied include the po tential onset of
pulsating and cellular instabilities in near-limit situations and their influences on flame extinction,
and soot formation. It is noted that each of these phenomena is a major area of study in its own right,
and the quality and meaningfulness of the study can be greatly facilita ted in microgravity
environments.
It is important to emphasize that while a major goal of the present investigation is to acquire

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame_SRD_20100125, p.21
text:
accurate data on phenomena affected by chemistry su ch as extinction, experiments performed in
ground-based low-gravity facilities could not una mbiguously demonstrate the occurrence of

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame_SRD_20100125, p.22
text:
18
extinction. Furthermore, wh ile extinction was indeed obser ved in the 1-g, low-buoyancy
experiments, the many special prov isions (low-pressure, low molecular-weight fuel, inverse flame)
required to achieve micro-buoyancy render the experi mental results of limited utility in terms of
kinetics studies. Long-duration, space-based experiments are therefore needed.
The last point we wish to mention is the proper strategy needed to tackle a research project of the
present nature, one that has an ex cessively long lead time before the first experimentation can be
conducted. It is important that during the time leading to the space expe rimentation, auxiliary
ground-based experiments complemented by com putational and analytical developments are
simultaneously conducted so as to produce as much supplemental information as possible in
anticipation of the eventual harvesting of the space-based da ta. Our low-buoyancy burner was
developed precisely with this objective in mind, and its usefulness has been repeatedly demonstrated.
Furthermore, while a substantial component of our program is based on quali tative and quantitative
verification, it must be recognized that some of the mechanisms and transport parameters to be
“validated” could actually be evol ving with time. Consequently the validation must be conducted

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame_SRD_20100125, p.22
text:
against the most current information that is availa ble at the time the space data are acquired. An
example is the soot formation kine tics. It would be ignorant of us to attempt to validate our space
data against any mechanism that is available at the tim e this document is prepared. It is precisely for
this reason that we have purposefully not menti oned any specific kinetic m echanisms for validation
because with the rapid rate with which research in this area is progressing, it is certain that our
understanding will be very different in several years. In order to be maximally benefited by costly
endeavors associated with space experimentation, one has to be informed and current in terms of
knowledge, and agile in adaptation and execution.

2.0 FLIGHT EXPERIMENT
2.1 Objectives of the Flight Investigation
Current experimental and theore tical capabilities make detailed, quantitative descriptions of
laminar flames situated in well-defined flow fields conceivable provi ded that comprehensive
chemical-kinetic and transport mechanisms are available. The comprehensiveness of these
mechanisms has been extensively tested for premix ed but not diffusion flames, especially in simple,
well-defined flow fields not comp licated by buoyant flows. A bur ner-generated spherical diffusion
flame provides a simple, one-dimensional flame ge ometry that permits a rigorous comparison
between detailed theory and experimental verifi cation. Existing theory and limited low-gravity
experimental results suggest th at quasi-steady spherical diffusi on flames can exist with some
combinations of fuel mixture supply rates and qui escent ambient oxidizers. With respect to the
steady flame conditions, altering fuel supply rates to limit flame residence time induces a convective-
kinetic extinction limit. Alternatively, very large residence times allow radiative heat losses and
diffusive transport mechanisms to quench the fl ame. Near these dual flammability boundaries of
quasi-steady flames, flame-front instabilities may appear before the flame is quenched.

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame_SRD_20100125, p.24
text:
We seek to investigate and improve the fidelity and comprehensiveness of the chemical kinetic
mechanisms and transport submodels used in th e simulation of aerothermochemical phenomena, and
consequently identify possible modifications, by ch aracterizing important unit combustion processes,
including: (1) the dynamics and extinction of diffusion flames, with emphases on fuel vapor
accumulation, radiation heat transf er, flame pulsation, and flame kinetics; and (2) the structure and
response of characteristically so oty flames, with emphases on fl ame front stability and soot
formation. Comprehensive predictive capability can be achieved by employing the simple flames of
Process (1) to interrogate and suggest modifications of the kinetic and transport data bases, and then
validate their adequacy in the chemically and aerodynamically more complex situation of Process (2).
A series of experiments is proposed with the fo llowing specific objectives , in both soot-free and
sooty flames, to compare with detailed computati onal simulation to assess transport properties and
detailed chemical kinetics (including chemiluminescence):
Objective A. Measure and characterize the transient st ructure (such as temperature and species
distribution) of diffusion flames established at in itially non-steady, spherical flame structures for

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame_SRD_20100125, p.24
text:
mixtures of different H 2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C 2H4/diluent ratios (sooty),
for different flow rates.
Objective B. Determine the quasi-steady convective/chem ical-kinetic extinction limits (low
system Damkohler numbers) and radiative/chem ical-kinetic extinction limits (high system
Damkohler numbers) for mi xtures of different H 2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-f ree) and different
C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty).
Objective C. Determine the existence (for different Zeldovich number, Ze), onset (as a
function Da), and nature (i.e. mode, frequency, amplitude) of pulsating inst abilities theoretically
predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that are
above a critical Lewis number.
2.2 Approach

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame_SRD_20100125, p.25

21
A series of experiments is proposed in which mixtures of various gaseous fuels and diluents will
be issued into an oxidizing envi ronment through a spherical porous burner and ignited to obtain,
nominally, a spherical, one-dimensional stabilized flame. Synchronized measurements are to be
made including spectrally resolved images, flame and burner temper atures, radiative flux
measurements, and system operating conditions (including reactant flow rates, ambient temperatures,
pressures and acceleration levels, etc.). These data are to be used for comparisons of flame behavior
and structure with detailed numerical simulations of the flames.
Conventional gaseous fuels including hydrogen, methane, and ethylene will be used. Hydrogen is
the simplest fuel and its reaction mechanism is also reasonably established. Methane is the simplest
hydrocarbon and extensive studies have been conduc ted on its combustion chemistry. Ethylene is a
typical sooty fuel and is also an important inte rmediate for the oxidation of higher hydrocarbons.
Diluents mixed with fuel are to include nitrogen and helium to adjust mixture diffusivities, and
carbon dioxide to influence flame radiation characteristics.
2.2.1 Flame Front Motion
To address the first experimental objective, fuel/dilu ent mixtures will be issued from the spherical

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame_SRD_20100125, p.25
text:
burner and ignited at flow rates expected to form flame fronts that move toward idealized steady-state
conditions. As the flame front move s, transient measurements of th e flame front velocity and flame
structure will be obtained using the imaging and radiometric system s. The flame characteristics will
be compared with predictions of the transient nume rical simulation of spherical diffusion flames for
evaluations of detailed chemical kinetic and transport sub-models.
2.2.2 Dual Quasi-Steady Extinction Limits at Low and High System Damkohler Numbers
The second experimental objective will be addre ssed in two parts, one each for low and high
system Damkohler number (Da) extinction-limit de terminations. To observe convective/chemical-
kinetic extinction at low Da, fuel/inert mixtures will be issued from the spherical burner and ignited
at initial flow rates expected (or known/observed) to form flames that evolve toward idealized steady-
state conditions. Following ignition and initial flame front movement, the fuel/inert flow rate will be
abruptly reduced to a second fl ow rate below the expected ex tinction limit. The quasi-steady
extinction is expected to occur as the flame adju sts to the reduced flow rate. To refine the
determination of the extinction flow rate for each fuel/diluent mixture, repeated tests are to be

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame_SRD_20100125, p.25
text:
conducted at successively lower initial flow rates and higher secondary flow rates.
To observe radiative/chemical-kinetic extinction at high Da, fuel/inert mixtures will be issued
from the spherical burner and ignited at flow rates above and beyond those expected (or
known/observed) to form steady flames when ra diative loss is consider ed. The quasi-steady
extinction is expected to occur as the flame fr ont moves outward before reaching the theoretical,
practically-non-attainable adiabatic steady-state radius.
At the low Da extinction limit, chemical kinetic rates will be retarded with respect to flow rates by
diluting the fuel stream with an inert gas that acts to decrease the flame temperature. Inert dilution
acts in principal to increase the extinction flow rate. Based on theoretical predictions, fuel/inert
mixtures are to be chosen for which the extinc tion flame radius is large enough to minimize the
effects of heat loss to th e burner. The surface temp erature of the burner will be directly measured to
quantify this loss.
At the high Da extinction limit, rates of ra diative emissions from the flame and radiative
reabsorption elsewhere are to be accentuated in so me cases by using a radiatively active diluent such
as CO2, recognizing the fact that it is chemically active as well. Sooty fuels could also be used to

30-day Operational Accomplishments Report
… for the International Space Station (ISS) Increment 63
ACME Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments
s-Flame Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames
The s-Flame investigation is one of several independent experiments that are part of the ACME
project, which uses a single modular set of hardware to carry out studies of flames burning
gaseous fuels in the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). The first round of s-Flame tests was
conducted during Increments 60 and 61, wh ile the second round was conducted fully within
Increment 63. There were no tests conducted in Increment 62 because of limited crew availability.
Prepared by the PI team and Dennis Stocker (dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov), the ACME Project
Scientist, who is the primary contact for s-Flame and ACME information.
Principal Investigator (PI): Prof. C.K. (Ed) Law, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ
Co-Investigator (Co-I): Prof. Stephen D. Tse, Rutgers University, Piscataway, NJ
Lead collaborator: Dr. Vladimir V. Gubernov, P.N. Lebedev Physical Institute of the
Russian Academy of Sciences , Moscow, Russia

I. Introduction

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.1
text:
Tests for the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment were
conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of
the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. The purpose of s-Flame
is to advance the ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction and
instabilities, of both soot-free and sooty flames. The results may contribute to the development
of lean-burn engines for improved efficiency and reduced pollutant emissions here on Earth.
The spherical flames are ignited at non -steady conditions and allowed to transition naturally
towards steady-state or extinction. Tests are conducted with various inert diluents in both the
fuel and chamber (oxidizer) atmosphere. The fuel gases include hydrogen and methane mixtures
for soot-free flames, and ethylene for sooty flames. One experimental objective is to identify the
extinction limits for both radiative and chemical kinetic extinction, i.e., where the flame
extinguishes from radiative heat loss or is “blown out, ” respectively. Another objective is to
determine the existence, onset, and nature of pulsating instabilities that have been theoretically
predicted to occur in flames with certain fuel/inert mixtures at near-limit conditions.

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.2
text:
ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63
2
More specifically, s-Flame has the following experimental objectives:
A. Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species
distribution) of diffusion flames established at initially non -steady, spherical flame
structures for mixtures of different H 2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot -free) and different
C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates.
B. Determine the quasi -steady convective/chemical -kinetic extinction limits (low system
Damköhler numbers) and radiative/chemical -kinetic extinction limits (high system
Damköhler numbers) for mixtures of different H 2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot -free) and
different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty).
A. Determine the existence (for different Zeldovich number, Ze), onset (as a function Da),
and nature (i.e. mode, frequency, amplitude) of pulsating instabilities theoretically
predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that
are above a critical Lewis number, at near-limit conditions.
As suggested by the experiment’s name, s-Flame features a spherically symmetric diffusion
flame, which is generated by discharging a fuel gas from a porous spherical burner into a still
oxygen/inert atmosphere in microgravity. The one-dimensional nature of the system facilitates

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.2
text:
data acquisition, data reduction, and computational simulation.
The space flight program consists of two main parts: (1) Mapping and characterization of the
motion (e.g., expansion) of spherical diffusion f lames subsequent to ignition and at extinction
because of the finite-rate chemistry and radiative heat loss. The study is focused on the thermal
radiation, the adequacy of the detailed chemistry and transport submodels used in
computational modeling, and the development of flame front instabilities that could modify the
extinction boundaries. (2) Studies of the response of cha racteristically sooty flames to ignition,
the onset of soot in the expanding flames, the soot radiation, and the soot’s effects on the flame
spread, extinction, and instability.
Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages
over normal -gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flame s, which is a buoyancy-
driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity.
Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame
structure. Momentum -dominated flames, whi ch are important for most practical combustion
systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.2
text:
much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of
characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.
The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many
microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames
advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.
For example, chemi-ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low
concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environme nt valuable for
evaluating the minor species chemistry. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to
new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational
environment of the combustion application.

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.3
text:
ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63
3
II. Methods/Research Operations
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol
The s -Flame investigation and other ACME experiments are configured, but not
conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc.
for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on th e modular ACME
chamber insert.
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload
Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the test s were all conducted in a
nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. As expected, no s-Flame tests
were conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in
response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry
stream. Thus far, that has been the case for all ACME tests, with the mundane exception
of ‘manually’ halting the test after the flame has extinguished or perhaps if a temperature
has reached a critical value.
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment.
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.3
text:
analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.
III. Results
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight
A total of 276 flames were ignited for the s-Flame experiment, with 29, 116, and 131
respectively ignited during Increment s 60, 61, and 63 . These numbers neglect some
flames which quenched promptly after ignition. In this regard, science testing began at
the end of Increment 60 and the first round of tests were completed during Increment
61. No tests were conducted in Increment 62 d ue to a lack of crew time , where the
second round of tests were fully conducted during Increment 63.
The tests were conducted in two rounds, where the first was conducted in increments 60
and 61 featured 145 flames (nominally) in which the fuel and oxygen (i.e., in the chamber
atmosphere) were diluted with nitrogen. The second round conducted in increment 63
featured 131 flames (nominally) in which the fuel and oxygen were instead diluted with
helium.
The s-Flame experiment does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but
the tests are i ndependently conducted with various gaseous fuels, including hydrogen,

for which the chemistry is relatively well understood.
No samples (e.g., of soot) were collected for s-Flame; all of the ISS results were

planned ACME experiments.

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.5
text:
ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63
5
B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies
1. Mission anomalies
While there were certainly issues with testing discussed in the next section, there
were no significant anomalies during s -Flame’s Increment 63 testing. However,
anomalies did occur during Increment 60 and 61 which led to corrective act ions
and/or make-up testing.
2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data
Ignition of the flames presented a significant challenge to the experiment during this
increment. All of the flame tests were conducted where the fuel and chamber
atmosphere were both diluted with helium rather than the nitrogen used in
Increments 60 and 61. The two gases’ properties are dramatically different making
comparison testing very desirable for ma nifestation of different phenomena .
Helium’s thermal conductivity is notably several times greater than that of nitrogen,
so considerably more energy and power was required to ignite the flames. The power
level was slowly increased from test to test unti l ignition was finally achieved on the
ninth test, where only seven flames were ignited of the 15 tests conducted on May 11
(20132), the first day for flames in Increment 63. The cautious approach was taken
because of concerns that the igniter tip might f ail (i.e., burn out) if too much power

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.5
text:
was applied. An igniter failure would have likely halted testing for weeks given the
need to schedule the commander’s time to replace the igniter tip.
After that first test day, the decision was made to have the igniter replaced with a coil
rather than loop design which was believed to be more robust because of the thicker
wire. Furthermore, the igniter tip had not been replaced in months, and the tips do
degrade with time, especially when they are not quickly retracted from the ignited
flames. The coil igniter was used successfully but still with caution, where flames were
not always ignited successfully. Subsequently, some tests were co nducted in
atmosphere with ~30% oxygen (by volume) instead of the planned ~21%. As one
would expect, that proved to be helpful for achieving ignition. But the end result was
that some tests were conducted with 21% oxygen, some at 30%, and some at both
nominal concentrations. Fortuitously, this mixture of conditions may provide deeper
insight into the mechanisms of flame dynamics and response.
Tests are also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite, where that occurred , for
example, during Increment 61 in tests 19304A4, 19304A6, 19308C1, and 20006A1.
That can be corrected by adjusting various test parameters and other settings. In this
case, adjustments were subsequently made to the ignition position (e.g., after

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.5
text:
19304A4 and 19304A6), the relative timing of the fuel flow and igniter activation (e.g.,
after 19308C1), and the duration of the igniter activation (e.g., after 20006A1). As
another example, failed ignition can result from false ignition detection and
deactivation resulting from the combina tion of settings for ignition and detection,
e.g., the gain for the Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module measuring the OH*
chemiluminescence. The latter, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.6
text:
ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63
6
ignited flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and
visible spectrum.
Testing on June 3 (20155) was cut short due to a combination of issues. The final test
was aborted due to an error with an Image Processing and Storage Unit (IPSU).
Consoles needed to be reset for the new increment, and there was an issue with the
Fuel Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA) Control Unit, i.e. the FCU. Rebooting
the FCU inadvertently set the valve safety timers to zero, which cannot be reset
without venting and refilling the combustion chamber with the intended atmosphere.
Those issues combined with an extended loss of commanding prevented further
science operations on that day. Therefore, an additional test day ( July 8, i.e., 20190)
was added to make up for lost science , e.g., whe re only one test was successfully
conducted at ~21% oxygen on June 3. The FCU was off nominal because of a high
carrier gas pressure in the Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP).
Imaging of the hydrogen flames was often an issue, where they were not apparent or hardly
visible to the operations camera and ACME DataCam, where the latter is the primary camera
for ACME testing. The testing with the extremely dim flames was limited to that conducted

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.6
text:
on Dec. 18 (19352), Jan. 24 (20024), June 3 (201 55), and July 8 (20190). This shortcoming
unfortunately inhibits assessment of the three -dimensional flame symmetry as the two
intensified cameras were opposite of each other.
The flow ranges of the selected Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) was found to be a
challenge, where it was discovered that the goal of studying both kinetic and radiative
extinction was not always satisfactorily achieved because of flow rate constraints.
At high flow rates, the burner does not produce spherically symmetric flames. While
nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center becomes increasing
offset from the burner center. More specifically, the flame is shifted toward the
supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of the porous sphere to the
supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the spherical burner. In other words, the
flow from the burner is not spherically symmetric. At sufficiently high flow rates, the
flame becomes obviously non-spherical, where it can appear to be ellipsoidal or even
parabolic in shape. In the latter case, the flame locally quenches near the supply tube.
When at a small fraction of the maximum flow rate, Mass Flow Controller (MFC)
performance has been seen to be poor during s-Flame testing, i.e., where actual flow
rate differed from that desired. However, this was not a surprise to those familiar

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.6
text:
with the hardware.
Flow perturbations have been noticed in some s -Flame tests, where ACME’s MFCs
used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and oxidizer have unfortunately not always
performed satisfactorily. In tests conducted using the 1 -slpm fuel MFC (where the
flow range is on a nitrogen basis), the flow has been seen to overshoot and
undershoot when first opening. Small flow irregularities have been most ap parent

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.7
text:
ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63
7
through their effect on the Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) measurements, e.g., of OH*
and CH* chemiluminescence. A momentary increase in fuel flow, as has occurred in
some s-Flame tests, naturally leads to increased light from the flame. The MFCs are
tested - without flames - after they are first installed. Adjustments are typically made
to (1) the setting that controls when the valves open and (2) the Proportional-Integral-
Derivative (PID) settings. This ACME activity has involved significant testing , where
there is an assortment of MFCs with different flow ranges for each of the three gas
types. While the MFC adjustments have been beneficial, they have not eliminated all
gas flow problems. It was seen in prior ACME testing that nitrogen oscillations (if any)
tend to damp with time, so a nitrogen pre -flow can be used so that such oscillations
might end before the flame is ignited. As another measure, the MFCs are re -zeroed
prior to each test, where that was another measure adopted in earlier ACME testing.
As mentioned previously, s-Flame tests have sometimes automatically aborted
(because of the controlling software script), where that is normally prior to gas flow
and the activation of the igniter – which is typical for other ACME experiments . As a

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.7
text:
result, there was little lost other than the available experimental time in the failed test
attempt. ACME aborts normally occur because of communication issues with an IPSU,
which for example happened for tests 19304A5, 19352D3, 19352P1, 20024N1, and
20024J1. A few other tests aborted because flow rates were accidentally specified
outside of the range of the installed mass flow controller(s), where that included for
example 19352A1, 19352D2, and 20013 C2. ACME aborts are infrequent, but there
are sometimes days when they occur repeatedly as can be seen here.
C. Completeness/Quality of Data
During Increments 60 and 61, nine days of tests were conducted during which 145 flames
were ignited for the first round of testing . In contrast, only 29 tests were specified as
required or highly desired in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Documen t
(ISRD) for that round. Therefore, a wealth of data was obtained for this round of testing
which featured gaseous fuels diluted by nitrogen.
However, there was a significant loss of data. Most importantly, the first fuel bottle
appeared to leak on installation (in Increment 60) and later on-orbit testing (in Increment
61) with other hydrogen/methane blends suggests that its fuel mixture would have been
ideal for achieving science success. Furthermore, there was significant image data loss

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.7
text:
on two different test days, specifically Sept. 13 (19256) and Dec. 18 (19352). As a result,
those test days were nominally repeated on Jan. 29 (20029) and Jan. 24 (20024),
respectively (i.e., in a reversed order). For these reasons, a simple comparison of the total
number of flames ignited (145) with that specified as required or highly desired (29) for
the first round of testing is somewhat misleading.
As discussed in the preceding section, the hydrogen and diluted -hydrogen flames were
not apparent or extremely dim in imaging from the operations camera and ACME
DataCam. Neglecting that factor, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.8
text:
ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63
8
gradually become ‘hot’ (i.e., dead) over time. While these bright spots are addressed in
image post-processing, they are a degradation of the image quality.
It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there
is not obvio us indication of this ; and it has thus far not been evaluated with available
measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS).
D. Status of Data Analysis [provided by Prof. Stephen Tse, Rutgers U.]
Image files are currently being processed. Radial position s of maximum CH*
chemiluminescence is being plotted against time. Different radii are being considered
and plotted together, as some flames are not completely symmetric. MFC and PMT data
are being compared with video images to assess and confirm experimental settings.
Radiometer data is being reviewed. Analy ses of the fiber pyrometry data are ongoing.
MATLAB code is used to isolate fiber images, which are then color assessed for
temperature.
Computational simulations with detailed chemistry and transport of the test cases are
underway. Time -dependent simulations will be compared with the time-dependent
experimental data , where tracking of the flamefront location is based on
chemiluminescent emission . Stea dy-state simulations will produce the Isola curves

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.8
text:
mapping flame response versus system Damkh öler number for given fuel mixtures. The
experimental cases will then be pin -pointed on the computational mapping s to assess
whether the experimental conditions are in quasi-steady state or near extinction limits,
either kinetic or radiative. Oscillation behavior will be correlated to possible pulsating
oscillations found in the simulations.
E. Preliminary Research Findings [provided by Prof. Tse and lightly edited by Stocker]
The s -Flame experiment utilize s spherically-symmetric diffusion flames and their
dynamics and responses to investigate fundamental processes, such as extinction,
instability, and soot formation.
The tests conducted on 19254 (near the end of Increment 60) revealed that a quasi-steady
flame could be attained for extended duration at low flow rate, i.e., 3 cc/s for 20%
C2H4/80% N2 (on a volume basis) . The flame was shut down by the automated system
because the burner reached a cut -off temperature of 250°C. Although the flame
oscillated near the end of the test, it was likely due to influence of the burner tube.
Comparisons with computation simulations will help to clarify the involved processes. For
higher flow rates, e.g., 5 -10 cc/s, with the same mixture, radiative extinctions were
observed. Generally, the flames showed unstable behavior near the burner tube prior to

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.8
text:
extinction, likely because o f lack of fuel mixture and heat loss in that region. Other
mixtures, e.g., 25% C2H4/75% N2 and 30% C2H4/70% N2, also showed radiative extinctions
at higher flow rates. For some cases, the pyrometry fiber interacted with the flame,
allowing determination of temperature in on -going analyses. Soot was observed only

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.9
text:
ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63
9
during ignition, which went away as the flame established itself. To assess whether these
nitrogen-diluted ethylene flames are non-sooty or sooty, cases were run where mixtures
were ignited and established at low flow rates (e.g., 3 cc/s) with low ethylene contents
(e.g., 25 -30% C2H4) and then ramped to high flow rates (e.g., 5 -10 cc/s) with higher
ethylene contents (e.g., 40 -50% C2H4). The flames all radiatively extinguished, but no
sooting was observed. Observations of such radiative extinction behavior at high flow
rates is an achievement because such phenomen on was not observed in our ground -
based studies, given the limited microgravity durations. Radiative reabsorption extends
flame size a t extinction. In ISS testing, radiative extinction has been found to be a
common event, which was predicted computationally, but not observed previo usly for
our flame conditions.
The 19256 tests (in Increment 60) were aimed at examining kinetic extinction. Similar to
the radiative extinction cases , sufficient microgravity duration is needed to observe
kinetic extinction because a near steady flame needs to be established first, before ramp
down in flow rate to find properly the chemical kinetic extinction limit. High flow rate
cases (e.g., 13.5 cc/s, 15 cc/s) showed asymmetrical flames which radiatively

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.9
text:
extinguished. Flow rates were lowered so that quasi-steady flames could be established
before ramp down in flow rate. The 15% C2H4 mixtures were not strong enough to sustain
a quasi-steady flame at 3 cc/s before ramp down. However, for stronger mixtures, i.e.,
20-30% C2H4, very nice flames were established at 3 cc/s; and kinetic extinctions were
observed during ramp down before reaching 1 cc/s. Radiative extinctions for ramp up
cases were also examined. Similarly, for stronger mixtures, i.e., 20 -30% C2H4, very nice
flames were established at 3 cc/s; and radiative extinctions were observed during ramp
up before reaching 8 cc/s.
Testing on 19304 investigated 45% CH4/55% N2 mixtures issuing into an air atmosphere.
The results indicated that the flow rates specified by the fuel MFC (0.5 slpm) were in the
regime of kinetic extinction. Quasi-steady flames could not be established. Furthermore,
larger flow rates could not be provided by the MFC, so observations of radiative extinction
could not be achieved. Even with a larger capacity MFC, characteristically larger flames
would be expected to be asymmetric. As such, nitrogen-diluted methane flames were
planned to be reexamined in increased oxygen atmosphere, i.e., 30% O2/70% N2.
Consequently, the 19308 tests investigated nitrogen-diluted methane flames in 30%

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.9
text:
O2/70% N2 atmosphere. Various methane concentrations from 45% down to 15% were
examined. For 45% CH4/55% N2, relatively long duration flames of ~15 s and ~10 s were
established at flow rates of 2 cc/s and 3 cc/s, respectively. At larger flow rates of 5 and
9.4 cc/s, the flames expanded to large radii and then extinguished. These flames
appeared to demonstrate radiative extinction. Reduction of flow rate from 2 cc/s to 1
cc/s resulted in extinction during ramp down, indicating kinetic extinction. For 30%
CH4/70% N2, flow rates of 3, 5, and 10 cc/s produced flames that expanded to extinction
(assumed radiatively); while reduction of flow rate from 3 to 1 cc/s resulted in presumably
kinetic extinction during ramp down. For 25% CH4/75% N2, flow rates of 5 and 10 cc/s

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.10
text:
ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63
10
yielded flames that expanded to extinction. For 20% CH4/80% N2, constant flow rate of
10 cc/s created a flame that expanded until extinction (assumed radiatively) ; while
reduction of flow rate from 10 cc/s to 1 cc/s resulted in wavering extinction during ramp
down, suggesting kinetic ex tinction. For 15% CH4/85% N2, flames were ignited, but
extinguished very quickly. These tests of 19308 suggest that they could manifest both
radiative and kinetic extinction for the conditions specified.
The 19352 tests examined various concentrations of H2 (45%-70%) diluted with N2 issuing
into air. The installed fuel MFC had a maximum output of 0.1 slpm, which unfortunately
provided a less-than-sufficient flow range where its use may have precluded the study of
radiative extinction corresponding to larger flame sizes. Imaging the diluted hydrogen
flames was a challenge, especially since the hobj image files from the ACME DataCam
were mis-formatted. Furthermore, little could be seen in the analog ops imaging, e.g.,
where it, like the DataCam and Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera, cannot
image the ultraviolet OH* flame emission (at 310 nm). Analysis of images from the Low
Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL -UV) camera and its OH* filter is ongoing. And as one might

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.10
text:
expect, little could be seen with the CFI intensified camera using its broadband CH2O filter.
Quasi-steady flames seem to be present at low flow rates (e.g. , 2.4 cc/s for 70% H2), as
inferred from PMT, pyrometry fiber emission, and b urner temperature observations.
Kinetic extinction seems to occur a s the flow rate is ramped down. There were various
problems with the IPSU and some tests aborted. Using the 100% H2 bottle with a higher
flow rate MFC was later performed for tests of 20024 (see below), which was a make-up
test day added because of the mis-formatting of the DataCam image files.
The tests conducted on 20006, using the 44.4% H2/55.6% CH4 bottle, examined 20%
H2/25% CH4/55% N2 mixtures issuing into air. Flames extinguished, some with wavy
oscillating behavior prior to extinction. However, it seems that even for very small flow
rates, e.g., 2 cc/s, extinction was by the radiative mechanism during flame
expansion. There was too little parameter room in terms of flow rate and burner size to
identify conclusively kinetic extinction durin g ramp down for these mixtures. In short,
radiative extinction (with local flame extinction and re -ignition seemed to occur prior to
ultimate extinguishment) during flame expansion after ignition was observed. However,
it is unclear whether ramping down the flow rate resulted in kinetic extinction. Detailed

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.10
text:
analyses of the data are needed. The various cameras seemed to capture the tests well.
The 20013 tests, which used the 66.7% H2/33.3% CH4 bottle, mainly investigated 30%
H2/15% CH4/55% N2 mixtures issuing into air. Radiative extinction was difficult to identify
conclusively because flames with larger flow rates, e.g. 15 cc/s, seemed to last, although
with patchy ex tinction areas, until time out. Larger flow rates could not be examined
either because of limited MFC range or distorted flame shape cause by burner limitations
at high flow rat es. Also, kinetic extinction during ramp down could not be identified
conclusively, as some flames seemed to extinguish because they were "going into the
burner."

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.11
text:
ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63
11
The 20024 tests using the 100% H2 bottle repeated and augmented conditions for those
of 19352 where the 0.1-slpm fuel MFC range was too low to examine radiative extinction
and the analog and intensified cameras did not pick up t he flame images at all or well.
Here, the 0.5-slpm fuel MFC was used and only a fused silica filter was used for the Cool
Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera. 45%-15% H2/N2 balance mixtures were
investigated. The flames at high flow rates, e.g., 10 cc/s, did not extinguish, appearing
quasi-steady until time out. The pyrometry fibers glowed, perhaps making good flame-
structure measurements, which will be evaluated subsequently. The flames seemed to
extinguish during ramp down, but further analysis is needed to assess kinetic extinction.
The tests conducted on 20029 used 50% C2H4/50% N2 and repeated and augment ed
conditions of 19256, when the images were not good. Again, the results indicated both
kinetic and radiative extinction phenomena under corresponding conditions . However,
no sooting flames were established, necessitating 100% C2H4 and an enriched oxygen
atmosphere to facilitate sooting behavior in possible future tests.
The 20132 tests kicked off a round of tests with helium -diluted fuel and oxidizer. The

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.11
text:
ambient was 21% O2 and 79% He. The fuel was composed of 25% H2, 20% CH4, and 55%
He. Using He as inert made igniting the mixture much more difficult compared to that for
the N2 inert cases of Round 1, using the same ignition parameters. The reason is believed
to be due to the 6X higher value in thermal conductivity of He versus that of N 2. As a
result, ignition parameters were varied, e.g., with a longer preheat time and higher
power, to achieve ignition for the He-diluted mixtures and ambient. The tests produced
flames at 3, 5, 7, and 10 cc/s that expanded outwardly quickly and extinguished. For 5, 7,
and 10 cc/s, the flames seemed to disappear and 're -ignite' with a "flash" before final
extinction. We are currently investigating the flash phenomenon. Moreover, the
radiation mechanism is not conclusive, as it appears different than for the N 2-diluted
cases. We did not have a chance to examine lowering of flow rates to assess kinetic
extinction.
The 20136 tests examined 20% H2/25% CH4/55% He issuing into 21% O2/He. For 5 cc/s
and 7 cc/s, the mixture ignites but imme diately extinguishes, with almost no observable
flame-front expansion. For 10, 13, 15, and 17.5 cc/s, the mixtures ignite, expand quickly,
and extinguish. We believe that the extinction mechanism is radiative and will compare
with computational simulations. For the cases with a ramp down in flow rate, the flames

seemed to extinguish before ramp down. Thus, we were not able to assess purely kinetic
extinction. Ignition parameters were varied to investigate thresholds for igniting the
mixture for differe nt flow rates. Only flow rates above 7 cc/s showed flame -front
expansion leading to extinction, with 17.5 cc/s showing a flash or wavering of the flame
before final extinction.
The test s conducted on 20142 investigated 30% H2/15% CH4/55% He issuing into 30%
O2/He. Elevated oxygen was approved for study, since ignition and extinction limits in
previous testing were affected by the high thermal conductivity of He. For 5, 7, 10, 15,

13, and 16.5 cc/s flow rates, nice flames were established that expanded to
wavy/oscillating extinction at the end, indicative of radiative extinction. For the cases
with a ramp down in flow rate, the flames seemed to extinguish during the ignition flow
rate stage before ramp down. Thus, we were not able to assess kinetic extinction.
The 20155 tests examined 45% H2/55% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He.
Previous tests using He as inert had shown that much larger energy and power are needed
to ignite the mixtures. For the 30% O2/H2 atmosphere, the tests produced flames at 10
and 14 cc/s (MFC limit of 1 SLMP) that expanded after ignition, but were extinguished by
the automated protocol because the burner reached the 250°C temperature limit before
any self-extinction could occur. The flames were not too large at the end. Presumably,
the thermally-conductive He diluent facilitates heat transfer to the burner. For the cases
with a ramp down in flow rate, i.e., starting at 10 and 14 cc/s and ramping down, the
flames seemed to self-extinguish during ramp down. Flow rate at 5 cc/s results in flames
that only existed briefly. Extinction at this lower flow rate is probably due to heat loss to
the burner, rather than pure kinetic extinction. Ramp down from 14 cc/s towards 5 cc/s

text:
resulted in the burner reaching the 250 °C limit during ramp down. More analyses are
needed. Tests at 21% O2/He atmosphere were limited. Fuel flow of 5 cc/s showed flash
ignition, but no sustained flame. Meanwhile, 10 cc/s resulted in a flame that seemed to
expand to self-extinction.
Testing on 20160 investigated 45% CH4/55% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He.
Without H 2 in the mixture, even larger energy and power were needed to ignite the
mixtures. For the 30% O2/H2 atmosphere, the 5, 10, and 15 cc/s flow rates were sooty
only at ignition; and the subsequent non-sooty flames expanded to self-extinction. At 3
and 4 cc/s, the mixtures flashed at ignition, and extinguished almost immediately. It was
not clear whether extinction was due to kinetic extinction or heat loss to the burner. At
6 and 7 cc/s, flames ignited with less soot, expanding with no soot to self-extinction. The
case with a ramp down in flow rate could not conclusively identify kinetic extinction.
More analysis is needed. Tests at 21% O2/He atmosphere needed even more energy and
power for ignition. At 5, 7, 10, and 15 cc/s, flames ignited with soot, and expanded quickly
to extinction.
The 20164 tests began study of ethylene-based flames, where 20% C2H4/80% He issued
into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He atmospheres. For 5 cc/s, the flame expanded and

remained quasi-steady until the burner limit temperature (250°C) was reached. At 6, 7,
10, and 15 cc/s, the flames expanded to extinction, with the higher flow rates (i.e., 10 and
15 cc/s) exhibiting sooty ignition. Fuel flow of 5.5 cc/s seemed to correspond to a
condition where the onset of oscill ating extinction was simultaneous with the burner
reaching the 250°C temperature limit. For the cases with a ramp down in flow rate, the
flames seemed to extinguish during ramp down, but heat loss to the burner may be the
mechanism of extinction. Althoug h 13 tests were conducted with the 21% O2/He

The tests performed on20170 investigated 25% C2H4/75% He issuing into 30% O2/He and
21% O2/He. At 5 and 5.5 cc/s, nice blue chemiluminescent flames were ignited, but
eventually were cut off because of the burner temperature limit being reached. At 6 cc/s,
a nice blue flame was ignited which expanded slowly to extinction. At 7, 10, and 15 cc/s,
sooty ignition occurred, but as the flames expanded, the soot went away, e ventually
resulting in radiative extinction. By ramping the flow rates up, starting at 5 cc/s, soot at
ignition was minimized, and the flames could expand to extinction. Ramp down of the
flow rate resulted in almost immediate extinction. For tests at 21% O2/He atmosphere,
cases at 5, 10, and 15 cc/s resulted in flames that expanded quickly to extinction. Less
soot was present at ignition compared with that for the 30 % O2/He atmosphere cases.
Consistent ignition was not always achieved for the same conditions, which is puzzling.
Testing on 20176 explored 30% C2H4/70% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He. At
5 cc/s, a long duration flame was established that eventually reached the burner
temperature limit. At 6, 7, 10, and 15 cc/s, the flames were sooty at ignition, but the soot
dissipated; and they expanded to extinction. Ramping up the flow rates, starting at 5 cc/s,

name: ACME s-Flame
title: ACME s-Flame: s-Flame 30-day report Inc 63 20201216, p.13
text:
minimized soot at ignition and resulted in flames that slowly expanded to extinction. For
tests at 21 % O2/He atmosphere, cases at 5, 10, and 15 cc/s resulted in flames that
expanded to extinction. At 4 cc/s, the flame lasted a while before eventual e xtinction.
The 3 cc/s case did not ignite. Ramp down of the flow rate seemed to result in flames
that extinguished quickly before the protocol could ramp down the flow rate.
The last testing of Round 2, which was a makeup of 20155, occurred on 20190, with 45%
H2/55% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 21 % O2/He. For both oxygen concentration
environments, flow rates resulting in expanding flames lasted for a while, but were cut
off by automated protocol before self-extinction when the burner temperature limit was
reached. As for cases where the flow rates were ramped down, extinction detection was
observed for both oxygen concentration environments. We are currently analyzing the
data to determine if extinction was kinetic or due to heat loss to the burner. A last set of
tests were conducted with a reduced oxygen concentration atmosphere, i.e., 17.5 %
O2/82.5% He. Some cases indicated that radiative and kinetic extinction were possibly
observed.
In summary, selected preliminary findings from this testing include:
o Cases run for nitrogen-diluted methane and ethylene flames and in air seemed to

indicate kinetic extinction at low flow rates and radiative extinction at high flow
rates. As previously mentioned above (and in our report for the pr eceding
increment pair ), such phenomena were not observed in our ground -based
research, given the limited microgravity durations. Nevertheless, comparisons
with computational simulations are needed to assess better the extinction
behavior.
o Cases run for nitrogen-diluted hydrogen flames seemed to show kinetic extinction
at ramp down. However, for the mass flow rates that could be accommodated,
radiative extinction was not observed.
