1.0 INTRODUCTION
1.1 Purpose
This document will eventually hold most of the info rmation needed to operate the SAME experiment on
ISS from the ground from the TSC. It will also descri be alternate methods of performing tasks when the
experiment hardware is not on ISS, but is instead e asily accessible. For now, however, this document is a
place to collect miscellaneous operational information and methods that need to be documented and under
configuration control.
1.2 Scope
TBD.
1.3 Applicable Documents
[1] SAME-DOC-005 Software Interface Control Document

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Operations Manual_007, p.7
text:
SAME-DOC-007
2
2.0 IN-FLIGHT FUNCTIONAL CHECKLIST
This is a list of items that should be addressed after the hardware is installed in the MSG and before any
samples are tested. Not currently in any order.
- Perform piston calibration and alter registry values as necessary. See procedure later in this
document. Run a test with heater setpoint below R0 and no use of the thermal precipitors in order
to confirm correct calibration.
- Figure out good values for STSPumpFailureLowLimit and STSPumpFailureHighLimit registry
values. These depend somewhat on atmospheric pressure and should be adjusted for the ISS
environment. Correctly set, these values help detect failure of the STS pump.
- Log some data with the P-Trak and DustTrak and confirm that their settings are correct. For
example: log interval, time constant, and date/time.
- Record some video, downlink, and examine.
- Experimentally determine the maximum setpoints that the mass flow controller will meet given
ISS vacuum and GN2 sources. Determine if any desired inlet velocities or diagnostic
combinations are affected.
- The registry value, DisableChecksumCheck, can be set to 1 to avoid the startup delay associated
with calculating the checksum each time.
- Revisit the decision about whether the heater controller offset correction will be done

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Operations Manual_007, p.7
text:
automatically as part of the test sequence or manually using the HeaterCorrectOffset utility prior
to the test sequence. Adjust the CorrectOffset registry value appropriately.

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Operations Manual_007, p.8
text:
SAME-DOC-007
3
3.0 STARTING THE SOFTWARE
3.1 Ground Computer
On the ground computer you’ll need to first log on. Then start TReK with SAME configuration files.
Also start SAMEDisplay. More TBD.
3.2 SAME Flight Software
The software that controls the system starts automa tically upon power on. Within 30 seconds of turning
on 120V power to the system there should be telemetr y data received at the SAMEDisplay application.
The GMT will be updating and startup messages will appear in the log window. The Run Mode will
change from Startup to Unitialized.

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Operations Manual_007, p.9
text:
SAME-DOC-007
4
4.0 TEST CHECKLIST
This is a list of important things to do or confirm pr ior to, during, and after the running of a sample test.
Placement of a highly visible printout of this lis t on console is recommended. Steps depend on whether
sample heater offset correction is being done automatically or manually. Check the CorrectOffset registry
value to find out (0=manual, >0=automatic).
- Once per carousel open the gate valves and turn on the diagnostics for TBD minutes. Downlink
the data and verify correctness. The purpose is to collect baseline measurements of the MSG work
volume required by the science team.
4.1 With Automatic Heater Offset Correction
- Power on the system, wait for telemetry reception.
- Send the Initialize command.
- If the desired sample is not engaged, engage it using the Self Test command.
- Turn on the 12VDC Heater Power.
- Note the sample resistance and compare to ground measured resistance. If they differ
significantly, TBD. Determine the setpoint.
- Look at test parameters and change as necessary. Use manual positioning option, but carousel and
sample number must be correct.
- Start the test.
- When the test pauses check the following:
o A “sample type is confirmed” message appears in the log.
o The offset correction returned a value less than 50uV in the log.
o The sample resistance is still good. Within TBD % of before.

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Operations Manual_007, p.9
text:
o The desired diagnostics are powered and readings are nominal.
o GN2 regulated pressure and vacuum pressure are good. Range is TBD.
- If the offset correction returned a value greater than 50uV, abort the test and restart. If the offset is
still greater than 50uV, change the CorrectOffset registry value to 0 (manual) and use the manual
heater offset correction checklist instead.
- Resume the test.
- Watch the log for details about when the sample heater will start. When it does, be ready to send
an Abort command.
- Watch the sample resistance and compare to the desired setpoint and MaxRt. The software will
too, and will abort heating if the resistance/temperature gets too high. But watch anyway and send
the Abort command in the highly unlikely event of too high resistance/temperature.
- After sample aging, during exhaust, watch the output of the diagnostics for unexpected results.
- After test is complete, power on any P-Trak or DustTrak that was used and retrieve the latest
logged test ids. Turn back off.
- As desired, force a transfer of the current housekeeping and log files to the MLC. Their transfer
during power down has a slight chance of failing. Doing it here ensures success.
- Perform any other desired OS or system maintenance, such as directory listings or self tests.
- Disengage the sample.

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Operations Manual_007, p.10
text:
SAME-DOC-007
5
4.2 With Manual Heater Offset Correction
- Power on the system, wait for telemetry reception.
- If the desired sample is engaged, DO NOT send the Initialize command.
- If the desired sample is not engaged, send Initialize, engage sample using the Self Test command,
and send Shutdown command with Restart option to bring system back to uninitialized state.
- Send the OSCommand command with parameter ‘/root/HeaterCorrectOffset_g’. If this command
returns 0 in the log, then proceed, otherwise repeat until it does. (Look at the value returned, not
the details message which always says the same thing.) See section 7.5 for details about the
HeaterCorrectOffset utility.
- Send the Initialize command.
- Turn on the 12VDC Heater Power.
- Note the sample resistance and compare to ground measured resistance. If they differ
significantly, TBD. Determine the setpoint.
- Look at test parameters and change as necessary. Use manual positioning option, but carousel and
sample number must be correct.
- Start the test.
- When the test pauses check the following:
o A “sample type is confirmed” message appears in the log.
o The sample resistance is still good. Within TBD % of before.
o The desired diagnostics are powered and readings are nominal.
o GN2 regulated pressure and vacuum pressure are good. Range is TBD.
- Resume the test.

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Operations Manual_007, p.10
text:
- Watch the log for details about when the sample heater will start. When it does, be ready to send
an Abort command.
- Watch the sample resistance and compare to the desired setpoint and MaxRt. The software will
too, and will abort heating if the resistance/temperature gets too high. But watch anyway and send
the Abort command in the highly unlikely event of too high resistance/temperature.
- After sample aging, during exhaust, watch the output of the diagnostics for unexpected results.
- After test is complete, power on any P-Trak or DustTrak that was used and retrieve the latest
logged test ids. Turn back off.
- As desired, force a transfer of the current housekeeping and log files to the MLC. Their transfer
during power down has a slight chance of failing. Doing it here ensures success.
- Engage the next desired sample using the SelfTest command. Engaging the next sample here
shortens the time for starting the next test.
- Perform any other desired OS or system maintenance, such as directory listings or self tests.
- Send the Shutdown command with Shutdown option and power off system, or proceed to next
test.

title: SAME: SAME_Operations Manual_007, p.11
text:
SAME-DOC-007
6
5.0 RUNNING A TEST
5.1 Initialization
Select the Initialize button on the System tab, sending the Initialize command, and wait until the Run
Mode changes from Unitialized to Ready.
5.2 Setting parameters
From the Testing tab, select Change… to change to the set of test parameters you want to look at. Create
a new test by selecting the CreateNew button. Select Set anywhere in the window to change the
parameter for the selected test.
The Test Setup group box is the way to choose which di agnostics to use. Select the Pri. or Sec. radio
button to see the difference in setup between primary and secondary aging.
Heater Control Setpoint should be set after knowing the unheated resistance of a sample, a.k.a. R0.
Nominal setpoints are a multiple, Rt/R0, of R0 depending on sample type:
Sample Type Setpoint Multiplier, Rt/R0
DBP TBD
Kapton 1.380
Lampwick 1.245
Silicone 1.327
Teflon 1.440
To find the R0 of a sample, engage the sample to th e inlet tube either by manual blocking or using the
SelfTest command with EngageSample option (on Syst em tab). Then on the Smoke Generation tab turn
on the 12 VDC Heater Enable (right click on the ‘ LED’ and select ‘Set On’). Sample Resistance will
settle to a valid measurement within 4 seconds.
5.3 Registry File Concerns
Assuming you’ve set the test parameters to a specif ic carousel number, sample number, heating setpoint

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Operations Manual_007, p.11
text:
and duration, you may think you are ready to go. Y ou may not be. There are a bunch of sample-related
limit checks that may cause an error or warning prior to heating. There are also many timing constants
that affect the system behavior. These can be cha nged by selecting Set Registry… on the System tab.
See SAME-DOC-005, Software Interface Control Document for key names and descriptions. A system
timing simulator, currently located in SAMEFluidMode l.xls, will be available on console to help see the
effect of registry value changes. Testing with the engineering unit is also recommended.
Alternately, registry values can be changed by editing the registry.txt file on the DACU. This file is
located in the /config directory. Also in that dir ectory is registry.orig.txt which contains the original
registry settings.
Important: Changes to registry values will not take e ffect until you restart the software. Follow the
steps for shutting down, below, but use the restart parameter option.

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Operations Manual_007, p.12
text:
SAME-DOC-007
7
5.4 Running the Test
From the Testing tab select Start… and enter the test number to run, if it hasn’t already been entered in
the field, and select Send.
After sample positioning and aging chamber setup has occurred the test will pause so you can examine
the log for any warnings or errors. Then send the Resu me button. The test should proceed to finish. You
can abort anytime by sending the Abort command. An abort causes all valves to be turned off as well as
all diagnostics.
5.5 Shutdown
It is recommended that the system be gracefully shut down using the Shutdown button on the System tab,
then cut power about 2 minutes later. Current housek eeping and log files are transferred to the laptop
during the first minute. Use the second minute to ensu re that the system did not restart, looking for the
restart of low rate telemetry packets and updating GMT. If the system restarts, select Shutdown again or
send the OS command with parameter, ‘/bin/shutdown –b’.
5.6 Self-Tests
The flight software has a few operations available through the SelfTest command. These may be useful
for other than self-test purposes, for instance to engage a sample to the inlet tube to check R0. Parameters
depend on the self test:
Self Test Parameter Definition
Disengage Carousel no parameters
Increment Carousel no parameters, rotates carousel one position
Engage Carousel no parameters

Parameter2: duration in seconds
ISS Detector no parameters
Fill Chamber Parameter1>0: Fill rate is this parameter divided by 10 in LPM
Parameter1=0: Fill rate is ChamberSelfTestFillRate registry value
Parameter2 not used.

value

Sample Heater Parameter1>0: Duration in seconds
Parameter1=0: Get previous run’s data and save to file. Do not heat

SampleHeatingSelfTestRatio registry value.
STS Detector no parameters
Watchdog Timer no parameters. System will reset in 2 minutes.

text:
SAME-DOC-007
8
6.0 PROCESSING FILES
6.1 Transferring files from DACU to the MLC
All files will be automatically transferred from th e DACU to C:\ftp on the MSG laptop. Housekeeping
files (.hkp) are transferred on the hour and upon shut down (with either the shutdown or restart option).
The Log file is also transferred upon shutdown. P- Trak, DustTrak, and heater files are transferred soon
after they are created. P-Trak and DustTrak file s are not automatically created since their data is
embedded in the housekeeping data. To explicitly retrie ve logged data select the Transfer Data button on
the DustTrak and P-Trak tabs. This should be do ne no more frequently than once per minute because the
filename is derived from the GMT, including the latest minute, but not the latest second.
If you need the data immediately or a file doesn’t get downlinked for some reason you’ll have to do it
manually using one of two methods described here:
6.1.1 Using SAMEDisplay and FTP Cmd command.
You’ll need to identify what file you need and the dir ectory it is in. Files are stored in a directory named
according to GMT year and day. For instance /data/2006_132/. The .log file will be named
2006_132_00.log in this example. Housekeeping files will be 2006_132_15.hkp, 2006_132_16.hkp, etc.
according to the GMT.

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Operations Manual_007, p.13
text:
With the flight software and SAMEDisplay running (does not need to be Initialized), select the FTP Cmd
from the System tab. Type: LCD /data/2006_132, for example, to change local directory (on the DACU)
and send the command. Then select FTP Cmd again a nd type: PUT 2006_132_16.hkp, for example, and
send the command. Watch your letter case – it matters.
6.1.2 Using SAME processor command line to transfer files
For this to work you’ll need a keyboard and mon itor connected to the GSE port on the SAME DACU.
Also, verify that the switch on the SAME DACU is sw itched to Override position. This is obviously a
ground use only method.
From the command line on the GSE monitor (if the so ftware is running you can get another console
window by typing <CTRL><ALT>n, where n is 1 or 2), na vigate using cd and ls to the directory with the
file you want to transfer. Type: ftp 192.168.1.1 <Enter>. Type: anonymous<Enter> for name and just
<Enter> for password. Then at ftp> prompt t ype: bin<Enter>, then t ype: put 2006_ 132_16.hkp, for
example. File should end up in C:\SAME Data on laptop. After done transferring file(s), type:
bye<Enter> on the DACU.
You can also use the two above methods to transfer files to the DACU using GET and get instead of puts.
6.2 Converting Housekeeping file to engineering units
Use SAMEFileConverter. More instructions TBD.

text:
SAME-DOC-007

7.0 MISCELLANEOUS PROCEDURES AND INFORMATION
7.1 Obtaining a directory listing
An example:
- OSCommand(‘ls –l /data/2006_237 > /data/dir.txt’).
- FTPCommand(‘LCD /data’).
- FTPCommand(‘PUT dir.txt’).
- Have MSG cadre downlink the file dir.txt.
7.2 Replacing the registry file
Normally you would change individual entries usi ng the SetRegistry command. This method could be
used to set the registry to a known state, perhaps a f ile under source control, using an uplinked file. And
this is the only way I could get the copied-over registry.txt file to ‘take’. If the system is shut down nicely
through the shutdown command then it appears to revert to the old registry file.
- FTPCommand(‘LCD /config’).
- FTPCommand(‘GET registry.new.txt’)
- OSCommand(‘cp /config/registry.txt /config/registry.old.txt’)
- OSCommand(‘cp /config/registry.new.txt /config/registry.txt’)
- Do a hard shutdown: power off
- Power on and the new settings should take effect.
7.3 Piston Calibration
Piston calibration, a.k.a. piston characterization, is a process of adjusting some registry values so that
piston rates and time marks are correct for current conditions. This process should be performed
whenever there is a change of hardware, especially the aging chamber and piston itself; a change of
environment, such as the move to the ISS; a change of fluid source strength; or a change of hardware

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Operations Manual_007, p.14
text:
condition, perhaps after many tests have been run.
7.3.1 Inlet Velocity
Actual inlet velocity is required to match desired inle t velocity to within +/- 0.5 cm/sec. Actual velocity
is not a directly measured value. It is a function of piston bottom to top travel time, chamber volume, and
inlet tube diameter. The equation is:

where, v = actual velocity (cm/sec)
V = chamber volume (L) = 5.65
t = piston travel time (seconds)
2.105 = conversion beween LPM and cm/sec
Increasing the registry value, FillLeakRateLPM, will in crease the actual velocity. To determine piston
travel time, perform the following steps:
- Run a test with the desired inlet velocity and no heating (setpoint set below R0 and/or heater
duration set to zero and/or no sample engaged.)
- Abort the test during or after the aging period.
- Obtain the drive side pressure data during chamber fill and graph it.

text:
SAME-DOC-007

- Pick the points where the piston begins moving, characterized by the start of increasing pressure,
and where the piston stops moving, characterized by drastically decreasing pressure.
- Subtract the start time from the stop time and calculate velocity. Adjust FillLeakRateLPM and
repeat as necessary.
7.3.2 Sample Heating Start Time
Ideally, the start of sample heating is calculated so that the end of sample heating occurs before the piston
reaches the top of the chamber. Actually, even before that, so that most of the smoke in the inlet tube at
the end of heating enters the chamber as well. And really, even before that, so that some clean air follows
the ‘last’ of the smoke and more of the smoke enters the chamber. The amount of the latter clean air is
determined by the BackEndCleanAirOffset registry value.
Because there is no direct physical measurement of where the piston is in the middle of its stroke, the
software must estimate when the stroke begins and how long the stroke will take. Then it can back off
from there to determine sample heating stop and start times. The registry values, FillWaita.b, where a.b is
0.0 to 5.0 by 0.5, help compensate for timing inconsis tencies which are a function of fill rate in LPM.
(These values were more drastically a function of f ill rate before the FillLeakRateLPM registry value was

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Operations Manual_007, p.15
text:
increased from 0.0. See section 7.3.1.).
Piston chamber fill movement begins by evacuating the the drive side of the piston at a rate of 3.0 LPM
until the drive side pressure reaches 13.2 psia. These values have been determined to be reliable, but can
be changed if necessary by altering the registry values, FillStartRateLPM and FillStartPressurePSIA.
Then the software waits for a period determined by th e desired fill rate, a function of inlet velocity, and
the FillWait registry values. For a fill rate of 3.0 the software waits for the value of FillWait3.0. For rates
in between, the wait time is interpolated. After wai ting this time the software marks the start of piston
movement, logging a message for the user. Sample heating and other start and stop times are based on
this mark. To determine the best FillWait registry values,

- Fill the chamber using the SelfTest command and the rate.
- Note when the drive side pressure reaches 13.2 psia. The software issues a “x seconds before
piston moving mark” message to indicate this point. The aim of this procedure is to get the ‘x’
right.
- Note when the piston reaches the top of the chamber. Visual confirmation is best, but

7.3.3 Secondary Aging Volume
When a secondary aging period and volume are speci fied, the piston must stop a percentage of the
distance between the top and bottom of the chamber. There is no direct physical measurement of the
running distance, therefore it is estimated from th e exhaust rate over time. The registry value,
ExhaustPercentageCorrectionFactor, is applied to the running percentage. To adjust this value,
- Perform a SelfTest to exhaust the chamber to a specific percentage. For best results use the
exhaust rate and secondary volume that will be used during the actual test. Or use 5 LPM and
50%.
- Perform a SelfTest to exhaust the chamber the rest of the way. Use the same rate and 100%.
- Calculate the time taken for each portion using log messages or pressure data and figure the
percentage of total time taken by the second exhaust. Adjust the registry value and repeat until
this percentage is within the desired accuracy of the secondary aging volume percentage.
7.3.4 Exhaust Rate
It was verified that the system exhausts at a rate sufficient to achieve overpressure of the diagnostic duct
for all combinations of diagnostic use except when usi ng the STS detector with both DustTraks. If this
situation changes, the exhaust rate can be increased using the ExhaustOverpressureRate registry value.
7.4 Changing flight software during flight

7.5 Description of HeaterCorrectOffset Utility
Sample heater offset correction is a feature of the sample heater microcontroller that reduces
measurement error by automatically removing off set voltages from the signal path. After offset
correction is performed, all subsequent resistance me asurements will include the o ffset correction. Until
the system is powered off, that is. At power up the offset correction is zero. Offset correction should be
run for each sample while the sample is engaged with the inlet tube and sample heater contacts.
Occasionally the offset correction circuitry produces a co rrection that is obviously too high. The result is
that subsequent reports of resistance are lower than ac tual. This can be detected at the time of the test

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Operations Manual_007, p.17
text:
pause by looking at the sample resistance and by lo oking for the log message indicating the value of the
offset correction. It should be approximately 200uV or less.
If the offset correction at the time of the test pause is too high, then the test must be aborted and restarted
to give the offset correction circuitry a second chan ce. To avoid this time-consuming detour a utility
separate from the flight software has been developed. It is HeaterCorrectOffset_g in the /root directory of
the DACU. It can be run from the flight software by sending the OSCommand command with a
parameter of ‘/root/HeaterCorrectOffset_g’.
The HeaterCorrectOffset utility app lies 12VDC to the sample heater , waits a few seconds, and then
requests an offset correction from the heater microcontro ller. If the returned off set is in range then the
utility exits, otherwise it requests the offset correction ag ain for several times until it is in range. Either
way, 12VDC is removed from the sample heater befo re the utility exists. As long as system power (not
12VDC) remains applied, the offset correction initiated by the utility will be used by the flight software.
If the utility fails to correct the offset to within the desired range then it returns a -1 (which is reported in
the flight software log as 65280), otherwise it returns a zero to indicate success.

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Operations Manual_007, p.17
text:
There is one caveat to running the HeaterCorrectOffset utility. The flight software must be either not
running, which will not occur during flight, or must be in the uninitialized state. Once the software is
initialized the utility cannot gain serial access to the heater micr ocontroller. Thus the sequence
gymnastics in section 4.0.
Additionally, if the HeaterCorrectOffset utility is used, then offset correction prior to the test pause should
be disabled. Otherwise an incorrect correction he re will negate the use of the utility. Setting the
CorrectOffset registry value to zero will disable au tomatic offset correction during the test, allowing the

8.0 KNOWN ISSUES
- Aborting a test occasionally causes the software to restart. If this should happen you’ll need to
reissue the Initialize command.
- Try to avoid running a test sequence through the change of hour (i.e. 12:45-13:05). Transfer of
the housekeeping file at the top of the hour takes a good bit of processor time and the processor is
close to 100% capacity, possibly affecting diagnostic measurement retrieval.
- It is recommended that the system be gracefully shut down using the Shutdown button on the
System tab, then cut power about 2 minutes later. However, about 20% of the time the software
will hang or restart before completely shutting down. If it restarts, issue the Shutdown command
again or issue the OS command with parameter, ‘/bin/shutdown –b’. If it hangs (you may only
know this if you have a monitor connected to the GSE port) a hard power off will have to suffice.
The operating system will clean up any file ‘litter’ on the next power up.
- Maximum inlet velocity with the FillLeakRateLPM registry value equal to 0.30 is 9.8 cm/sec.
Above this the software does not correctly use the FillWait registry values to time chamber fill
operations, including sample heating start time. 10.0 cm/sec can be achieved if FillLeakRateLPM
is 0.25 LPM or less. But timing is affected in other ways and ground testing or flight testing

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Operations Manual_007, p.19
text:
without sample heating is recommended.
- Whenever the P-Trak is on, the DACU requests a measurement from it once per second.
Occasionally the P-Trak does not respond with a measurement and the DACU substitutes a -999
value instead to mark this occurance. If the P-Trak is logging during this time, that missing data
can be recovered by issuing the Transfer Data command to retrieve the logged data. It is
recommended that this be done for each test, soon (within days) after the test is complete.
- The P-Trak memory can hold approximately 60 20-minute tests. When all memory is used the
unit does not respond with any serial measurements while logging. In other words, continuous -
999 readings is one indicator of full memory. It is suggested that memory be cleared after 50
tests to be safe.
- Sample heater offset correction occasionally produces an incorrect correction factor. The result is
that reported sample resistance is lower than actual. For more information see section 7.5.
- Using ground support equipment there was insufficient fluid flow during chamber exhaust to
maintain overpressure of the diagnostic duct, as required, when the STS detector and both
DustTraks are in use. When the STS detector is used it is recommended that at most one
DustTrak is used.
- If the heater gives an “Abort on MaxRt” error, the system must be power cycled before

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Operations Manual_007, p.19
text:
proceeding. Otherwise, as will be apparent, the resistance measurement will be in error.
- When specifying inlet velocities below 2 cm/sec, the FillWait registry values may not be
accurate. The registry value, BackEndCleanAirOffset, must be adjusted to ensure correct heater
timing. For 1 cm/sec, a value of 170 seconds is good. But run a test with no heating to be sure.
- During ground testing the connection between the DACU and the MSGSimulator occasionally
drops out. Packet count numbers of the MSGSimulator no longer increment and change from
green to blue. To reestablish the connection deactivate it and activate it again.

title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.3
text:
iii
Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)
Abstract
Leaks, fires, and spills are some of the most significant hazards that must be accounted for in the
design of the environmental control and life-su pport system on spacecraft. While prevention is
certainly the first line of defens e against a fire, early detection of a overheat event or an actual
fire allows the crew to res pond before the hazard gets out of control. The limited options
available for response to a spacecraft fire increas e the importance of dete cting the fire in an
earlier stage of its development than is typical for terrestrial applications. This report describes
the outcomes of the Smoke Aerosol Measurements Experiment (SAME), an experiment
conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) on the International Space Station (ISS)
to characterize the size distribution of smoke part iculate produced in low- gravity from a variety
of overheated spacecraft material s The absence of gravity can im pact not only the formation of
the smoke particulate but also th e aging and coagulation processes that occur as the particulate
are transported from their source to a detector.
Based on the results of an earlier flight project carried out in th e Glovebox of the Space Shuttle,
(Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD)), the soot particles gene rated and observed in low gravity

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.3
text:
environment tend to be larger in size than t hose in earth conditions. Ho wever, the preliminary
results of CSD project were not conclusive because of a minor variation of the temperature of hot
wire which heated the test sample to generate smoke, and also because the CSD apparatus could
not measure the liquid drops existing in the smoke produced by several of the samples.
Furthermore, the CSD project was not designed to provide on-orbit measurement of the particle
size distribution. The Smoke Aerosol Measurement E xperiment was designed to obtain this data
that could then be used to design the next-generation smoke detectors for space exploration
missions. Unfortunately, because of the relati vely small volume of the MSG, it cannot
accommodate the instruments normally used in a ground-based laboratory to measure the size
distribution of smoke particul ate. Therefore, a new proce dure was developed, the moment
method, from which the characteristics of the part icle size distribution can be inferred using a
minimum number of portable instrument.
The SAME experiments were conducted during E xpedition 15 on the ISS. Four materials,
typical of those found in spacecr aft, were tested including cellulose (lamp wick), Kapton,
silicone rubber, and Teflon. A fift h material, dibutyl-phthalate (D BP) retained in a cotton wick

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.3
text:
was used as a reference. In order to simulate the detection of a pre-fire overheated-material event,
samples were heated to temperatures below th e ignition point. The smoke generation conditions
were controlled to provide repeatable sample surface temperatures and air flow conditions. The
transport time from the smoke source to the det ector was simulated by holding the smoke in an
aging chamber for times ranging from 10 seconds to 1800 seconds. Smoke particle samples
were collected on Transmission Electron Microsc ope (TEM) grids for post-flight analysis. The
smoke properties were measured using particulat e aerosol diagnostics that measure different
moments of the size distribution. These statistic s were combined to determine the geometric
mean particle sizes and geometric standard devia tion, which is sufficient to describe the entire
smoke distribution if a lognormal distribution is assumed. For comparison, smoke detectors from

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.4
text:
iv
the ISS and the space shuttle we re also included in the SAME apparatus. The experimental
results show that, for the materials tested, a su bstantial portion of the smoke particles are below
500 nm in diameter. The smoke transport model demonstrated that mixing dominates the smoke
transport and that consequently detection time lags are longer than in normal gravity. The
knowledge gained from SAME can be used to es tablish design requirements for smoke detectors
used in future spacecraft.

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.11
text:
1
1. Introduction
Appropriate design of fire detection systems require s knowledge of both the expected signature of the
events to be detected and the bac kground levels of the measured parame ters. Terrestrial fire detection
systems have been developed based on extensive study of terrestrial fires. 1, 2 Unfortunately, there is no
corresponding data set for spacecraft fires and cons equently current spacecraft fire detectors were
developed based upon experience on normal gravity fi re behavior and propertie s. This approach was
necessary given the absence of data concerning microgravity smoke particulate. However planned
spacecraft and their planned missions outside of low earth-orbit will requi re increased reliability of fire
detection systems in addition to robust false alar m resistance. Extended lunar-surface missions will
require systems that are not influenced by lunar dust and other nuisance dust sources.
The absence of buoyant flow increas es the residence time in microgra vity fires causing substantial
changes in flame structure. Given the large changes in fire beha vior seen in reduced gravity, it is
reasonable to expect that the signatures and detection requirements of these fires will change. There are
a number of factors that can be expected to aff ect the particle size distri bution of the smoke from

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.11
text:
spacecraft fires. The absence of buoyant flow in low-gravity increases the residence time in
microgravity fires and increases the transit ti me from the reaction zone to the detector. 3 The materials
used in spacecraft are different from those typically used in terrestrial applications where smoke
properties were previously evaluate d. More importantly, the limited options available to respond to a
spacecraft fire increase the importance of detecting the fire in an earlier stage of its development than is
typical for terrestrial applications. All of these effects can be expected to change the smoke particle size
distribution. The objective of this work was to ma ke sufficient measurements of smoke from spacecraft
fires to enable improved design of future detectors.
2. Smoke Background
Smoke is a general term that encompasses aerosol materials produced by a number of processes. In
particular for non-flaming combustion, the aerosol incl udes recondensed original material or pyrolysis
products that can be either liquid or solid. For flaming combustion, the aerosol includes soot particulate,
condensed water vapor, and ash particles. Soot part icles dominate the smoke pa rticulate in established
flaming fires while unburned pyrolysis products and recondensed polymer frag ments are produced by

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.11
text:
smoldering and pyrolysis in the early stage of fi re growth. Given the constrained space on any
spacecraft, the target for the fire detection system is necessarily the early phase and not established
flaming fires; consequently, the primary target for detection is the pyrolysis products and not the soot.
The background regarding fire detection in US spacecraft is summarized in this paper but is discussed in
more detail in papers by Friedman and Urban4, 5 In the Mercury, Gemini a nd Apollo missions, the crew
quarters were limited and mission durat ions were short, consequently it was considered reasonable that
the astronauts would rapidly detect any fire. The S kylab module, however, included approximately 30
UV-sensing fire detectors. 4 These devices were limited to line-of -sight and were reported to have
difficulties with false alarms.
Details of the ISS and STS detector require ments are described by Steisslinger et al. 6 A brief overview
of the requirements is given below.

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.12
text:
2
Space Shuttle Detectors:
At the time the Space Shuttle Orbiter (Space Tran sportation System (STS)) was developed, smoke
detection for terrestrial applic ations was becoming commonplace. 1 In particular, ionization detectors
were readily available but photoelectric
(scattering or obscuration detectors) were
generally unavailable due to the difficulty of
producing stable light sources. There were
no data available concerning the smoke or
dust particle size dist ribution in low-gravity
and the database for normal-gravity smoke
characteristics was a fraction of what is
available today. Consequently, the STS
smoke detector (Fig. 1) employed a variant
of the accepted ground-based approach
(ionization detectors). The Orbiter has nine
particle-ionization smoke detectors in
avionics cooling air return lines in the mid-
deck and flight deck and the SpaceLab had
six additional partic le-ionization smoke
detectors in the avionics lines. 7 While the
design rationale is not completely known,
Celesco™ (later Brunswick Defense™)
based their design on data that suggested
incipient fires could be discriminated by looking for particulate in the 0.4 μm to 0.7 μm range.8 The use
of a pump provided the opportunity to use a particle separator that re jected particulate larger than 1 μm.
This air pump increased the power requirements a nd reduced the operational lif e of the detector. The

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.12
text:
STS detector as built was designed to alarm at a particle loading of 2 mg/m 3 for 5 seconds (based on 1
micron particles) or a 0.022 mg/m3/s rise in concentration for 20 seconds9.
ISS Detectors:
The International Space Station (ISS) smoke detector de sign took advantage of the availability of stable
laser-diode light sources, mirroring a tr end in terrestrial detectors toward light scattering devices. This
provided the opportunity to produce a detector that required substantially less power, (1.5 Watts versus 9
Watts for the orbiter detector) 6 and, with no moving parts, was quiet er with a much longer operational
life. The choice was supported by data indicating that early smoldering fires produce larger particulate
than established flaming fires. 1 The ISS detectors (Fig. 2) are lase r-diode, forward-scattering, smoke or
particulate detectors. The sensitivity extends down to 0.3 μm but is greatest for particles larger than 1
μm. The current requirements for the ISS call for tw o detectors in the open ar ea of the module, and
detectors in racks that have cooling air-flow.10
The design developed for the ISS by Allied Signal™ (Fi g. 2) consists of a 2-pass laser diode to sense
forward scattered light ( 30 degrees). There is also a light tran smission sensor to monitor the beam
intensity. The system is designed to alarm base d on the magnitude of th e scattered light signal

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.12
text:
referenced to the beam intensity. The system is less se nsitive to particles smaller than the wavelength of
the laser (near IR) than it is to larger particles. The mini mum reported sensitivity is 0.3 μm.6 The ISS
detector was designed to alarm at 1% obscuration per foot using an Underwriters Laboratory (UL)
Figure 1 . Brunswick Defense™ smoke detector used in the
NASA orbiter fleet. The inlet is on the right and the gas is
expelled out the small plate on the top.

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.13
text:
3
smoke box and white light extinction. This
was implemented using a transfer standard
detector and a 0.5 m polystyrene-bead
aerosol system that was used to set the
amplifiers on each unit. The transfer
standard was calibrated in the smoke box
and then used to set the levels with the
aerosol system.
As a result of these de sign decisions, the ISS
and the Orbiter detectors have particle
sensitivities that do not overlap. In both
cases the designs were based upon the best
available data at the time. However, due to
the complete absence of low-g data
concerning the nature of particulate and
radiant emission from incipient and fully
developed low-g fires, different conclusions
were drawn concerning the optimal design
for spacecraft fire detection.
As described by Friedman 4 there have been
six overheat and failed component failures in
the NASA Orbiter fleet in addition to several
similar incidents that have occurred on the
ISS. None of these events spread into a real fire but as mission durations in crease, the likelihood of
failures increases. The experience on Mir in 1997 has shown that fa ilure of oxygen generation systems
can have significant consequences. As a result, impr oved understanding of spac ecraft fire detection is
critically needed.11
Previous work on smoke particles from low-gravity sources by Urban et al. 5 indicated that the

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.13
text:
particulate produced by low-gravity fl ames (soot or unburned fuel partic les) tends to have larger size
particles than in normal gravity. Results from the CSD (Comparative Soot Diagnostics) Experiment 5
which studied smoke properties in low-gravity from several spacecraft materials suggested that liquid
smoke particles could achieve sizes larger than 1 µm while solid particulate remained in the sub-
micrometer range. However, the CSD experiment di d not produce sufficient data concerning the size of
the liquid smoke particles to guide detector design. The combined im pact of these lim ited results and
physical expectations is that, ba sed on the increased sm oke residence time in low gravity, direct
knowledge of low-g combustion partic ulate is needed for the confident design of smoke detectors for
spacecraft rather than extrapolation from 1-g data
Any effort to detect fires must be able to discriminate against the ambient background and nuisance
signals. In the case of smoke detection, the background dust aerosol conditions must be considered. The
only spacecraft background aerosol particulate measurem ents to date were made on the Orbiter on STS-
32 in 199012 and on the ISS.5
Figure 2. Allied Signal/Honeywell light-scattering smoke
detector used in the ISS. The near IR laser beam emerges from
the enclosure into the top assemb ly (A) and is reflected by two

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.13
text:
mirrors (one visible at top right (B)) and is then reflected back to
the sensors in the enclosure (C). One sensor detects the forward
scattered light and is referenced by another sensor that looks
directly at the incident beam.

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.14
text:
4
The STS measurements included the results from two cascade impactors and a light scattering device.
The two impactors reported a bimodal particle size distribution with ~ 40% of the particles in each of the
2.5 μm to 10 μm and >100 μm ranges. The other two ranges <2.5 μm and 10 μm to 100 μm were very
lightly populated. Each impact or sampled approximately 15 m 3 of air over approximately 30 hours.
These results showed substantially higher concentr ations than typical indoor measurements (over a
factor of 5 for the two most populat ed size ranges). These data were supported by the li ght scattering
instrument which made 17 measurements in 12 loca tions, all of these reported mass concentrations
ranging from 50 μg/m3 to 70 μg/m3. The ISS results of Urban et al. 5 were obtained from a feasibility
experiment to validate the operation of an aerosol particle counter in low-gravity (DAFT). The
measurements were made in the US Lab on Increment 10 and the particle count levels were at the noise
level for the instrument (less than 5 particles/cm 3). The low particle levels in the < 2.5 μm bin for the
STS and the low overall numbers for the ISS suggest a zone of opportunity for spacecraft fire detection
since typical normal gravity fires produce su bstantial particulate in this size range 5,2 However more
complete particle size statistics are needed.
3. SAME Experiment

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.14
text:
To address the limited data from the CSD experime nt concerning the likely size of spacecraft smoke
particulate, the Smoke Aerosol Measurement E xperiment (SAME) was developed. The SAME
experiment sought to avoid the problems experi enced by the CSD experiment by obtaining the
particulate size statistics on-orbit with a reduced dependence upon sample return to Earth. This is a
challenging endeavor because existing aerosol instrumentation is typica lly too large to be compatible
with spacecraft experiment constraints. Thus, to obtai n particulate size statistics with existing aerosol
instrumentation would require the return of numerous samples to Earth. As will be described below, an
alternative approach was employed that used three discrete instruments to measure separate moments of
the size distribution. When combine d, these moments provide useful a ggregate statistics of the size
distribution if a lognormal distri bution is assumed. The measurem ents were made using smoke
generated by overheated spacecraft materials in much the same manner as the CSD experiment however
the sample temperature, flow field, and particle aging time were more rigorously controlled.
A. The Moment Method
The approach used by the SAME experiment is termed the ‘moment method’ for convenience. 13 This

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.14
text:
approach consists of measuring three moments of the size distribution (the zeroth, first and third moment)
on orbit, using several small, light -weight instruments. By applyi ng the properties of the lognormal
distribution to the measured moments, the total number concentration, Nt, the geometric mean diameter,
Dg, and the geometric standard deviation, g, of the aerosol can be estimated. Once these three
parameters are known, the size distribution of the m easured aerosol is uniquely defined, assuming that
the distribution is lognormal. In what follows, we will explain how the moment method works.
A.1. Principle of the moment method
The number (or count) distribution of an aerosol descri bes the number of particles that fall into a certain
size range in a unit volume of aerosol. The number distribution is sometimes also called size distribution.
Mathematically, a distribution function can be expresse d in four different, but related, forms. First, a
distribution function can be expre ssed as a frequency (or density) di stribution function or a cumulative
distribution function. Then, each of the two can be expressed in terms of its normalized form or non-

The SAME project assumes a lognorm al distribution function for the aer osol size distri bution. Since a

denoted by D1.5 or md . The subscripts of 0.5 and 1.5 used for these two diameters follow an existing
naming convention.

A.2. Implementation of the moment method in SAME experiment
In the SAME experiment, the zeroth moment, M0, was measured using a c ondensation nuclei counter
called the P-Trak TM (TSI Inc.). The first moment, M1, was approximately pr oportional to the output
signal of an ionization detector, which was a modified ionization chamber taken from a commercially-
available smoke detector. The third moment, M3, was inferred from the li ght scattered by the smoke
aerosol when illuminated by a red laser. For particles in th e size range of 0.2 μm to 2.0 μm, , the light

instrument used to obtain the third moment is called a DustTrakTM (TSI Inc.). Calibration measurements
were made for the DustTrak to account for th e departure of the scattering signal from the 3 rd moment.
More detailed information of instruments and thei r operations can be found in the Instruments section
below. The instruments used in SAME were compact enough to be installed in the ISS MSG.
Extensive calibrations of these instruments were performed at NIST to ensure that correct values of each
moment were obtained from the instrument output sign als. The results of these calibrations showed that
the instrument signals correlate well with corresponding moments ex cept for the third moment. The
third moment was found to be a function of the DustTr ak output and the particle diameters. This led to
an iterative procedure to find the best-fit results of Dg and g.

B. Instrumentation
The moment measurements were made using an a ssembly of three separate instruments. Two are
industrial hygiene instruments manufactured by TSI and one is a modified residential smoke detector.
The zeroth-moment instrument is a condensation nuclei counter, the P- Trak™ (TSI Inc.). This device
operates by passing the aerosol-laden air stream through a region satura ted with isopropanol vapor and
then into a cooler region where the vapor condenses onto the particles increasing their diameter such that
they can be readily counted by a light scattering devi ce. This instrument is very robust and operates
over a range of 0 to 10 5 particles/cm3 and 20 nm to 1 μm diameter. Some diluti on is required since the
smoke concentration in SAME ranges from about 0.5 × 10 6 to 5 × 10 6 particles/cm3. There was also a
concern that the isopropanol condensate woul d not return to the wick in low-gravity. 5 To mitigate this

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.20
text:
10
issue, the condensing section of the device was modified with very small grooves to improve
conductance of the condensate back to the wick. These changes were tested in a separate space
experiment with good results indicating the modified device could be used successfully in low gravity.5
The first-moment instrument is the ionization cham ber taken from a resident ial smoke detector. This
device uses an alpha-particle emitter to generate ions in a region within a DC electric field. Normally,
the ions drift toward an electrode inside the ioni zation chamber producing a current. When particulate
are present, the ions attach themselves to the pa rticles thereby charging the particles. Because the
charged particles have a much smaller mobility than ions alone, the current is reduced. The required
particle concentrations are on the order of 105 particles/cm3, thus no sample dilution was required.
The third-moment instrument is a light scattering de vice, the DustTrak™ (TSI In c.). The device uses a
90 degree light scattering signal to quantify the aerosol mass density. For terrestrial dust particulate, this
signal correlates well with the mass concentration, however additional comp ensation was needed to
account for the range of particle sizes observed in the SAME experiment. The device operating range is

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.20
text:
from 0.001 mg/m3 to 100 mg /m3. These devices are equipped with an aerodynamic impactor at the inlet
which captures particles larger than the selected size. The SAME experiment included 2 DustTraks™,
one with a 1 μm impactor and the other with a 10 μm impactor. The differen ce in the signal from the
two devices provided a measure of the fraction of the particulate that was larger than 1 μm. In some
cases dilution was required owing to the high smoke concentration levels.
A schematic of the assembled hardware appears in Fig. 4. The system was installed in the Microgravity
Science Glovebox, an ISS facility that provides ma ny resources including: containment, power, data,
video and uplink commanding. Smoke was generated by resistively heating small samples of spacecraft
materials. Sample heating wa s achieved by heating a steel wire that was wrapped around an
approximately 3 mm diameter cylinder of the sample material. The steel wire was resistively heated and

C. Instrument Calibration
Calibration of these instruments was essential to prope rly interpret the flight data and was performed on
the ground before the flight. Calibra tion was accomplished using two different aerosol generators; one
generates mono-disperse particle using dioctyl phthalate (DOP) according to the approach by

functioned by producing a spray of DOP diluted with isopropanol wh ich is then evaporated and
recondensed producing monodisperse droplets. The droplet size is controlled by the DOP dilution level.
The generator will operate stably for tens of minutes. The aerosol from the generator was sampled
simultaneously by the SAME instru ment under test and a reference instrument. For the number count,

4. Flight Tests
The SAME hardware installed in the ISS MSG is shown in Fig 10. The SAME tests were performed on
board ISS in September and early October of 2007. Overall 30 sample materials were tested. These
were comprised of six samples each of 5 materials: Teflon™, Kapton™, silicone rubber, cellulose, and
dibutyl-phthalate deposited on a por ous wick. These samples were test ed at different airflow rates,
pyrolysis temperatures, and smoke aging durations.
Realizing that crew time was the most precious I SS resource, SAME was desi gned to be operated both
autonomously and from the ground to the greatest exte nt possible. The SAME hardware was organized

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.24
text:
into a number of smaller modular un its to facilitate stow age for launch, provide for easy change out,
increase the reliability a nd reduce risk. The downside of this st rategy was that the assembly of the
experiment involved many connections and required approximately 5 hours of crew time. Once installed,
however, SAME was easily and effectively operated fr om the Tele Science Center (TSC) at the Glenn
Research Center (GRC), and this ca pability enabled the ground team to achieve roughly a 50% greater
number of test points (and data) than was originally planned.
The on orbit operations were scheduled around the availability of the crew for installing the next Sample
Carousel and Thermal Precipitator (and removing and stowing the used ones). Typically, the crew would
install the next units during the morning, and operati ons would be scheduled for later that day. SAME
would be nominally scheduled by the ISS staff for two test points on each of the following days.
Figure 10. SAME Experiment installed in the ISS MSG Facility.

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.25
text:
15
Because the allowed operations windows were sufficiently large, the ground team was frequently able to
perform four test points in the allowed time.
The staffing level of the ground team varied between two and five me mbers from the engineering team
with additional support from up to three members of the Science team. Most of the time, there would be
one person operating the linked co mputer that controlled the expe riment, one providing verbal
communication to the ISS cadre an d doing data reduction and a third recording video and performing
other miscellaneous functions.
Uplink parameter sheets were generated by the Science team and most times, emailed to the engineering
team the day before operations, although when additional unplanned test points were performed during a
session, the Science team provided a hard copy of the parameters during the interim between test points.
These sheets were printed and checked, and in most cas es, signed. The parameters were entered into the
ground computer by a team member and then the en try was checked both by means of a checksum and
by the other member on consol before uplinking them to the DACU.
The test points were scheduled by the ground team to coincide with Ku and S band coverage so that
video of the heating and the measurement data coul d be obtained Near Real Time (NRT) and recorded

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.25
text:
on the ground. Because the data reduction software was already in place, processing of the data could be
done immediately after the test point had been completed, and in all cases, before the next test point was
performed. Periodically during the overall operations, downloads from the DACU were commanded as a
backup to the NRT data to insure that the most complete compilation was available.
Detailed chronological record of the SAME flight tests can be found in Appendix A.
5. Test Results and Discussions
The analog signals from various instruments were digitized at 1 Hz by an 8 bit A/D converter. Figure 11
contains the signal traces from a typical run for silicone rubber. The difference in the signals for the two
DustTrak’s indicates that a substan tial portion of the aerosol mass is in particles that are larger than 1
μm.
For comparison, Fig. 12 contains similar data for a Teflon run where little difference is evident between
the two DustTrak instruments, indicating that the bulk of the aerosol mass is in particles below 1 μm.
Figure 13 shows that the effect of is a substantial decrease in the number concentration (Ptrak) while the
mass concentrations (DustTraks) remain relatively stea dy. This behavior is consistent with particle
coagulation with limited wall loss. It is also inte resting to compare the response of the ISS and STS

name: SAME
title: SAME: SAME_Final Science Report, p.25
text:
detectors for silicone rubber and Teflon. In figure 11, both the ISS de tector and the STS detectors show
strong signals. (Note that the presence of smoke yi elds a positive deflection of the ISS signal and a
negative deflection on the STS signal). This is reasonable because the silicone rubber smoke has a larger
diameter of average mass in Table 1. In figure 12, the STS detector provided a strong signal, whereas
the signal from the ISS detector was more erratic, because the Teflon smoke is comprised primarily of
particles having diameters less than 1 m, as mentioned above. This s hows that the smoke detectors
used in STS and ISS have different response to particle size range.
Results from the moment instruments for baseline runs (no aging) and 720 second aging runs are
summarized in Table 1.

text:
ABSTRACT
Title of Document: SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND
NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION
FLAMES
Keenan Thomas Dotson, M.S., 2009
Directed By: Assistant Professor, Peter B. Sunderla nd,
Department of Fire Protection Engineering
Smoke points were measured in microgravity aboard t he International Space Station
(ISS) as part of the Smoke Points in Coflow Experim ent (SPICE), and in normal
gravity conditions. In microgravity conditions incr easing the coflow velocity or
decreasing the burner diameter increased the smoke point flame length. A simplified
prediction of centerline jet velocity did not yield residence-time-based criticalities or
data collapse. Simulation of non-reacting flows sho wed that the simplified centerline
velocity prediction was able to predict velocity de cay for only relatively weak
coflows. An improved model may yield different resu lts. In normal earth gravity
coflow velocity exhibited mixed effects. For burner diameters of 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6
mm, smoke points increased with increases of coflow velocity. For an unconfined
coflow burner with a burner diameter of 13.7 mm smo ke point length decreased with
increasing coflow velocity for ethylene and propyle ne, while increasing for propane
flames.

title: SPICE: SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES_DotsonThesis, p.11
text:
1
Chapter 1. Introduction
Soot formation is an important but unresolved probl em in combustion science. In
many circumstances soot production in flames is des ired. Nevertheless, once soot
escapes the flame and becomes smoke, it is rarely i f ever wanted in a combustion
system. Soot is estimated to be responsible for up to 52,000 premature deaths in the
U.S. 1 and is believed to contribute to climate change an d glacial melting. 2 Radiation
from soot in flames allows reading by candlelight, provides heat to campers, and
cooks our food. On the other hand this radiation ca n represent a loss of efficiency and
increased heat loads in engines. Also the spread of unwanted fires is in many cases is
through the radiation heat transfer originating fro m soot particles. Smoking flames
emit carbon monoxide, which is the major cause of death in fires. 3
1.1. Smoke Point
The laminar smoke point is the condition (or lumino us flame length) where a laminar
diffusion flame begins to emit soot. Smoke points a re the prevalentmethod used to
determine fuel sooting propensity in diffusion flam es. The longer the luminous
(visible) flame length at its smoke point, the lowe r the sooting propensity of the fuel.
In normal gravity, laminar smoke points have been m easured for many gaseous and
condensed fuels. 4,5,6,7,8,9 Laminar smoke points have been found to correlate with soot
source: data/raw/PSI-107/Reports/PSI-107_Reports_SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES_DotsonThesis.pdf#page=11

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES_DotsonThesis, p.11
text:
volume fractions 10 and radiative loss fractions 11 of turbulent diffusion flames. Yang et
al. 12 found that gas turbine soot emissions correlate wi th a threshold sooting index
(TSI) based on fuel molecular weight divided by the laminar smoke point. Smoke
points have been shown to correlate with the smoke release from turbulent buoyant
4 -6, 7 -9
source: data/raw/PSI-107/Reports/PSI-107_Reports_SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES_DotsonThesis.pdf#page=11

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES_DotsonThesis, p.12
text:
2
flames, 13 and have been applied to developing general soot m odels for computation
combustion simulations 14 and heat release measurements. 15
Smoke points for gaseous fuels are determined from a jet flame apparatus. A
surrounding coflow of excess oxidant (over-ventilat ed conditions) is typically
necessary for buoyant flames to reduce flame flicke ring. It is also most common to
confine the coflow and jet within a quartz chimney to reduce disturbances from
exterior flows. Shorter smoke point flame lengths a re indicative of a higher sooting
propensity. A flame that has a lower inclination to form soot will exhibit a smoke free
flame for longer flame lengths; that is longer flam e residence times are required to
create the necessary amount of soot to reach the smoke point condition.
1.2. Soot Formation, Growth, and Oxidation
General consensus has that the soot formation proce ss begins with the formation of
polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). From these precursors fine soot particles
nucleate. These particles grow by addition of PAHs or through surface reactions. The
Hydrogen Abstraction by Carbon (Acetylene) Addition (HACA) mechanism is one of
the most often cited for soot growth mechanisms. I n addition, coagulation, in which
small particles coalesce into larger particles and agglomeration, where multiple
source: data/raw/PSI-107/Reports/PSI-107_Reports_SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES_DotsonThesis.pdf#page=12

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES_DotsonThesis, p.12
text:
particles combine into larger pearl-necklace-like s tructures, also contribute to
morphology. Soot oxidation occurs from participatio n from species such as O 2, O,
and OH present near and downstream of the flame she et. OH-based oxidation is the
most dominant soot oxidation mechanism, occurring f rom slightly rich to lean
source: data/raw/PSI-107/Reports/PSI-107_Reports_SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES_DotsonThesis.pdf#page=12

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES_DotsonThesis, p.13
text:
3
conditions within the flame. O 2-based oxidation becomes more important as the flame
becomes leaner and the super-equilibrium levels of OH decline.16 Both soot formation
and soot oxidation are temperature dependent.
Detailed measurements have provided greater insight into sooting phenomena. In
premixed ethylene flames, Harris and Weiner 17,18 determined that soot reaches a final
particle size due to a decrease in reactivity of th e particle that stops surface growth,
and the dominate growth mechanism is by acetylene. In diffusion flames Kent et
al. 19,20 have shown that soot particles are formed primaril y on the fuel side of the
flame reaction zone. The number of particles decrea ses by coagulation away from the
peak formation zone (a few millimeters inside the r eaction zone on the fuel side),
while particle size and soot volume fraction increa se by the addition of hydrocarbon
species. Soot typically convects towards the fuel s ide of the flame after it has formed
from buoyancy. The soot path ultimately follows on the local streamlines.
Thermophoretic forces modify these paths slightly t owards cooler regions within the
flame.
Santoro et al. 21,22 discovered a unique feature of coflow diffusion fl ames. The
annular region near the base of the flame is a loca tion of intense nucleation and
agglomeration of soot. This formation region is the cause of the soot 'wings' seen in
source: data/raw/PSI-107/Reports/PSI-107_Reports_SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES_DotsonThesis.pdf#page=13

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES_DotsonThesis, p.13
text:
diffusion flames near their smoke points. Gomez et al. 23 found that soot formation
begins at a temperature around 1350 K in diffusion flames and that dilution does not
change this temperature but rather shifts the locat ion at which this temperature
source: data/raw/PSI-107/Reports/PSI-107_Reports_SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES_DotsonThesis.pdf#page=13

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES_DotsonThesis, p.14
text:
4
occurs. Sunderland and Faeth 24 determined soot nucleation to become significant a t
1250 K. Kent and Wagner 25 found that smoke burnout in the oxidative region o f the
flame ceases when the tip of a buoyant diffusion fl ame cools to approximately
1300 K. This is the direct cause of the smoke poin t flame. Urban et al. 26 found that
the luminous tip of a nonbuoyant (microgravity) fla me reaches 1000 K at its smoke
point. In buoyant flames this decrease in temperatu re is attributed primarily to heat
conduction, and in nonbuoyant flames this can be si gnificantly enhanced by radiative
quenching. 16 Radiative quenching is believed to also cause the visible tip opening in
nonbuoyant smoke points of flames of relatively long residence times.26
In diffusion flames, oxygen and fuel meet at a narr ow reaction zone, the flame sheet.
Kinetics does not determine the location or tempera ture of this zone, but rather
stoichiometry does. Diffusion limits the flow of th e reactants to this narrow flame
sheet and, for strong flames, is much slower than t he kinetic reaction rate.
Furthermore the soot formation/oxidation times are believed to be greater than the
time necessary for diffusion of reactants. 27 If chemical kinetics is practically
instantaneous, then residence time becomes the dete rmining factor for soot formation
source: data/raw/PSI-107/Reports/PSI-107_Reports_SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES_DotsonThesis.pdf#page=14

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES_DotsonThesis, p.14
text:
and oxidation. It has also been suggested that the ratio of soot formation and soot
oxidation times also determines when the smoke poin t will occur. Lautenberger et
al. 27 describe this process for buoyant laminar flames. “Increasing the flame height
increases the residence time and allows more time f or the flame to produce soot.
Once formed, this soot requires additional time to oxidize in the upper parts of the
source: data/raw/PSI-107/Reports/PSI-107_Reports_SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES_DotsonThesis.pdf#page=14

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SMOKE POINTS OF MICROGRAVITY AND  NORMAL GRAVITY COFLOW DIFFUSION  FLAMES_DotsonThesis, p.15
text:
5
flame if it is to be entirely consumed below the fl ame tip. As soot travels through the
flame (in a Lagrangian sense), it radiates away energy and cools the flame gases.”
Also corroborating what was mentioned previously ab out a limiting temperature at
which soot oxidation ceases, typically at the smoke point flame height, the radiative
heat loss from the flame by soot radiation is about 30% of the total heat release rate of
the flame. 28 The cooled flame gases can no longer oxidize the s oot and one could
consider the soot formation/oxidation time to appro ach the diffusion time. 27 Smoke is
then released from the tip of this flame and it has just surpassed its characteristic
smoke point because the required time for soot oxidation is now less than the time the
soot is capable of being oxidized post flame sheet.
Important review articles on soot formation mechani sms are available from
Frenklach 29 , Mansurov 30 , and Glassman. 31 Richter and Howard 32 in a particularly
detailed fashion reviewed the formation of PAHs and their growth to soot. Soot
oxidation is well covered by Stanmore et al. 33
1.3. Fuel and Diluent Effects
For diffusion flames, work by Schalla and McDonald 34 showed that fuel sooting
propensity decreases with hydrocarbon family in the following order: aromatics >
alkynes > alkenes> alkanes. According to Glassman 31 , increasing the molecular

is only an indirect measure of the pyrolysis rate of the fuel.
In diffusion flames H radicals are important to the fuel pyrolysis process, facilitating
the initial pyrolysis of the virgin fuel as well as the subsequent attack on fuel
intermediates. H radicals facilitate abstraction reactions much faster than hydrocarbon
radicals do. Despite this importance of H radicals, Schug et al. 4 have shown that the
initial overall carbon-hydrogen (C/H) atom ratio of the fuel does not determine the
sooting propensity. Nevertheless the degree of mole cular unsaturation correlates with
higher sooting propensity, perhaps likely due to th e greater ease these molecules can
form acetylenes and PAHs.
In over-ventilated coflow diffusion flames, additio n of inert to the fuel stream
typically reduces sooting propensity. Longer smoke points result. However the
addition of inert can also alter the flame temperat ure. This occurs by the inert acting
as a heat sink, this effect depending on the heat c apacity of the inert. 4,35 The peak
flame temperatures will be reduced, which for a dif fusion flame reduces soot
formation, increasing the smoke point. Additionally , the temperature field of the
flame can be altered through transport effects. Ine rt species with high thermal

the soot formation rate peaks around 1900 – 2300 K.31
1.4. Buoyancy Effects
Soot is transported in flames primarily by convecti on, modified slightly by
thermophoresis. The primary difference between a bu oyant and nonbuoyant jet
flames is that, in general, a buoyant flame, the fl ow is accelerating, while for a
nonbuoyant jet the flow is decelerating. This is of course neglecting volumetric
expansion from combustion related heating. In gener al, for a buoyant flame the flow
streamlines move towards the flame axis, while for the nonbuoyant flame the flow
streamlines are drawn outwards from the flame axis. 16 Therefore in a buoyant flame,
once soot is nucleated in the soot production regio n near the flame sheet, it is drawn
into the fuel rich core, allowing continued growth. In a nonbuoyant flame as the flow
is drawn outwards, the soot moves in a more direct path to the flame sheet and
oxidative region downstream. 16
It had been predicted that smoke points would not o ccur in nonbuoyant gas-jet
flames. 37 This was based on the assumption that residence ti me would be independent
of flow rate in microgravity flames. As flame lengt h and mass flow rate are directly
proportional, an increase in velocity would lead to proportional increase in length and

1.5. Velocity Field Effects
By varying the burner diameter, coflow velocity, an d fuel dilution, flame shape and
residence times in the soot formation and soot oxid ation regions can be changed.
Reductions in the burner (fuel jet exit) diameter i ncrease the mean fuel jet velocity,
reducing overall flame residence time, assuming tha t flame length only depends on
the mass flow rate of fuel. There has not been subs tantial research into the burner
diameter effect on smoke points. The work of Kent a nd Wagner 25 showed that
reducing burner diameter (increasing fuel jet veloc ity) shifts the centerline soot-
volume-fraction profile downstream, without modifyi ng peak values. Therefore it
should be expected that the smoke point luminous fl ame length should increase from
the soot profile shifting downstream, directly leng thening the flame or reducing the
region of the flame where soot formation is possibl e. Increasing fuel dilution, in
addition to modifying soot propensity by volumetric and thermal effects, increases the
