text:
Smoke Point In Coflow Experiment
“SPICE”
Microgravity Science Glovebox
Increment 19-20 (30 Day Report)
Investigators: David Urban NASA GRC, Peter Sunderland: Univ. Maryland
Project Scientist: Zengguang Yuan, National Center for Space Exploration Research
Project Manager: Robert Hawersaat NASA GRC
I. Introduction
A. Hypothesis
The hypothesis of the SPICE investi gation is that smoke point behavior
will be observed for co-flowing flames and that it will show
dependence on nozzle diameter and coflow velocity.
B. Objectives of Investigation
The objective of the SPICE experiment is to find the laminar smoke-point
properties of nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the properties of the
largest laminar jet diffusion flames that do not emit soot) for several fuels
under different nozzle diameter/ co-flow velocity configurations.
Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify
models of the flame shapes under co-flow conditions.
C. Previous Mission Experience
N/A
D. Background/History of Project (Optional)
The SPICE experiment was an outgrow th of the Laminar Soot Processes
Experiment (LSP) which flew on STS 83, 94, and 107. SPICE utilized the
design heritage and modified the hardware from the Enclosed Laminar Flames
Experiment (ELF) which flew in the Middeck Glovebox on STS 87.
II. Methods/Research Operations
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_30-DayPostFlightReport, p.1
text:
Most tests were conducted by setting the coflow velo city, igniting the flame,
and adjusting the fuel flow rate. Appr oximate smoke points were identified in
the video by the flight crew and simultaneously by the ground support crew in
Cleveland. Typical burn times were 60 s, and after each two such burns the
MSG contents were flushed with ISS cabin air. After the tests the video
record was analyzed to identify sm oke point conditions. The associated
coflow and fuel flow rates were obtain ed from digital data recorded in the
video. The smoke point lengths, LSP, we re obtained from the video record
and are the measured distance from the burner tip to the tip of the luminous
flame on the flame axis.

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_30-DayPostFlightReport, p.2
text:
III. Results
A. List of Preflight, In-f light, Postflight Anomalies
SPICE operated very successfully with the only significant anomaly being the
accumulation of soot in the outlet screen which changed the flow behavior in
the duct. This was corrected by a crew member using the vacuum to clean the
outlet screen on June 15.
B. Completeness/Quality of Data
During Increment 18 SPICE conducted 108 test points completing its nominal
test matrix. During Increments 19/20 SPICE conducted 155 additional test
points the provided improved resolution of the smoke points and allowed us to
explore further limits in the parameter space.
C. Status of Data Analysis: The data from the down linked video have been analyzed
for flame length and smoke point flow rate. These have resulted in a meeting apper
and a draft journal paper. More work will be conducted with analysis of the digital
luminance data from the Nikon.
D. Preliminary Research Findings:
See attached paper below

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_30-DayPostFlightReport, p.3
text:
1
2009 Fall Technical Meeting
Organized by the Eastern States Section of the Combustion Institute
and Hosted by the University of Maryland College Park
October 18-21, 2009
Laminar Smoke Points of
Microgravity Coflow Diffusion Flames
K.T. Dotsona, P.B. Sunderlanda, Z.–G. Yuanb, D.L. Urbanc
aDepartment of Fire Protection Engineering, University of Maryland, College Park, MD, USA
bNational Center for Space Exploration Research, Cleveland, OH, USA
cNASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH, USA
Laminar smoke points were measured in nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in air coflow aboard the
International Space Station as part of the Smoke Points in Coflow Experiment (SPICE). Smoke points were found
for ethylene, propane, propylene, and mixtures of 50 and 75% propylene by volume in nitrogen. Burner diameters
were 0.41, 0.76 and 1.6 mm and coflow velocities varied from 5.4 – 65 cm/s. These flames afford good control over
residence time via variations in dilution, burner diameter , and coflow velocity. Increasing coflow velocity decreases
luminous flame lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths.
Smaller burners have longer smoke points for coflowing flames. These trends can be explained qualitatively by
considering total residence time effects. The luminous flame lengths generally correlate with fuel mass flow rate

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_30-DayPostFlightReport, p.3
text:
divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they increase slightly as air velocity decreases.
1. Introduction
Soot formation is an important unresolved problem in combustion science. Soot is estimated to
be responsible for up to 50,000 prem ature deaths in the U.S. [1] a nd is believed to contribute to
climate change and glacial melting [2]. Radiation from soot in flames allows reading by candle-
light but also contributes to he at loads in engines and the spread of unwanted fires. Smoking
flames emit carbon monoxide, which is the major cause of death in fires [3].
The smoke point is the condition (or length) where a flame begi ns to emit soot. Smoke points
indicate the sooting propensity of a fuel in diffusion flames. In normal gravity, laminar smoke
points have been measured for many gaseous a nd condensed fuels [4–9]. Laminar smoke points
have been found to correl ate with soot volume frac tions [10] and radiative loss factions [11] of
turbulent diffusion flames. Yang et al. [12] found that gas turbine soot em issions correlate very
well with a threshold sooting i ndex (TSI) based on fuel molecula r weight divided by the laminar
smoke point. Smoke points have been shown to co rrelate with the smoke release from turbulent
buoyant flames [13] and have been applied to developing general soot models for computational

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_30-DayPostFlightReport, p.3
text:
combustion simulations [14] and heat release measurements [15].
In a 1988 paper [16], Glassman predicted that smoke points would not occur in nonbuoyant gas-
jet flames. He based this on the assumption that residence time scales with the square root of fuel
flow rate in normal gravity but is independent of flow rate in microgravity flames. Subsequent
work [17] observed smoke points of nonbuoyant fl ames aboard a parabolic aircraft and used
numerical predictions to show that residence time increases with flame length for nonbuoyant
flames without co-flow. Urban et al. [18] reported smoke points of microgravity flames observed
on a space shuttle. Microgravity smoke point meas urements are difficult in parabolic aircraft

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_30-DayPostFlightReport, p.4
text:
2
owing to g-jitter and in drop facilities owing to limited test times.
Attributing smoke point behavior to total resi dence time helps with qualitative explanations of
smoke point behavior but to date has not yielded successful quant itative correlations [8]. This
may be because smoke points arise from a comp etition between the times available for soot
formation and soot oxidation. De lichatsios and co-workers suggest ed that smoke point length is
proportional to soot formation time [19–20]. Quantitative correlations may also be possible from
an examination of radiative losses, which have been observed to be 20 – 30% for normal-gravity
smoke point flames and to increase with adiabatic flame temperature [5].
Soot is transported in flames by convection and thermophoresis. By varying the burner diameter,
coflow velocity, and fuel dilution, flame shape and residence times in the soot formation and
soot oxidation regions can be changed. A decrease in coflow velocity will generally increase
entrainment of flow towards the flame axis.
Kent and Wagner [21] found that smoke burn out in the oxidat ive region of the flame ceases
when the tip of a buoyant diffusion flame cools to approximately 1300 K. Urban et al. [22] found
that the tip of a nonbuoyant (microgravity) fl ame reaches 1000 K at its smoke point. In buoyant

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_30-DayPostFlightReport, p.4
text:
flames this decrease in temperature is attr ibuted primarily to he at conduction, while in
nonbuoyant flames it is attributed largely to ra diative quenching [23]. The radiative quenching
effect causes a visible tip openi ng in nonbuoyant smoke points of flames of relatively long
residence time [22].
A recent 2.5 s drop tower study by Jeon et al. [24] found that for small coflow velocities the soot
volume fraction increases with coflow velocit y. This was attributed to an increase in
temperature. Lin and Faeth [7,25] studied the effects of coflow velocity on weakly-buoyant
flames near the smoke point. They observed flam es in normal gravity, but at low pressures to
reduce the effects of gravity. They found that increasing the coflow velocity reduced soot
volume fractions and increased the smoke point le ngth. This was attributed to decreased flame
residence time and modified soot pathlines. Refs. [7 and 24] both showed that luminous flame
lengths decrease with increasi ng coflow velocity. Their bur ner diameters, 7 and 10 mm,
respectively, were much larger than those considered here.
Faeth and co-workers [25–27] applied the fl ame shape analyses of Spalding [28] and
Mahalingam et al. [29] to nonbuoyant gas-jet flames to obtain

Reynolds number, Sc is the Schmidt number, and Zst is the stoichiometric mixture fraction. The
Reynolds number is defined as ρ d u / μ, where ρ is density, d is burner diameter, u is velocity,
and μ is dynamic viscosity. The Schmidt number and vi scosity in Eqs. (1–2) were those of air at
the mean of the adiabatic flame temperature and the ambient temperature.
Schmidt number and viscosity, defined in this fashion, do not vary substantially for the flames in
this study, and are not considered significant. In addition the virtual origin correction was
neglected. With this in mind, Eqs. (1–2) can be rearranged to

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_30-DayPostFlightReport, p.5
text:
3
L f = C m˙ f / Zst , (3)
where C is a constant and m˙ f is the fuel mass flow rate.
Thus motivated, the objectives of this study are:
1. to measure nonbuoyant smoke points of propane, ethylene, propylene, and
propylene/nitrogen mixtures,
2. to identify the effects of coflow velocity and burner diameter on the smoke points, and
3. to correlate the luminous flame lengths.
2. Experimental
The Smoke Points in Coflow Experiment (SPI CE) module was brought to the International
Space Station (ISS) in 2008. It was operated in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) by
various crew members in 2009. Smoke points were at tempted for all fuels for fuel jet diameters
of 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm. The conditions for which smoke points were found are summarized in
Table 1. In some cases (e.g., te sts involving ethylene) the fuel supply was depleted before
desired smoke points could be found, as the supply was limited to two 75 cc bottles of each fuel
at gage pressures of 760 – 1440 kPa, depending on the fuel.
The SPICE module contains a rectangular duct th at has an approximately 76 mm square cross
section with rounded corners. A DC fan supplie s coflowing air from the glovebox contents. The
air passes through a honeycomb and screen to reduce swirl and then enters the duct. The air and
combustion products leave the duct through a pe rforated copper plate followed by a copper

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_30-DayPostFlightReport, p.5
text:
screen. The screen is 50 mm upstream of th e burner discharge and the plate is 120 mm
downstream. Fan voltage is varied to control the coflow velocity, which is measured with a hot-
wire anemometer between the inlet honeycomb a nd screen. This anemometer was calibrated in
normal gravity using a hot-wire anemometer 36 mm downstream of the duct entrance. Fuel flow
rate was adjusted manually and controlled with a mass flow meter. The flames were ignited with
a hot-wire ignitor. Video was recorded with an analog color video camera and downlinked in real
time. Still images were recorded with a 12 bit Nikon™ D100 single-lens reflex color digital still
camera (with 3008 × 2000 pixels) with a 60 mm lens.
Most of the tests were conducted by setting the coflow velocity, igniting the flame, and adjusting
the fuel flow rate. Approximate smoke points were identified in the video by the flight crew and
simultaneously by the ground support crew in Cleveland. Typical burn times were 60 s, and after
each two such burns the MSG contents were flushed with ISS cabin air.
After the tests the video record was analyzed to identify smoke point conditions. The associated
coflow and fuel flow rates were obtained from digital data r ecorded in the video. The smoke
point lengths, LSP, were obtained from the vi deo record and are the measured distance from the

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_30-DayPostFlightReport, p.5
text:
burner tip to the tip of the luminous flame on the flame axis. The luminous flame tips were not
sharply defined in most images, but rather involved a transition from bright yellow to black
across an axial distance of 2 – 5 mm. Flame hei ght was thus measured to the point where the
centerline grayscale intensity changed most rapidly between these yellow and black regions. This
helped reduce the sensitivity of measured flame height to camera exposure settings.
Smoke points were obtained for five fuels, as summarized in Table 1. Smoke points were

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_30-DayPostFlightReport, p.6
text:
4
attempted with methane, but could not be obtained before the flames impinged on the plate at the
end of the duct. Also shown in Table 1 are the ranges of various parameters for which
microgravity smoke points were observed.
3. Results and Discussion
Some smoke points, propane and ethylene in part icular, were identified by the onset of gradual
(rather than sharp) dimming and reddening of the luminous flame tip in the downstream
direction. Rounding of the tip al so was associated with th e smoke point. For conditions
sufficiently above the smoke point, quenched soot could be seen leaving the flame. The brightest
flames did not always display significant redden ing or darkening near their tips, except well
above the smoke point. This occurred for the pu re propylene and propylene mixtures, and the
smoke point was identified by the rapid transition to an open-tipped, soot emitting flame.
The flames generally reached steady conditions within 5 s of ignition or a change in flow rate of
fuel or air. Flames of propylene and propylene mixtures were generally more luminous than
those of methane, ethylene, and propane, attribut ed to their higher propensity to form soot. The
smoke point transition was more abrupt in th e propylene-based fuels than for propane or
ethylene. Periodic flame motion was observed in some flames, especially those with high coflow,

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_30-DayPostFlightReport, p.6
text:
long length, and low fuel velocity, and is attributed to non-uniform coflow. This effect was small
and did not prevent clear measurement of flame length.
Figure 1 shows images for representative flames near their smoke points. Two sequences are
shown, and in both the smoke point occurs betw een the third and fourth flames. In the top
sequence, coflow velocity decreases from left to right at constant fuel flow rate. This increases
luminous flame length and reduces the smoke poi nt leading to soot emission. The luminous
length decreases in the fourth image owing to incomplete combustion. In the bottom sequence
fuel flow rate is increased at constant coflow velocity, increasing flame length as expected. As
seen in Fig. 1, luminous length is more sensitive to changes in fuel flow rate than to changes in
coflow velocity.

4. Conclusions
Smoke points of microgravity gas-jet
diffusion flames were observed.
Conditions emphasized small burners
and effects of coflow velocity. These
flames allow extensive control of
residence time, which is important in
smoke point phenomena. The major
conclusions are as follows.
1. An increase in coflow velocity
increases the smoke point length.
2. A decrease in burner diameter
increases the smoke point length.
3. These two effects can be
explained qualitatively by
considering residence times;
increased fuel and/or coflow
velocities yield increased smoke
point lengths.

ii
Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE)
Abstract
The laminar smoke point is the condition (and the l uminous flame length) where a flame begins
to emit soot. Smoke points indicate the sooting pro pensity of a fuel in diffusion flames. In normal
gravity, laminar smoke points have been measured fo r many gaseous and condensed fuels.
Laminar smoke points have been found to correlate with soot volume fractions and radiative loss
fractions of turbulent diffusion flames. SPICE pro ject measured laminar smoke points in non)
buoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in co)flowing air aboard the International Space Station.
Fifty)two smoke points were found for ethylene, pro pane, propylene, and propylene/nitrogen
mixtures. Burner diameters were 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm and co)flow velocities varied from 5.4 –
65 cm/s. These flames afford extensive control over residence time via variations in dilution,
burner diameter, and co)flow velocity. Increasing c o)flow velocity decreases luminous flame
lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths.
Smaller burners have longer smoke points for co)flo wing flames. These trends can be explained
qualitatively by considering total residence time e ffects. The luminous flame lengths generally
correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoic hiometric mixture fraction, although they

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_FinalReport, p.2
text:
increase slightly as air velocity decreases. The me asured smoke point lengths were found to
correlate with burner diameter to the –0.91 power t imes coflow velocity to the 0.41 power. The
measurements allow estimates of pseudo threshold so ot indices (TSI) for microgravity diffusion
flames, indicating an unusually high sooting propen sity for propane in microgravity. A model of
residence times in coflowing flames is developed, a nd although residence time helps explain
many of the observations, it does not correlate the measured smoke points. The measurements
yielded estimates of sooting propensities of the present fuels in microgravity diffusion flames.
Acknowledgments
The authors acknowledge G.M. Faeth for conceiving this work, the SPICE engineering team, and
the astronauts that conducted the tests (M. Barratt , E.M. Fincke, S.H. Magnus, and K. Wakata).
The SPICE project was conducted through the ISS Exploration Research Project of the
Exploration Technology Development Program. The sup port of this program is also
acknowledged.

INTRODUCTION
SPICE project, from it was rewarded in 1997 to it w as conducted onboard ISS in 2009, covered
more than a decade time span. During these years, t he project experienced a few cycles of active and
inactive status. A brief project history is given b elow. SPICE project was awarded on December 3,
1997 by the Microgravity Science and Application Di vision of NASA Headquarters to Professor
Gerard M. Faeth of the University of Michigan for h is proposal titled as Laminar Smoke Point
Properties of Nonbuoyant Round-Jet Diffusion Flames in response to NASA’s 1996 Solicitation for
Glovebox Investigations issued in late 1996. The or iginal proposal of Professor Faeth was meant to
be a supplement to the Laminar Soot Processes Exper iment which was a combustion project under
NASA Grant No. NAG3-1245, conducted onboard STS-73 and STS-94 in 1997. In the awarding
letter, the experiment was planned to be carried out onboard STS-107, for which the launch date was
then scheduled in May 2000. From December 1997 to t he end of 1999 was the first phase of the
project. In this period, the experiment was planned to be conducted in the Middle Deck Glove Box
of a Space Shuttle and the SPICE hardware was fabri cated and assembled in GRC. Various project
reviews necessary for the flight project, were comp leted. In addition, significant efforts on science

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_FinalReport, p.7
text:
side were made to explore proper camera settings fo r different flame conditions by conducting
reduced gravity experiment in parabolic flight on board the KC-135 aircraft. From the end of 1999 to
March 2002, the project was inactive. The second p hase of the project was from March 2002 to
January 2005. In this period, SPICE was a part of MRDOC contract to ZIN Inc., for a potential UF-1
Flight. Since the target facility of SPICE was swit ched from Space Shuttle’s Middle Deck Glove
Box to the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), ZIN’s major effort was to retro-fit hardware
for use with MSG in International Space Station (IS S), which included: designed and assembled
Power/Video Unit to support MSG video interfaces, d esigned and fabricated a new mechanical
camera supports, redesigned fuel bottle assemblies and developed new cabling. Project was
cancelled again at the end of 2004. ZIN developed s torage plan for hardware which was presented to
NASA in December, 2004. The SPICE apparatus was put in storage in January 2005 and all the
documents were archived waiting for future flight o pportunities. At that time, the LSP project and
the re-flight LSP-2 were completed, thus the object ives of SPICE were later changed to a stand-
alone investigation of smoke point of jet diffusion flames with coexistence of air flows. One

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_FinalReport, p.7
text:
important event soon after the SPICE became inactive again was the sudden death of Professor Faeth
of the University of Michigan, the PI of the projec t. It was not until March 2006 that the SPICE was
resurrected in May, 2006 as part of the Small Paylo ads Projects Task under MRDOC that Dr. David
Urban, the Co-I of the project, succeeded Professor Faeth as the PI of the project. In addition,
Professor Peter Sunderland of University of Marylan d, former Ph.D. student of Prof. Faeth was
recruited as a Co-I of the project. An updated Scie nce Requirement Document was edited. The test
matrix was finalized. Additional tests in camera were conducted.
Minor hardware modifications were made and a number of project reviews were conducted. The
SPICE hardware was shipped to KSC on June 18, 2008 and later lifted up to ISS by ULF-2 in
October 2008. SPICE experiments were finally conduc ted in ISS MSG from February through June
of 2009. What Follows is the science significance and justification of the SPICE project.
Soot formation in hydrocarbon-fueled flames is an i mportant unresolved problem in combustion
science. Soot is estimated to be responsible for up to 52,000 premature deaths annually in the U.S. 1
and is believed to contribute to climate change and glacial melting. 2 Radiation from soot in flames is

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_FinalReport, p.7
text:
beneficial in many applications but also contributes to unwanted heat loads in engines and the spread
of fires. Carbon monoxide emitted by smoking flames is the major cause of death in fires. 3
Knowledge of Soot formation is needed for developing computational combustion.

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_FinalReport, p.8
text:
2
The differences between soot processes in buoyant a nd nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames can
be seen by comparing their soot production regions as plotted in Fig. 1. Soot formation in diffusion
flames generally is limited to fuel-equivalence rat ios, φ, in the range 1-2, which are marked on the
plots. Unlike gases, which both convect and diffus e, soot mainly convects with the flow velocity so
that it moves along the streamline. For buoyant fl ames, the dividing streamline generally is inside
the soot formation region so that most of the soot initially forms near the flame sheet, where φ, =1,
and then moves radially inward toward cooler region s having higher fuel concentrations. The soot
formation process for nonbuoyant flames is complete ly different: most of the soot initially forms
near the cool core of the flame, where φ is close to 2, and is drawn directly toward the fl ame sheet.
Results from an MSL-1 combustion project, the Lamin ar Soot Processes (LSP), revealed that the
smoke height phenomenon in microgravity can be subs tantially different form that seen in normal
gravity. The removal of buoyancy induced accelerat ion can cause the smoke point phenomenon to
be dominated by radiative heat losses for condition s of low overall flame velocity. Under these
conditions the flame extinguishes at the flame tip allowing soot to be emitted. In spite of this effe ct,

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_FinalReport, p.8
text:
it is still possible to have flames that either emi t soot along all stream lines or do not emit soot
anywhere, for conditions where radiation losses do not dominate.
Figure 1. Soot path lines through buoyant and non-b uoyant flames
The information of smoke-point properties and flame shapes is needed to improve our understanding
of heat and mass transfer mechanisms for different flame conditions. Unfortunately, while the
laminar smoke-point properties of buoyant jet diffu sion flames at normal gravity are well known,
corresponding information for nonbuoyant flames is limited and questionable. Thus the insights of
soot generation and oxidation processes under micro gravity conditions are critical to devise better
fire safety strategy in spacecraft needed for long term space travels and other space exploration
activities. In addition, the improved understanding of soot processes in laminar flames will help us,
by analogy, to gain better understanding of soot processes in practical turbulent flames.
The objectives of the SPICE experiments is to find the laminar smoke-point properties of non-
buoyant jet diffusion flames for several fuels unde r different nozzle diameter/co-flow velocity
configurations. Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify models of the

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_FinalReport, p.9
text:
3
flame shapes under co-flow conditions. In particula r, the experiments are planned to be conducted
under the following conditions: six types of fuels: methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, 75%
propylene mixed with 25% nitrogen in moles, and 50% propylene mixed with 50% nitrogen in moles;
three nozzles: 0.4, 0.8 and 1.6 mm ID and two air v elocities: 100% and 50% of the maximum air
flow velocity (near 50cm/s). The operation procedur es are as such that the air velocity is set first,
then start the fuel flow and ignite the flame. Fuel flow rate is adjusted until the smoke point is
reached. Thus, for each combination of a fuel and a nozzle size, two smoke point fuel flow rates are
obtained. One is under 100% air velocity and the ot her is under 50% air velocity. Then in the case of
50% air velocity, the fuel flow rate is reduced to 50% of the smoke point fuel flow rate to get a flame
length with that fuel flow rate.
SPICE EXPERIMENT SETUP
A. The SPICE Apparatus
The SPICE project utilized and modified an apparatu s constructed for a previous project, Enclosed
Laminar Flames (ELF), which was conducted in the Mi ddle Deck Glovebox of Space Shuttle
Columbia during mission USMP-4/STS-87 in November, 1997. The SPICE apparatus configuration
and the connection to the MSG power supply are show n in Figure 2. The upper right portion in the

Inside the Glovebox, the core of the apparatus is t he Experimental Assembly which consists of a
flow duct and its accessories. In this flow duct bu rns the flame under investigation. More detailed
discuss of this part will be given below. An imagi ng system, including a still digital camera and a
video camera is mounted outside the flow duct to re cord the flame images. Inside the Glovbox there
are two additional enclosures. One is the Power Uni t that converts the electrical power provided by
the Glovebox Power Supply (single voltage) to vario us voltages needed by different part of the
SPICE apparatus. The second enclosure is the Video Unit which has the following functions: a)
controls the shutter of the still cameras based on the signal received from the control box, and b)
merges the video camera signal with the signal from a title generator which includes air and fuel
flow rates and outputs the merged signal to a VCR o utside the Glovebox for recording and
displaying on a monitor. The feature of merging fla me image and the flow rates to a single video
image is very important improvement of SPICE over E LF. With the real time flow rates stamped on
the flame image, the data reduction process, after the experiment, is greatly simplified by eliminating
the need of synchronizing the flame image and the f low data manually, which would be very tedious
and time consuming.

Experiment Assembly: Figure 3 shows a photo of the Experiment Assembly.
The flow duct is the core of the Assembly. The inte rior dimensions of the flow duct are 172mm x
43mm x 43mm. It has two Lexan windows on its top an d front sides through which the still camera
and the video camera can image the flame.
A retractable ruler 105mm in length is placed insid e the flow duct. It is used to generate a reference
image for flame length measurement. This ruler is n ormally rests at the far, bottom corner of the
flow duct. When a reference image is taken, it is m oved in line with the nozzle tip. Since its surface
is 45 degree tilted, it can be seen both by the sti ll camera and the video camera. After the reference

A hot wire igniter, a coiled Kanthal wire, was used to ignite the flame. During ignition, it is moved
to the nozzle tip through a handle next to the rule r handle and electrically powered up with about 4
amps of electric current that makes the wire bright red hot. Once the flame ignition is confirmed, the
igniter is then moved away from the nozzle tip to i ts home position. The two handles are designed in
such that only one of the two, the igniter and the ruler, can be moved to the nozzle at a certain time .
This provides a safety feature of the system that p revents the ruler from being burned by the igniter.
There is a small magnet mounted on the linkage to t he igniter and a Hall-effect sensor mounted on
the hinge of the front door. This sensor controls t he igniter power circuits that when the front door is
in open position or when the igniter is at its home position, the igniter power circuit is disabled. I n
other words, the igniter can be powered only if the front door is closed and the igniter is at the nozzle
tip. The igniter is replaceable. When replacing the igniter, the astronaut must open the front door so
that the igniter will not be powered during the replacement.

B. Air velocity distribution in the flow duct
An important feature of SPICE is that it has air co -flow surrounding the flames. SPICE is the first
experiment that studies soot processes of laminar j et diffusion flame under long term microgravity
condition with air coflow. Because the velocity dis tribution in or near the flame is complicated by
the varying gas property and thermal expansion, the coflow air velocity can only be specified in far
field and the inlet of the flow duct as boundary co nditions of the flame under investigation. For this
reason, the information of air velocity distributio n before igniting of the flame is needed. The air
velocity was measured with an anemometer at differe nt locations in the flow duct at different fan

name: SPICE

accommodate anemometer prob. Figure 13 shows vario us hole locations through which air
velocities were measured. Some expressions used in describing a spatial location are explained as
follows. A “Station” refers to a plane perpendicula r to the flow direction. The value of a “Station”
indicates the distance between the nozzle tip and t he plane. There are only two Stations in use: 13
mm and 56 mm, defining two planes 13 mm and 56 mm d ownstream of the nozzle tip. “Height Off
Floor” refers to the distance above the floor of th e flow duct. The Floor of the flow duct is the lowe r
wall of the flow duct, perpendicular to the front w indow. The three positions in Height Off Floor in
use are 19 mm, 36 mm, and 57 mm define three planes in parallel with the flow duct floor. The 36
mm one is in the middle of the flow duct so that it includes the nozzle. The third direction is
expressed in terms of “Centerline”, “20 mm to the Inside” and “20 mm to the Outside,” which define
three planes in parallel with the front window of t he flow duct. There are totally 18 intersections of
these three sets of planes. Air velocities were mea sured at these 18 locations at 6 different fan dial
settings. Note that for the safety concern, even at 0 fan dial setting, there is a minimum DC voltage

SPICE FLIGHT TESTS
The actual SPICE tests were conducted in SMG in twelve sessions from February 14, 2009 to June
23, 2009. In each session, the SPICE science team and engineering team were in the TeleScience
Center (TSC) in GRC to support the tests conducted on MSG. Real-time flame images were
available as long as air-to-ground communication channel was available. In addition, the team was
able to communicate with the astronaut who conducted the experiment to answer questions or to
clarify any ambiguities.
Most tests were conducted by setting the coflow vel ocity, igniting the flame, and adjusting the fuel
flow rate. Approximate smoke points were identified in the video by the flight crew and

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_FinalReport, p.19
text:
simultaneously by the ground support team in TSC. Typical burn times were 60 s, and after each two
such burns the MSG contents were flushed with ISS c abin air. The oxygen mole fraction of this
cabin air is maintained within 19 – 24%.
After the tests the video record was analyzed to id entify smoke points. The smoke point lengths, LSP ,
(and the flow conditions) were obtained from the vi deo record and are the measured distance from
the burner to the tip of the luminous flame on the flame axis. The luminous flame tips were not
sharply defined in most images, but rather transiti oned from bright yellow to black over an axial
distance of 2 – 5 mm. Luminous lengths were measure d to the point where the centerline grayscale

Totally 526 flames were ignited and studied, which were much more than originally planned. The
reason more flames can be studied was owing to the increasing familiarization for astronauts to the
apparatus, so that the flame adjusting time and smo ke point realization time became shorter and
shorter. This leads to plenty unused fuel for new t est points. The entire test matrix and measured
flame data are listed in Appendix A.
The flames generally reached steady conditions within 5 s of ignition or a change in flow rate of fuel
or air. Flames of propylene and propylene mixtures were generally more luminous than the others,
attributed to increased soot volume fractions. Peri odic flame motion was observed in some flames,
especially those with high air velocity, large burn ers, and long flames, and is attributed to coflow
perturbations. This increased slightly the uncertainties in smoke points for these conditions.
TEST RESULTS
Smoke points were attempted for all fuels. The cond itions for which smoke points were found are
summarized in Table 1. In some cases (e.g., tests i nvolving ethylene) the fuel supply was depleted
before all desired conditions could be tested, as t he supply was limited to two 150 cc bottles of each

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_FinalReport, p.20
text:
fuel at gage pressures of 760 – 1440 kPa. Smoke poi nts were attempted with methane, but could not
be obtained before the flames impinged on the copper plate at the end of the duct.
Some smoke points (particularly for propane and eth ylene) were identified by the onset of gradual
dimming, reddening, and rounding of the luminous fl ame tip. Conversely, the brightest flames
(particularly for propylene and propylene mixtures) normally did not display significant dimming
and reddening near their tips, except when much lon ger than their smoke points. For these flames,
smoke points were identified by the rapid transitio n to open-tipped flames. Open-tipped flames are
common in microgravity when smoke points are far ex ceeded 4 and are associated with flame
extinguishment along the centerline and soot that e scapes in an annular shell. For conditions
sufficiently above the smoke points, quenched soot could be seen leaving the flames despite the dark
background in the video.

Figure 17 shows images for representative flames ne ar their smoke points. Two sequences are
shown, and in both, the smoke point occurs between the third and fourth images. In the top row,
coflow velocity decreases from left to right at a c onstant fuel flow rate. This increases luminous
flame length and leads to soot emission in the four th image. The luminous length decreases in the
fourth image owing to flame extinction and extensiv e reactant leakage. In the bottom row, fuel flow
rate is increased at a constant coflow velocity, in creasing luminous lengths. The luminous lengths of
the flames in Fig. 17 are more sensitive to changes in fuel flow rate than to changes in coflow
velocity. For a jet diffusion flame, the fuel flow rate is the limiting factor of the flame length because
there is almost unlimited amount of oxidant (air in this case) available. This is why the flame length
is more sensitive to the change of fuel flow rate.
In Fig. 18 the measured smoke point lengths are plo tted with respect to coflow velocity. For a given
choice of fuel and burner diameter, an increase in coflow velocity generally increases the smoke
point length. This behavior is attributed to decrea sed residence times and radiative losses as coflow
velocity increases, and is an important issue for f urther consideration. The slope of the correlations

Also shown in Fig. 18 are smoke points of microgravity flames in still air. 5 The limited smoke points
at different diameters actually increase with burne r diameter. When the present measurements are
extrapolated to zero coflow velocity, the dependenc e on burner diameter diminishes. Normal gravity
smoke points are also generally found to have only a weak dependence on burner diameter. 5,6
However, testing in normal gravity 8 has shown that coflowing normal gravity smoke poin ts for
propylene decrease with increasing burner diameter for the present range of diameters. The present
smoke points generally were repeatable. An exceptio n was the tests with the 0.41 mm burner (for
which only propylene smoke points were possible). T esting on different days yielded different
smoke points for this burner.
The sooting propensity of the present fuels, identi fied from the smoke point lengths for fixed burner
diameter and coflow velocity, generally increases f rom propane to ethylene, to 50% propylene, to
75% propylene, and to propylene. This is consistent with normal gravity results in the same
apparatus. 7 The only exception was that, for the 0.76 mm burne r, ethylene has a longer smoke point
length than propane. The lower density of ethylene results in a decreased residence time, but this is
unlikely to explain such a long smoke point relative to that of propane.

title: SPICE: SPICE_FinalReport, p.22
text:
In Fig. 19 the smoke point flame lengths are plotte d with respect to m ˙f / Zst . This is motivated by
Eq. (2) for stoichiometric lengths and the past obs ervations that flames at their smoke points
typically have luminous lengths that are twice as l ong as their stoichiometric lengths. This choice of
axes yields a reasonably good single correlation of the luminous lengths of all fuels. These results
are similar to those of Lin and Faeth 1 in that flames with low ua / u f are generally longer than those at
otherwise matched conditions. This occurs in Fig. 1 9 for propylene, propane, and ethylene flames
with the smallest burner, for which ua / u f < 0.08.

respect to coflow velocity. The lines shown are fit s for each

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_FinalReport, p.23
text:
17
DISCUSSION
Although it is convenient to classified all flames, laminar vs. turbulent and diffusion vs. premixed,
into two categories based on their soot emission co nditions, i.e., soot emitting flames and non-soot
emitting flames, the conditions delineating the two or the conditions of onset of soot emission are
difficult to define. Up to date, these conditions h ave been documented solely based on experimental
observations. Many efforts have been made to dev elop a universal method of defining the onset of
soot emission, i.e., smoke point, conditions, in terms of primary parameters of the flame. But none of
these efforts has been quite successful yet. The primary parameters of the flame mentioned here refer
to parameters used to set the flame, not those gene rated by the flame. The primary parameters of jet
diffusion flames include fuel type, fuel and oxidiz er supply rates, ambient temperature and pressure,
and configuration of the device where the flame takes place, such as nozzle diameter and dimensions
of the combustion chamber. The flame temperature, g as velocity and species distributions as well as
flame shapes and derived parameters such as heat ge neration and heat loss, are the parameters
generated by the flame which is not considered as p rimary parameters. If a method that relates

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_FinalReport, p.23
text:
smoke point to those primary parameters were found, we would be able to predict whether a flame
emits soot or not based on the planned flame condit ions. In the course of pursuing such a universal
method, a number of surmises of the mechanism of so ot emission have been proposed to associate
smoke point with certain flame generated parameters . Those surmises served as a middle step in
hoping to help further development of the aforement ioned method. The first surmise, and least
controversial, is that smoke points occur when soot temperature drops below a critical temperature
prior to soot burnout. This temperature is about 13 00 K in normal gravity 8,9 and 1000 K in
microgravity.10,11 The second is that smoke point occurs when radiati ve loss fraction reaches 0.2 –
0.4 for normal-gravity flames 12-16 or 0.4 – 0.6 for microgravity flames. 17 Since the radiative fraction
of heat loss increases with fuel flow rate, smoke p oint will occur as the fuel flow rate is higher tha n
Figure 19. Smoke point luminous length plotted with
respect to fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiom etric mixture
fraction. A linear fit that intersects the origin is shown.
Urban et al. (2000)
at ua = 0.

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_FinalReport, p.24
text:
18
certain value. This is consistent with experimental observations. The third surmise is that the smoke
point correlates to the ratio of luminous length di vided by stoichiometric length. This ratio increase s
with flow rate. Once it reaches about 2, smoke poin t occurs. 15,18,19 The last surmise suggests that
smoke point correlates with the centerline flame re sidence time. This is the most complex 8-11,17,18,20-
24 surmise because flame residence time affects the s oot processes in twofold. An increase in
residence time can lead to soot emissions by increa sing the time available for soot formation.
Because this generally also increases the time avai lable for soot oxidation, it has been proposed that
smoke points are associated with conditions where t he time available for soot formation exceeds that
for soot oxidation to certain extent. 21 This is difficult to prove because to evaluate the flame
residence time requires the velocity distribution a lone the centerline and the flame length, both of
which are resulted flame parameters, not readily av ailable from primary parameters of the
experiment. In addition, the soot formation time an d oxidation time are conceptually defined.
Practically, these times are not measurable and the y might be overlapped, i.e., for the same soot
aggregate, adding and oxidizing carbon particles ma y happen simultaneously. Because of these

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_FinalReport, p.24
text:
difficulties and ambiguities, the fame residence ti me theory cannot be proved or disproved
rigorously. However, these obstacles do not preven t us from checking the residence time theory
against the observed smoke point data with the help of some approximated velocity distribution and
flame length information. More detailed discussion of this effort can be found in the publications
resulted from the SPICE project listed in Appendice s B through F. The results showed that although
residence time is helpful in understanding the pres ent smoke points, it does not yield quantitative
correlations.
CLOSING REMARKS
Smoke points of 55 microgravity gas-jet diffusion f lames in coflowing air were measured in earth
orbit. The conditions emphasized small burners and the effects of coflow velocity. These flames
allow extensive control over residence time, which is important in smoke point phenomena. The
major conclusions are as follows:
1. An increase in coflow velocity increases the smoke point length.
2. A decrease in burner diameter increases the smoke point length.
3. These two effects can be explained qualitatively by considering residence times; increased
fuel and/or coflow velocities yield increased smoke point lengths.
4. The sooting propensities of the present fuel mixtur es in microgravity increase according to

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: SPICE_FinalReport, p.24
text:
ethylene < propane < 50% propylene < 75% propylene < propylene. This is the same as in
normal gravity except for the exchanged positions of ethylene and propane.
5. Consistent with past theory and experiments, lumino us length at the smoke point is
proportional to fuel mass flow rate. However there is a slight increase in luminous length as
ua / u f decreases.
6. Although residence time is helpful in understanding the present smoke points, it does not
yield quantitative correlations of smoke points.
7. The present smoke point lengths scale with d –0.91 uair 0.41 . Either a decrease in diameter or an
increase in coflow velocity decreases residence time and radiative loss fraction, which in turn
leads to a longer smoke point.

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: IP-C Crew training 2010, p.3
text:
INTRODUCTION
• Three investigations will be performed: SPICE, SLICE, and BASS.
• These investigations will be performed inside the Microgravity Science
Glovebox (MSG).
• SPICE is based on the Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) hardware which
flew on STS-87 in 1997.
• SPICE hardware is already on-orbit. It has successfully completed all of its
objectives with the collection of 200 data points in the first half of 2009.
Spare gas onboard will now be used to collect additional data. New fuel is
being flown on ULF5 to support the SLICE and BASS experiments.
• SPICE hardware will also be used to perform SLICE and BASS.
• SPICE burns different fuels to investigate the point at which they begin to
smoke.
• SLICE burns different fuels to investigate the structure of flames when lifted
from the fuel nozzle.
• BASS burns different materials to investigate how they burn in microgravity.

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: IP-C Crew training 2010, p.4
text:
The objective of the SPICE experiment is to find
the laminar smoke-point properties of
nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the
properties of the largest laminar jet diffusion
flames that do not emit soot) for two fuel types
under different nozzle diameter / co-flow velocity
configurations.
SPICE will stabilize an enclosed laminar flame,
measure the overall flame shape to validate the
theoretical and numerical predictions, measure
the flame stabilization heights, and measure the
temperature field to verify flame structure
predictions.

SLICE Science Background
• The goal of the SLICE investigation is to investigate the structure of lifting
and lifted flames; whereby the flame detaches from the nozzle and
stabilizes at a downstream position.
• The results of the SLICE experiment will be used to minimize risk and
maximize the scientific return of the CLD (Coflow Laminar Diffusion)
Flame experiment, which is one of the four ACME (Advanced Combustion
via Microgravity Experiments) investigations that are currently in
development for conduct within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).
6

flame base in the example images below (which are not at the same scale) and
the distance from the nozzle tip (which is not visible).

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: IP-C Crew training 2010, p.7
text:
BASS Science Background
• The BASS investigation tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity burn as well
if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being
identical (ie. pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature).
• To test this hypothesis with any but the thinnest materials requires extended
microgravity time – longer than available in drop towers or parabolic aircraft. If this
hypothesis is true, it implies serious safety concerns over the utility and margin of
safety provided NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 (upward flammability test used to evaluate
materials intended for use in the habitable environments of US spacecraft). Practical,
realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames
which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire
burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).
• There are important differences in the suppression of fires in space compared to on
Earth. On Earth it is understood that best results are generally obtained when the
extinguisher “attacks” the base of the flame, which is both the stabilization point and
the point of fresh air entrainment. For a fire burning in microgravity, the best point of
application of suppressant may not be immediately apparent, especially for a partially

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: IP-C Crew training 2010, p.7
text:
obstructed flame or a wake-stabilized flame. Depending on the geometry of the flame
and the characteristics of the extinguisher (distance from flame, dispersion angle) it is
possible that the suppressant stream will be ineffective or might actually make the
flame worse through the entrainment of oxygen.

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: IP-C Crew training 2010, p.9
text:
Earth Applications
• SPICE
The smoke-point phenomena is a classical metric in the understanding of the heat
release and spread rate of fires. It is commonly used in fire modeling on Earth and to
understand the soot growth and emission by flames. The dominant characteristics of
many flames of practical interest are nonbuoyant. SPICE seeks to extend our
understanding by looking at the interaction of ambient flow with the smoke point,
enabling us to better predict heat release from non-buoyant flames in practical
combustors (e.g. jet engines and furnaces).
• SLICE
The twin purposes for the SLICE research are increased efficiency and reduced
pollutant emission in practical combustion devices. More explicitly, the experiment is
being conducted to advance combustion modeling capability, which “allows system
designers to improve efficiency and reduce harmful pollutants in ways never before
possible” (as stated by an external reviewer of the SLICE experiment). In other
words, the SLICE research is being conducted to advance energy technology and
improve our global environment.
• BASS
It is highly desirable to develop a new and/or improved Earth-based test method for
material flammability. The data obtained in this experiment will begin to bridge the
gap between the normal gravity method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual
material flammability in microgravity 9

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: IP-D Crew training 2011, p.3
text:
Introduction
• Three investigations will be performed: SPICE, SLICE, and BASS.
• These investigations will be performed inside the Microgravity Science
Glovebox (MSG).
• SPICE is based on the Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) hardware which
flew on STS-87 in 1997.
• SPICE hardware is already on-orbit. It has successfully completed all of its
objectives with the collection of 200 data points in the first half of 2009. New
fuel is being flown on ULF5 to support the SLICE and BASS experiments.
• SPICE hardware will also be used to perform SLICE and BASS.
• SPICE burns different fuels to investigate the point at which they begin to
smoke.
• SLICE burns different fuels to investigate the structure of flames when lifted
from the fuel nozzle.
• BASS burns different materials to investigate how they burn in microgravity.

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: IP-D Crew training 2011, p.4
text:
The objective of the SPICE experiment is to find
the laminar smoke-point properties of
nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the
properties of the largest laminar jet diffusion
flames that do not emit soot) for two fuel types
under different nozzle diameter / co-flow velocity
configurations.
SPICE will stabilize an enclosed laminar flame,
measure the overall flame shape to validate the
theoretical and numerical predictions, measure
the flame stabilization heights, and measure the
temperature field to verify flame structure
predictions.
SPICE Science Overview
4

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: IP-D Crew training 2011, p.5
text:
Target Setting: The target setting is just above the setting that
produces a distinct edge (only a small portion of the tip will emit
smoke). The smoke will probably emerge from the center of the tip
but may emerge at the tip edges (horns) for the larger nozzle. The
pictures show the onset of smoke points for various fuels on the
KC-135. The size of the flame when it emits smoke is a fuel
property. The expected size sequence will be Propylene, Ethylene,
Propane and Methane (probably no smoke point). The diluted
propylene smoke points will be longer than pure propylene.
SPICE Smoke Point Determination Cue Card
Background: The smoke point is the flame length,
above which, soot particles are no longer consumed in
the flame and instead emerge through the flame tip
and glow as they cool. The glowing soot causes a
change from a sharp edge to a gradual transition
between the bright flame and black background.
Advisory note: For the test points with the 0.4 mm
nozzle, the possibility exists that the flame could blow
off. When this happens, the blue flame-base no longer
touches the nozzle. When the base of the flame starts
to separate from the nozzle, reduce the flow rate until
it is well attached as the smoke height is not
achievable.

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: IP-D Crew training 2011, p.6
text:
SLICE Science Background
• The goal of the SLICE investigation is to investigate the structure of lifting
and lifted flames; whereby the flame detaches from the nozzle and
stabilizes at a downstream position.
• The results of the SLICE experiment will be used to minimize risk and
maximize the scientific return of the CLD (Coflow Laminar Diffusion)
Flame experiment, which is one of the four ACME (Advanced Combustion
via Microgravity Experiments) investigations that are currently in
development for conduct within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).
6
The lifted nature of the flames can be discerned from the outward flare of the
flame base in the example images below (which are not at the same scale) and
the distance from the nozzle tip (which is not visible).

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: IP-D Crew training 2011, p.7
text:
BASS Science Background
• The BASS investigation tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity burn as well
if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being
identical (ie. pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature).
• To test this hypothesis with any but the thinnest materials requires extended
microgravity time – longer than available in drop towers or parabolic aircraft. If this
hypothesis is true, it implies serious safety concerns over the utility and margin of
safety provided NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 (upward flammability test used to evaluate
materials intended for use in the habitable environments of US spacecraft). Practical,
realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames
which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire
burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).
• There are important differences in the suppression of fires in space compared to on
Earth. On Earth it is understood that best results are generally obtained when the
extinguisher “attacks” the base of the flame, which is both the stabilization point and
the point of fresh air entrainment. For a fire burning in microgravity, the best point of
application of suppressant may not be immediately apparent, especially for a partially

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: IP-D Crew training 2011, p.7
text:
obstructed flame or a wake-stabilized flame. Depending on the geometry of the flame
and the characteristics of the extinguisher (distance from flame, dispersion angle) it is
possible that the suppressant stream will be ineffective or might actually make the
flame worse through the entrainment of oxygen.
7

name: SPICE
title: SPICE: IP-D Crew training 2011, p.9
text:
Earth Applications
• SPICE
The smoke-point phenomena is a classical metric in the understanding of the heat
release and spread rate of fires. It is commonly used in fire modeling on Earth and to
understand the soot growth and emission by flames. The dominant characteristics of
many flames of practical interest are nonbuoyant. SPICE seeks to extend our
understanding by looking at the interaction of ambient flow with the smoke point,
enabling us to better predict heat release from non-buoyant flames in practical
combustors (e.g. jet engines and furnaces).
• SLICE
The twin purposes for the SLICE research are increased efficiency and reduced
pollutant emission in practical combustion devices. More explicitly, the experiment is
being conducted to advance combustion modeling capability, which “allows system
designers to improve efficiency and reduce harmful pollutants in ways never before
possible” (as stated by an external reviewer of the SLICE experiment). In other
words, the SLICE research is being conducted to advance energy technology and
improve our global environment.
• BASS
It is highly desirable to develop a new and/or improved Earth-based test method for
material flammability. The data obtained in this experiment will begin to bridge the
gap between the normal gravity method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual
material flammability in microgravity 9

minutes to promote air mixing to dilute any HF concentration
byproduct produced during combustion.

Assembly is present, MSG Air Cir must be ON.
• The inside of the Experiment Assembly must be permitted to
cool to a temp below 49°C before crew access is permitted.

name: PSI-115
title: PSI-115: NNX17AF08A_FinalReport, p.3
text:
1 Executive Summary
This work examines how microgravity conditions on spacecraft change the development of smoke
aerosol relative to smoke on Earth. We perform simulations of particle formation and growth with
the goal of capturing smoke dynamics similar to those realized in experiments performed aboard the
International Space Station. The simulations provide detailed information about ﬂuid/thermal/particle
interactions that cannot be acquired experimentally on orbit. A surrogate material, dibutyl pthalate, is
expelled from a hot surface in a rectangular chamber while ambient air is blown through the domain,
convecting the developing smoke downstream. The study considers two ﬂow rates, two geometric con-
ﬁgurations, and the isolated effects of gravitational particle settling and thermophoresis. In Earth gravity,
buoyancy produces asymmetries in all ﬁelds of interest and ampliﬁes vapor-to-particle conversion near
room temperature surfaces at the upper boundary of the simulation domain. Gravitational settling re-
moves large particles from the aerosol, limiting the maximum particle size to ∼ 40 µm and the mode
particle size to∼ 5µm. Without buoyancy or settling, the microgravity smoke plume is spatially symmet-
ric and contains very large particles (> 40µm). A bimodal particle size distribution results in microgravity

name: PSI-115
title: PSI-115: NNX17AF08A_FinalReport, p.3
text:
when prominent recirculation occurs behind the hot vapor source. The distribution is comprised of large
particles (> 20µm) associated with long residency time, vapor rich, high temperature recirculation, and
smaller particles (< 10µm) that originate farther downstream of the hot vapor source. A distinct large
particle mode does not appear in microgravity ﬂows that do not have prominent high temperature re-
circulation, although the aerosol still contains large particles. Without recirculation, the mode particle
diameter in microgravity is∼ 10µm, or approximately twice that of terrestrial smoke. Results show that
future experiments should carefully consider and quantify surface interactions and the presence of hot,
recirculating vapor, in order to control geometry-dominated features of the particle size distribution.
A manuscript based on this work will be submitted to the journal Aerosol Science & Technology. The
ﬁnal document, when accepted, will be provided to NASA.
UTILIZATION OF THE SAME DATA FOR ADVANCED MODELING AND SIMULATION OF SMOKE GENERATION IN
MICROGRAVITY
3 SEAN C. GARRICK

name: PSI-115
title: PSI-115: NNX17AF08A_FinalReport, p.4
text:
2 Introduction
Gravity affects the evolution of aerosols by introducing buoyancy and particle settling. Buoyant convec-
tion modiﬁes the time-temperature history of the aerosol, as well as the spatial distribution of particles,
condensing vapor, and thermal energy. Gravity also causes the settling of large particles out of the
aerosol, provided the chemistry and vapor concentrations allow for the generation of large particles
with appreciable settling velocities. These factors combine to increase particle residency times in high
temperature, vapor rich regions in microgravity systems relative to terrestrial or Earth gravity systems
(Urban et al., 1998, 2005). As a result, smoke particles produced in microgravity tend to be larger than
those produced on Earth (Ku et al., 1995, Urban et al., 1998). Measurements suggest microgravity
smoke particles to be 2− 8 times larger than terrestrial smoke particles (Urban et al., 2005). Moreover,
large particles (not only smoke particles) persist in microgravity, with mass concentrations of particles
with diameter > 100 µm measured at ten-times that of a nominal terrestrial environment (Liu et al.,
1991). Total particulate mass concentrations are also more than ﬁve times greater in microgravity (Liu
et al., 1991). Understanding gravitational effects is of practical interest because it assists in the design

name: PSI-115
title: PSI-115: NNX17AF08A_FinalReport, p.4
text:
of mission-critical smoke detection systems for use in microgravity environments, including the Interna-
tional Space Station (Mulholland et al., 2015); systems developed and calibrated for terrestrial use may
not perform correctly in microgravity because of inappropriate particle size sensitivities (Urban et al.,
2005).
The present work uses numerical simulation to explore the inﬂuence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke
growth from a fundamental perspective. We simulate the formation and growth of dibutyl-phthalate
(DBP) particles in Earth gravity and microgravity environments. We utilize direct numerical simulation
via a Navier-Stokes nodal approach. The smoke originates from pyrolysis vapor expelled from a heated
sample in a geometry similar to that considered in the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al., 2015). The
intention of this effort is to quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth gravity smoke, and
to identify the ﬂuid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences. This study considers two cross-
ﬂow velocities of sufﬁciently low speed that buoyancy cannot be neglected in the presence of gravity.
Simulations are presented to assess the dependence of particle size distributions on thermophoresis,
particle settling, and ﬂow geometry. The paper is organized as follows: we introduce the simulation and

name: PSI-115
title: PSI-115: NNX17AF08A_FinalReport, p.4
text:
modeling methodology, followed by a description of the ﬂow geometry and the parameter space under
consideration; we then examine differences in the wake geometry attributable to buoyancy for the lower
of two ﬂow speeds; next, we present and discuss instantaneous scalar ﬁelds as a means to describe
particle accumulation and growth in the buoyant and non-buoyant wakes that form downstream of the
hot vapor source; after developing an understanding of how the particle ﬁelds interact with the ﬂuid
dynamics for the low speed cases, we consider the effects of thermophoresis, particle settling, ﬂow
geometry, and the higher ﬂow speed; we conclude with a discussion of the results, summarize ﬁndings
relevant to future experimentation, and outline directions for future work.
UTILIZATION OF THE SAME DATA FOR ADVANCED MODELING AND SIMULATION OF SMOKE GENERATION IN
MICROGRAVITY
4 SEAN C. GARRICK

We simulate the formation and growth of DBP particles in air ﬂowing over a heated sample that expels
DBP vapor. The simulation mimics the smoldering or pre-conﬂagration stage of a ﬁre studied in experi-
ments performed aboard the ISS (Mulholland et al., 2015). A schematic of the computational domain is
shown in Fig. 1. Room temperature air enters a long chamber and ﬂows over a heated rectangular sam-
ple. Vapor released from the sample nucleates into particles that grow and are subsequently collected
downstream for analysis. The ﬂow is laminar and steady, allowing the two-dimensional representation
to present physical characteristics largely representative of the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al.,
2015). DBP is used as the surrogate material because its properties are known and its use in modeling
is well-established (unlike the materials used in the SAME experiments).
4.2 PHYSICAL CONDITIONS
Constant ﬂuid properties for air and DBP are provided in Table 1, and variable DBP properties are
provided in Table 2. The enhancement factor required for the nucleation expression, Eqn. (20), is
deﬁned for DBP ascnuc = 3.2× 10−4 (Nguyen et al., 1987, Pyyk¨onen and Jokiniemi, 2000).
The thickness of the heated DBP source serves as the reference length scale,Lo = 0.0044 m (illustrated

name: PSI-115
title: PSI-115: NNX17AF08A_FinalReport, p.9
text:
in Fig. 1), which is representative of the length scale in the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al.,
2015). The air enters from the left with velocity Uo and temperature To = 300 K . We consider two
inlet velocities: Uo = 0.08 m/s, the velocity considered in the SAME experiments, and a slightly faster
ﬂow ofUo = 0.10 m/s. The upper and lower boundaries are impermeable, no-slip, iso-thermal surfaces
(Twall =To). The heated rectangle is also no-slip, has a ﬁxed temperature ofTs = 473.2 K, and releases
DBP vapor at a constant mass ﬂux ofq′′ = 8.4× 10−5 kg/m2· s. The mass ﬂux has been selected to be
representative of the mass loss data presented by Mulholland et al. (2015). Zero-derivative conditions
are imposed for all species and particle ﬁelds at the inlet and outlet. The gravitational acceleration is
considered at terrestrial (go = 9.81 m/s2) and microgravity (go = 0 m/s2) conditions.
The inlet velocities and the gravitational accelerations considered represent four cases with varying
Reynolds and Froude numbers. A summary of the simulations performed at the two ﬂow speeds and
gravitational levels is given in Table 3. The ﬂags “EG” and “MG” identify the “Earth gravity” and “micro-
gravity” conditions, while 1 and 2 identify the Uo = 0.08 m/s andUo = 0.1 m/s conditions, respectively.
Case 1MG is therefore deﬁned to have an inlet velocity of Uo = 0.08 m/s and go = 0 m /s2, corre-

title: PSI-115: NNX17AF08A_FinalReport, p.9

sponding to a Reynolds number Re = 22.3 and a Froude numberFr =∞. In addition to the four base
cases listed in Table 3, we examine the aerosol development sensitivity to: (1) particle settling, (2) ther-
mophoresis, and (3) the ﬂow geometry. For this purpose, a series of additional cases, deﬁned in Table
3, are constructed by modifying the setup of Case 1MG and/or Case 1EG. Case 1EG-NS (where NS
stands for “no settling”) is identical to Case 1EG, but the settling mechanism has been neglected. Case
1MG-NT (where NT stands for “no thermophoresis”) is identical to Case 1MG, but the thermophoresis
transport mechanism has been neglected. Cases 1MG-R and 1EG-R (where R stands for “rotated”) are
identical to Cases 1MG and 1EG, except the heated vapor source has been rotated 90◦. In all cases,
data is collected and presented at a time oft = 7 seconds.
4.3 NUMERICAL SPECIFICATIONS
The domain is non-uniformly discretized by 960 grid points in the x direction and 240 grid point in
the y direction. The governing equations are solved on this computational mesh with a second-order
MacCormack scheme. The particle size space is discretized by 45 particle nodes, with the volume of
each successive node increased by a factor of 2.25, i.e.vk = 2.25×vk−1. The volume of the ﬁrst node
is selected to be the volume of a DBP molecule, v1 =vm = 4.44× 10−28 m3. Boundary conditions are

name: PSI-115
title: PSI-115: NNX17AF08A_FinalReport, p.10
text:
implemented by considering the characteristic relations for the Euler equations accounting for gravity
(Poinsot and Lele, 1992). The computational tool used for this work has been well-validated and used
for prior studies of aerosols (Garrick, 2011, 2015, Garrick and Khakpour, 2004, Garrick et al., 2001,
Khakpour and Garrick, 2003, Modem and Garrick, 2003).
4.4 PHYSICAL ASSUMPTIONS
All assumptions utilized in this work are listed below.
• From the perspective of thermal conductivity and viscosity, the condensing vapor phase is con-
sidered sufﬁciently dilute such thatµ andk are computed for air as a function of temperature and
density (Kadoya et al., 1985). Both the air and the condensing vapor are considered calorically
perfect gases with constant properties deﬁned in Table 1.
• The Mach number M is only important for ﬂows with M & 0.3. Although the physics are insen-
sitive to variation in Mach number when the Mach number is small, the ratio of sound speed to
convective speed imposes a large computational burden. The computational challenge is often
remedied with a Boussinesq approximation, but this approach is not valid in the presence of large
density variations. Additionally, an elliptical solve for pressure is computationally intractable for the
number of iterations required to resolve the particle time scales. We instead use a scaled dynamic

name: PSI-115
title: PSI-115: NNX17AF08A_FinalReport, p.10
text:
pressure as the reference pressurePo =ρo (c1Uo)2, such thatP⋆ = ραRαT Po , wherec1 is speciﬁed to reduce the effective speed of sound to 8 m/s. The ﬂow ﬁeld was found to be independent of c1
for the values used.
• All particles are assumed to be spherical.
• Condensed phase DBP properties are deﬁned by their continuum values.
• There is no momentum exchange between the particles and the ﬂuid (the air/DBP vapor mixture);
the particle velocity equals the ﬂuid velocity, augmented by the thermophoretic velocity and the
stokes settling velocity. The stokes settling velocity is assumed to apply for all particles in the
domain (including the large particles).
• The ﬂuid and particles are in thermal equilibrium and have the same temperature.
• Particle diffusion coefﬁcients decrease rapidly with diameter. This poses a numerical challenge
due to the lack of a physical mechanism for diffusing numerical errors. For this reason, the mini-
mum diffusion coefﬁcient considered in the particle mass fraction transport equations corresponds
to the ﬁfth particle size node – any node greater than the ﬁfth node is assigned the particle diffu-
sion coefﬁcient of the ﬁfth node.
• The mass ﬂux of DPB from the heated rectangle is spatially uniform and all surfaces have spatially
uniform temperature.
• Particles that impact a solid surface “stick” with 100% efﬁciency, and are removed from the ﬂow.

name: PSI-115
title: PSI-115: NNX17AF08A_FinalReport, p.10
text:
• The aerosol does not achieve a rigorous steady-state because particle evolution continues (slowly)
in regions of the ﬂow with recirculation, particularly behind the hot vapor source. The recirculation
is characterized by high temperatures, long particle residency times, and the continuous intro-
duction of additional vapor. The hydrodynamic and thermal ﬁelds, conversely, become steady
after only a few seconds. Although a rigorous steady-state does not exist, all aerosol features
develop and effectively stabilize shortly after the hydrodynamic ﬁelds. We therefore present all
results at timet = 7 seconds, which is considered to be the effective steady-state. At his time, all
ﬁelds are either steady, or changing at a rate that does not affect the conclusions drawn from the
simulations.

4.5 FLUID FLOW, TEMPERATURE, AND MASS FRACTION
The velocity ﬁeld controls the convection of thermal energy, condensible species vapor, and particles.
Vorticityω, deﬁned as the curl of the velocity vector
ω =∇× u, (31)
is positive in regions of the ﬂow where ﬂuid rotates counterclockwise, and is negative in regions where
the ﬂuid rotates clockwise. The sign and magnitude of vorticity therefore identiﬁes the location, orienta-
tion, and intensity of vortices and boundary layers.
Figure 2 shows the steady dimensionless vorticity. Panel (a) shows Case 1MG and panel (b) shows
Case 1EG. The grey rectangles represent the heated vapor source. Red ﬂuid rotates counterclockwise
(positive vorticity) and blue ﬂuid rotates clockwise (negative vorticity). Immediately upon entering the
channel, the ﬂuid at the walls is brought to rest by the no slip condition, signiﬁed by the large vorticity
gradients in the upper and lower left corners of panels (a) and (b). As the ﬂuid travels downstream
from left to right, boundary layers develop symmetrically on the upper and lower walls due to viscous
diffusion. Further downstream, the heated rectangle reduces the cross-sectional ﬂow area, and the
pressure ﬁeld accelerates the ﬂuid through ﬂow paths above and below the heated vapor source. The
microgravity case in panel (a) remains symmetric near the heated vapor source, whereas the Earth

title: PSI-115: NNX17AF08A_FinalReport, p.11

gravity case in panel (b) develops an asymmetry with the majority of ﬂuid passing below the heated
vapor source (indicated by larger vorticity magnitudes below than above). Comparatively low vorticity
values on the downstream side of the rectangles indicate the presence of low speed, recirculating
wakes. The microgravity wake in panel (a) is symmetric, whereas the Earth gravity wake in panel (b) is
asymmetric. As the ﬂuid continues to ﬂow downstream, the boundary layers thicken in both cases and
the ﬂuid exits the domain to the right. Variations in density due to heat transfer from the rectangle have
inﬂuenced the vorticity ﬁelds via baroclinic torque and buoyancy. Because there is no gravity in Case
1MG in panel (a), density variations due to heating do not disturb the symmetry of the ﬂow ﬁeld. The
asymmetry apparent in panel (b) is due to buoyancy effects.
Temperature ﬁelds with overlaid velocity vectors are shown in Fig. 3 at time t = 7 seconds. Panel (a)
shows Case 1MG and panel (b) shows Case 1EG. The downstream portion of the domain has been
expanded for clarity. Velocity vectors in panel (a) show a symmetric wake proﬁle with two counter-
rotating vortices surrounded by dividing streamlines. Panel (b) shows an asymmetric buoyant wake,
also with two counter rotating vortices: one near the lower right corner of the heated vapor source, and

another near the upper right corner of the heated vapor source. Both panels show hot ﬂuid in white,
warm ﬂuid in red, and room temperature ﬂuid in black. Thermal energy diffuses from the heated vapor
source to the adjacent ﬂuid. Hot ﬂuid convects energy downstream and cools while diffusing energy
to cooler ﬂuid and the isothermal upper and lower walls. The highest temperatures appear near the

4.6 P ARTICLE NUCLEATION, NUMBER DENSITY , AND SIZE
The particle nucleation rate is a function of vapor mass fraction and temperature (and pressure). Figure
5 shows the DBP nucleation rate at time t = 7 seconds for Case 1MG in panel (a) and Case 1EG in
panel (b). Panel (a) shows that nucleation occurs exclusively downstream of the heated vapor source in
Case 1MG, and most rapidly at a rate of∼ 1012 [ m3· s ]−1 near the periphery of the recirculating wake.
Nucleation does not occur at a signiﬁcant rate anywhere in the wake. The nucleation rate decreases
quickly after approximately ten dimensionless length units downstream of the heated vapor source.
Panel (b) shows two primary zones of nucleation in Case 1EG: downstream of the upper wake vortex
and in the region downstream and above the upper wake vortex, near the upper surface. Nucleation
occurs at a higher rate,∼ 1014 [ m3· s ]−1 , in Case 1EG than in Case 1MG.
Particle number densities at timet = 7 seconds are shown in Fig. 6 for Cases 1EG and 1MG in panels
(a) and (b), respectively. Panel (a) shows a particle number density of∼ 1010 m−3 at the center of each
counter-rotating wake vortex. Thermophoretic forces prevent particles from contacting the downstream
surface of the heated vapor source (this will be demonstrated in Section 4.8), resulting in a void of

name: PSI-115
title: PSI-115: NNX17AF08A_FinalReport, p.12

particles between the heated vapor source and the particle-dense wake vortices. Particles are also
less numerous on the downstream side of the recirculating wake: particles do not nucleate in this
region, dividing streamlines prevent particles from being convected into this region, and low diffusion
rates limit particles from rapidly diffusing into this region. Even further downstream, the particle number
density remains symmetric, with the largest particle number densities of∼ 1011 m−3 appearing slightly
separated from the symmetry line on top and bottom. No particles appear near the upper and lower
surfaces. Panel (b) shows the particle number densities for Case 1EG. More particles accumulate in
the upper wake vortex than in the lower wake vortex. The Case 1EG wake contains fewer particles than
the Case 1MG wake. In Case 1EG, a high particle concentration of nearly ∼ 1012 m−3 appears over
a large area near the upper surface due to the high nucleation rate in the region. Signiﬁcantly more
particles appear in this near-wall region than anywhere in the Case 1MG particle ﬁeld. Unlike Case
1MG, Case 1EG contains particles throughout the entire vertical span of the ﬂow chamber: particles
that appear in lower concentrations near the bottom wall have arrived there via the gravitational settling

In order to isolate the effects of particle settling, we modify Case 1EG by neglecting the settling mecha-
nism (by settinguss⋆ j,k = 0). This case is referred to as Case 1EG–NS, where NS stands for “no settling”.
Figure 9 compares size distributions for Case 1MG, Case 1EG, and Case 1EG–NS at measurement
planex′ = 26 at timet = 7 seconds. The Case 1EG–NS distribution is considerably wider than the other
cases. It contains particles ranging in size from nanometers to 100 µm. Case 1EG–NS also contains
